parts.problemMd:
A student investigates how changing the temperature and pressure affects the volume of a gas.

The student fills a balloon with helium gas and places it in a freezer.

i) Predict what happens to the volume of the balloon as the temperature decreases. Explain your answer using the kinetic particle theory.

[2]

ii) The balloon is removed from the freezer and taken to a mountain where the atmospheric pressure is lower.

Predict what happens to the volume of the balloon and explain your answer.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
i) When the temperature decreases:

- The volume of the balloon decreases; **[1 mark]**
- Because the gas particles move more slowly and exert less pressure on the balloon walls; **[1 mark]**

ii) When the atmospheric pressure is lower:

- The volume of the balloon increases; **[1 mark]**
- Because the external pressure is lower, so gas particles push outward more; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

This question tests your understanding of how gas particles behave when conditions change

For part (i), remember that temperature affects particle energy:

- When a gas gets colder, its particles move more slowly

  - They have less kinetic energy
- The particles collide with the container walls less often and with less force
- So, the volume decreases

For part (ii), focus on how external pressure affects a gas:

- At higher altitudes, the pressure outside the balloon is lower
- This means that there is:

  - Less pressure squeezing it from the outside
  - Less resistance to the particles inside pushing outward
- So, the volume increases

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows a gas jar that initially contains bromine gas at the bottom and air above it. After a few minutes, the two gases have mixed more evenly.

![Diagram of a vertical gas jar with a lid, containing air at the top and bromine as a darker gradient at the bottom, labelled accordingly.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-chemistry-23/1-states-of-matter/1-1-solids-liquids-and-gases/assets/007-diagram-of-a-vertical-gas-jar-with-a-lid-contain.png)

Describe and explain what has happened to the bromine gas in the jar over time.
parts.solutionMd:
Over time, the bromine spreads throughout the gas jar because:

- The particles move randomly and spread out due to kinetic energy; **[1 mark]**
- They diffuse from an area of high concentration to low concentration; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

Even though bromine starts at the bottom, its particles spread out and mix because they are always moving in all directions

At the start:

- The bottom of the gas jar is in an area of high bromine concentration
- The top of the gas jar is in an area of low bromine concentration

Diffusion moves particles from an area of high concentration to low concentration. This means that the bromine spreads upward and mixes with the air.

It’s important to remember that diffusion depends on concentration difference, not gravity. Particles spread because of random motion, not because they rise or fall.

parts.problemMd:

To compare how fast gases diffuse, look at the mass of their particles. Lighter gas particles move faster because they have higher average speeds at the same temperature.

Since chlorine particles are lighter than bromine particles, chlorine diffuses more quickly.

Just remember: the smaller the relative molecular mass, the faster the gas will spread.

> **[exam-tip]**

parts.problemMd: Iron reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to form iron(II) chloride, which is a soluble salt. Describe the steps a student should use to prepare **pure, dry crystals of iron(II) chloride** from excess iron powder and dilute hydrochloric acid.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**

> - Filter (to remove the unreacted iron) **[1 mark]**
> - Heat the filtrate to the point of crystallisation / heat to concentrate the solution / heat to evaporate the solvent / heat to form a saturated solution **[1 mark]**
> - Filter crystals after cooling / leave to cool/crystallise **AND** dry the crystals with filter paper / dry on filter paper / dry between sheets of filter paper / dry in a desiccator **[1 mark]**

Atoms with the same number of protons; **[1 mark]**

A different mass number; **[1 mark]**

State why these two isotopes of chlorine have the same chemical properties.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The reason these two isotopes of chlorine have the same chemical properties is:
> 
> - Same number of electrons **[1 mark]**
> - Same electronic configuration **[1 mark]**
> 
> Stating the electronic configuration as 2,8,7 is accepted for the second mark.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The two isotopes differ only in their number of neutrons. Neutrons carry no charge and sit in the nucleus, so they take no part in bonding.

|---|---|---|---|

parts.solutionMd:
The completed table is:

|   | number of electrons | number of neutrons | number of protons |
|---|---|---|---|
| `{}_{17}^{35}{Cl}` | **Final answer:** **17** | **Final answer:** **18** | **Final answer:** **17** |
| `{}_{17}^{37}{Cl}^{-}` | **Final answer:** **18** | **Final answer:** **20** | **Final answer:** **17** |

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for both values in the number of electrons column
> 
> 1 mark for both values in the number of neutrons column
> 
> 1 mark for both values in the number of protons column

> **[exam-tip]**
> Work across one row at a time and take the two numbers in the symbol in turn.
> 
> The bottom number is the proton number, so both particles have 17 protons. That number never changes, because changing it would make it a different element.
> 
> The number of neutrons is the top number minus the bottom number:
> 
> - 35 - 17 = 18 neutrons.
> - 37 - 17 = 20 neutrons.
> 
> Electrons are where most marks are lost. A neutral atom has as many electrons as protons, so <sup>35</sup>Cl has 17. The negative sign on the chloride ion means one electron has been gained, so <sup>37</sup>Cl<sup>-</sup> has 18.
> 
> The trap is to assume the charge changes the number of protons. It never does. Only the electron count moves.

#### Separate: Chemistry and Extended Only

In the above experiment, 50.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of hydrochloric acid of concentration 2.0 mol / dm<sup>3</sup> was used. 6.4 g of SrCl<sub>2</sub>.6H<sub>2</sub>O was made.

Calculate the percentage yield.

number of moles of HCl used = ............................

number of moles of SrCl<sub>2</sub>.6H<sub>2</sub>O which could be formed = ............................

mass of one mole of SrCl<sub>2</sub>.6H<sub>2</sub>O is 267 g

theoretical yield of SrCl<sub>2</sub>.6H<sub>2</sub>O = ............................g

percentage yield = ............................%
parts.solutionMd:
c) To calculate the percentage yield:

- Number of moles of HCl used = 0.05 × 2 = 0.1;** [1 mark]**
- Number of moles of SrCl<sub>2</sub>.6 H<sub>2</sub>O which could be formed = 0.05; **[1 mark]**
- Theoretical yield of SrCl<sub>2</sub>.6 H<sub>2</sub>O = 0.05 × 267 = 13.35 g; ** [1 mark]**
- Percentage yield = 6.4/ 13.35 × 100 = 47.9% 
**OR** 
48%; ** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *To calculate the number of moles use the equation: concentration x volume *

  - *Don't forget to convert volume into dm*<sup>*3*</sup>* by dividing by 1000*
  - *So 0.05 x 2 = 0.1 mol*
- *In the first equation, the molar ratio of HCl to SrCl*<sub>*2*</sub>* is 2:1 *

  - *So the number of moles of SrCl*<sub>*2*</sub>*.6H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O which could be formed is 0.01/2 = 0.05 mol *
- *To find the maximum (theoretical) mass that could be obtained use molar mass x number of moles*

  - *So 267 x 0.05 mol = 13.35 g*
- *Percentage yield is calculated using: *$\frac{\mathrm{actual} \mathrm{yield}}{\mathrm{theoretical} \mathrm{yield}}\times100$

  - *So *$\frac{6.4}{13.35} \times 100 = 47.9 \%$

parts.solutionMd:
For calculating the relative atomic mass, you must use the following equation:

`relative atomic mass ( A _ r ) = (% of isotope 1 x mass number of isotope 1 + % of isotope 2 x mass number of isotope 2 +...)/(100 %)`

relative atomic mass (*A*<sub>r</sub>) = **24.3** **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd: Phosphorus(V) oxide, P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub>, is an acidic oxide. Phosphorus(V) oxide, P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub>, reacts with aqueous sodium hydroxide to form a salt containing the phosphate ion $\mathrm{PO}_{4}^{3-}$. Water is the only other product. Write a chemical equation for the reaction between phosphorus(V) oxide and aqueous sodium hydroxide.
parts.solutionMd:
d)

The correct equation for the reaction between phosphorus(V) oxide and aqueous sodium hydroxide is:

P<sub>4</sub>O<sub>10</sub> + 12NaOH → 4Na<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> + 6H<sub>2</sub>O

- Formula: Na<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub>; **[1 mark]**
- Rest of the equation completely correct; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *You are told that "phosphorus(V) oxide, P*<sub>*4*</sub>*O*<sub>*10*</sub>*, reacts with aqueous sodium hydroxide" and you should know the formula for sodium hydroxide*
- *This gives the reactants to be:*

  - *P*<sub>*4*</sub>*O*<sub>*10*</sub>* + NaOH →*
- *You are also told that they "form a salt containing the phosphate ion PO*<sub>*4*</sub><sup>*3-*</sup>*" - the salt will contain the negative phosphorus ion and the positive ion, Na*<sup>*+*</sup>* from the sodium hydroxide*
- *For the compound to be neutral overall, 3 Na*<sup>*+*</sup>* ions are required for every 1  PO*<sub>*4*</sub><sup>*3-*</sup>*, so its formula is Na*<sub>*3*</sub>*PO*<sub>*4*</sub>

  - *P*<sub>*4*</sub>*O*<sub>*10*</sub>* + NaOH → Na*<sub>*3*</sub>*PO*<sub>*4*</sub>
- *Finally, you are also told that water is the only other product which gives the unbalanced equation:*

  - *P*<sub>*4*</sub>*O*<sub>*10*</sub>* + NaOH → Na*<sub>*3*</sub>*PO*<sub>*4 *</sub>*+ H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
- *Now the equation needs balancing*
- *There are 4 P atoms on the left-hand side, so balance the right-hand side to give 4 P atoms:*

  - *P*<sub>*4*</sub>*O*<sub>*10*</sub>* + NaOH → **4**Na*<sub>*3*</sub>*PO*<sub>*4 *</sub>*+ H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
- *There are 12 Na atoms on the right-hand side, so balance the left-hand side to give 12 Na atoms:*

  - *P*<sub>*4*</sub>*O*<sub>*10*</sub>* + **12**NaOH → 4Na*<sub>*3*</sub>*PO*<sub>*4 *</sub>*+ H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
- *There are 12 H atoms on the left-hand side, so balance the right-hand side to give 12 H atoms:*

  - *P*<sub>*4*</sub>*O*<sub>*10*</sub>* + 12NaOH → 4Na*<sub>*3*</sub>*PO*<sub>*4 *</sub>*+ **6**H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
- *There are 22 O atoms on both sides of the equation, so the equation is now balanced*

parts.problemMd:
#### Separate: Chemistry and Extended Only

Basic lead(II) carbonate has a formula of the type xPbCO<sub>3</sub>.yPb(OH)<sub>2</sub> where x and y are whole numbers. Determine x and y from the following information.

PbCO<sub>3</sub>  → PbO + CO<sub>2</sub> Pb(OH)<sub>2</sub> → PbO + H<sub>2</sub>O

When heated, the basic lead(II) carbonate gave 2.112 g of carbon dioxide and 0.432 g of water. Mass of one mole of CO<sub>2</sub> = 44 g Mass of one mole of H<sub>2</sub>O = 18 g Number of moles of CO<sub>2</sub> formed = .....................

[1]

Number of moles of H<sub>2</sub>O formed = .....................

[1]

x = ..................... and y = .....................

Formula of basic lead(II) carbonate is ........................................................................

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
c) The formula of basic lead(II) carbonate can be found by:

- Number of moles of CO<sub>2</sub> formed = mass/molar mass = 2.112/44 = 0.048 moles; **[1 mark]**
- Number of moles of H<sub>2</sub>O formed = mass/molar mass = 0.432/18 = 0.024; **[1 mark]**
- x = (0.048/0.024 =) 2 and y = (0.024/0.024 =) 1

Formula of basic lead(II) carbonate is 2PbCO<sub>3</sub>.Pb(OH)<sub>2</sub> / Pb(OH)<sub>2</sub>. 2PbCO<sub>3</sub>; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

  - *1 mole of CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* is produced by 1 mole of PbCO*<sub>*3*</sub>* and 1 mole of H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O is produced by 1 mole of Pb(OH)*<sub>*2*</sub>
- *You can then divide by the smallest number of moles to find the value of x and y*

parts.problemMd:
#### Extended Only

Magnesium oxide, MgO, is formed when magnesium burns in oxygen.

Write the chemical equation for the reaction that occurs when magnesium burns in oxygen.
parts.solutionMd:
c) The chemical equation for the reaction that occurs when magnesium burns in oxygen is:

2Mg + O<sub>2</sub> → 2MgO

- Correct species;** [1 mark]**
- Correct balancing;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *You are given the formula of magnesium oxide*
- *You are expected to know that magnesium, as a metal, has the formula Mg and that oxygen is diatomic, O*<sub>*2*</sub>*. *

  - *The unbalanced equation is Mg + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → MgO*
  - *Balance the oxygen atoms first:  Mg + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → **2**MgO*
  - *The balance the magnesium atoms: **2**Mg + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → **2**MgO*

parts.problemMd:
#### Separate: Chemistry and Extended Only

The structures of five organic compounds, A, B, C, D and E, are shown. Answer the questions that follow. Each letter may be used once, more than once or not at all.

![q1a-0620-s20-qp-43](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-chemistry-23/3-stoichiometry/3-1-formulae-and-relative-masses/assets/005-q1a-0620-s20-qp-43.png)

Give the letter of the compound that has the empirical formula CH<sub>2.</sub>
parts.solutionMd:
a) The letter of the compound that has the empirical formula CH<sub>2 </sub>is:

- C;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

- *The molecular formula is the actual number of atoms of each element in a compound*
- *The empirical formula is the simplest ratio of atoms of each element in a compound *
- *C has the molecular formula C*<sub>*3*</sub>*H*<sub>*6 *</sub>
- *This can be simplified to CH*<sub>*2*</sub>* *

parts.problemMd:
An endothermic reaction occurs when calcium nitrate is heated.

Balance the equation for this reaction.

.....Ca(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> → .....CaO + .....NO<sub>2</sub> + .....O<sub>2</sub>
parts.solutionMd:
b) The balanced equation for this reaction  is:

- **2**Ca(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> → **2**CaO + **4**NO<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub>; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

- *There are six oxygen atoms on the left hand side, and five on the right hand side*
- *Placing a 2 in front of CaO gives six oxygen atoms on the right hand side *

  - *Ca(NO*<sub>*3*</sub>*)*<sub>*2*</sub>* → **2**CaO + NO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + O*<sub>*2*</sub>*;*
  - *If you placed a two in front of the other molecules, this would result in 7 oxygen atoms on the right hand side and you would not be able to balance the reactants correctly *
- *Balance the calcium atoms next:*

  - *2**Ca(NO*<sub>*3*</sub>*)*<sub>*2*</sub>* → **2**CaO + NO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + O*<sub>*2*</sub>
- *There are now four nitrogen atoms on the right hand side, and 12 oxygen atoms*
- *To balance these, add 4 in front of NO*<sub>*2*</sub>* *

  - *2**Ca(NO*<sub>*3*</sub>*)*<sub>*2*</sub>* → **2**CaO + **4**NO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + O*<sub>*2*</sub>

parts.problemMd:
The equation shows the effect of heat on anhydrous zinc sulfate.

ZnSO<sub>4</sub> $\overset{\mathrm{heat}}{\rightarrow}$ ZnO + SO<sub>3</sub>

When 12.60 g of anhydrous zinc sulfate is heated, the mass of zinc oxide formed is 6.34 g.

Calculate the mass of zinc oxide formed when 63.0 g of anhydrous zinc sulfate is heated.

mass of zinc oxide = _______________
parts.solutionMd:
d) The mass of zinc oxide formed when 63.0 g of anhydrous zinc sulfate is heated is:

- *The mass of zinc sulfate produced from 12.60 g is multiplied by 5*

  - *6.34 x 5 = 31.7 g*

parts.problemMd:
Complete the table to calculate the relative formula mass of anhydrous zinc sulfate, ZnSO<sub>4</sub>. Use your Periodic Table to help you.

| type of atom | number of atoms | relative atomic mass |   |
|---|---|---|---|
| zinc | 1 | 65 | 1 × 65 = 65 |
| sulfur |   |   |   |
| oxygen |   |   |   |

relative formula mass = _________________
parts.solutionMd:
e) The relative formula mass is:

- 161; **[2 marks]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *The completed table is:*

| > *type of atom* | > *number of atoms* | > *relative atomic mass* |   |
|---|---|---|---|
| > *zinc* | > *1* | > *65* | > *1 × 65 = 65* |

parts.problemMd:
#### Extended Only

Fluorine forms both ionic and covalent compounds. Magnesium reacts with fluorine to form the ionic compound magnesium fluoride. The electronic structures of an atom of magnesium and an atom of fluorine are shown.

![q2a-0620-s20-qp-42](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-chemistry-23/3-stoichiometry/3-1-formulae-and-relative-masses/assets/004-q2a-0620-s20-qp-42.png)

What is the formula of magnesium fluoride?
parts.solutionMd:
a) The formula for magnesium fluoride is:

- MgF<sub>2</sub>; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

- *Magnesium has two outer shell electrons *
- *Fluorine has seven outer shell electrons *

  - *It can only gain one electron to achieve a full outer shell *
  - *Two fluorine atoms are therefore needed for every one magnesium atom when an ionic bond forms*

parts.problemMd:
When copper is reacted with hot concentrated sulfuric acid, sulfur dioxide gas is formed.

Balance the chemical equation for this reaction.

Cu + .......H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → CuSO<sub>4</sub> + SO<sub>2</sub> + .......H<sub>2</sub>O
parts.solutionMd:
b) The balanced equation for this reaction  is:

Cu + **2**H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4 </sub>→ CuSO<sub>4</sub> + SO<sub>2</sub> + **2**H<sub>2</sub>O

- Left hand side; **[1 mark]**
- Right hand side; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *There are two sulfur atoms on the right hand side and one on the left hand side*
- *Add a 2 in front of H*<sub>*2*</sub>*SO*<sub>*4*</sub>* *

  - *Cu + **2**H*<sub>*2*</sub>*SO*<sub>*4 *</sub>*→ CuSO*<sub>*4*</sub>* + SO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
- *There are now four hydrogen atoms on the left hand side*
- *Add 2 in front of H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O *

  - *Cu + **2**H*<sub>*2*</sub>*SO*<sub>*4 *</sub>*→ CuSO*<sub>*4*</sub>* + SO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + **2**H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
  - *This also balances the oxygen atoms*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

When copper is reacted with hot concentrated sulfuric acid, sulfur dioxide gas is formed. Balance the chemical equation for this reaction. Cu + .......H~2~SO~4~ → CuSO~4~ + SO~2~ + .......H~2~O

#### Extended Only

When sulfuric acid reacts with ammonia the salt produced is ammonium sulfate.

Write the chemical equation for this reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
c) The balanced equation for this reaction  is:

2NH<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → (NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>

- Correct formulae; **[1 mark]**
- Correct balancing; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *The formula for sulfuric acid has been given in part b) - H*<sub>*2*</sub>*SO*<sub>*4*</sub>
- *You are expected to know the formula of ammonia is NH*<sub>*3 *</sub>
- *To deduce the formula of ammonium sulfate:*

  - *The ammonium ion is NH*<sub>*4*</sub><sup>*+*</sup>
  - *The sulfate ion is SO*<sub>*4*</sub><sup>*2-*</sup>
  - *The overall charge of the compound is 0 so these charges should cancel each other out *
  - *You therefore need two ammonium ions for every one sulfate ion, (NH*<sub>*4*</sub>*)*<sub>*2*</sub>*SO*<sub>*4*</sub>
- *The balancing should be straightforward once the equation has been written*

parts.problemMd:
#### Extended Only

Barium sulfate is an insoluble salt. Barium sulfate can be made from aqueous ammonium sulfate using a precipitation reaction.

Write an ionic equation for this precipitation reaction. Include state symbols.
parts.solutionMd:
d) An ionic equation for this reaction is:

Ba<sup>2+ </sup>(aq) + SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2- </sup>(aq) → BaSO<sub>4 </sub>(s)

- Correct formulae; **[1 mark]**
- Correct state symbols;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *Barium ions have the formula Ba*<sup>*2+*</sup>
- *Sulfate ions have the formula SO*<sub>*4*</sub><sup>*2-*</sup>

parts.problemMd:
#### Extended Only

Oxygen is produced by the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide. Manganese(IV) oxide is the catalyst for this reaction.

Oxygen can also be produced by the decomposition of potassium chlorate(V), KClO<sub>3</sub>.

The only products of this decomposition are potassium chloride and oxygen.

Write a chemical equation for this decomposition.
parts.solutionMd:
e) The balanced equation for this reaction  is:

2KClO<sub>3</sub> → 2KCl + 3O<sub>2</sub>

- Correct balancing; **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
#### Extended Only

This question is about titanium.

Titanium is a transition metal that is extracted from titanium dioxide in a two-stage industrial process.

In the first stage, titanium dioxide reacts with carbon and chlorine to form titanium tetrachloride and carbon monoxide.

Write the balanced symbol equation for this reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
a) The balanced symbol equation for this reaction is:

TiO<sub>2</sub> + 2C + 2Cl<sub>2</sub> ⟶ TiCl<sub>4</sub> + 2CO

- TiO<sub>2</sub> + C + Cl<sub>2</sub> as reactants; **[1 mark]**
- TiCl<sub>4</sub> + CO as products; **[1 mark]**
- Correct balancing;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *You have all the information to be able to write a word equation:*

  - *Titanium dioxide + carbon + chlorine → titanium tetrachloride + carbon monoxide*
- *You would be expected to deduce the formula of titanium dioxide and titanium tetrachloride from their names*

  - *Titanium = Ti*
  - *Dioxide = two oxygens (O*<sub>*2*</sub>*)*
  
    - *Therefore, titanium dioxide is TiO*<sub>*2*</sub>
  - *Tetrachloride = four chlorine (Cl*<sub>*4*</sub>*)*
  
    - *Therefore, titanium tetrachloride is TiCl*<sub>*4*</sub>* *
- *You are expected to know the chemical symbol/formula of some substances, e.g. C, Cl*<sub>*2*</sub>*, CO*
- *Balancing the equation:*

  - *You must use 2Cl*<sub>*2*</sub>* to have enough chlorine to make the TiCl*<sub>*4*</sub>* *
  - *You must form 2CO using the TiO*<sub>*2*</sub>
  - *This means that you must have 2C to make the 2CO*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

In the first stage, titanium dioxide reacts with carbon and chlorine to form titanium tetrachloride and carbon monoxide. Write the balanced symbol equation for this reaction.
The balanced symbol equation for this reaction is: TiO~2~ + 2C + 2Cl~2~ ⟶ TiCl~4~ + 2CO

Explain how your chemical symbol equation in part (a) demonstrates the law of conservation of mass.
parts.solutionMd:
b) The chemical symbol equation in part (a) demonstrates the law of conservation of mass because:

- There is the same amount / number of each atom on the reactants and products 
**OR **
There is the same amount / number of each atom on the left and right hand side of the equation; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

- *Don't be put off by the question starting with the phrase "explain how your answer to part (a)"*
- *The answer to this question is true for any balanced chemical symbol equation*

  - *There should always be the same number of each atom in the reactants and products*
  - *This is because any chemical reaction does not have any atoms being added or removed, they are simply rearranged to make other chemicals*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

This question is about titanium. Titanium is a transition metal that is extracted from titanium dioxide in a two-stage industrial process. In the first stage, titanium dioxide reacts with carbon and chlorine to form titanium tetrachloride and carbon monoxide.

Identify **two** hazards associated with Stage 1.
parts.solutionMd:
c) **Two** hazards associated with Stage 1 are:

Any **two** from:

- Chlorine is toxic / poisonous; **[1 mark]**
- Carbon monoxide is toxic / poisonous; **[1 mark]** *Ignore harmful / deadly / dangerous*
- Titanium chloride is corrosive; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *You are expected to use the correct chemical term when talking about hazards*

  - *Harmful is not a correct term as this suggests that it can make you ill*
  - *Toxic and poisonous imply that it can kill*
  - *Dangerous and deadly are not acceptable as they are not specific*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

This question is about titanium. Titanium is a transition metal that is extracted from titanium dioxide in a two-stage industrial process. In the first stage, titanium dioxide reacts with carbon and chlorine to form titanium tetrachloride and carbon monoxide.
TiO~2~ + 2C + 2Cl~2~ ⟶ TiCl~4~ + 2CO

#### Separate: Chemistry and Extended Only

Calculate, to three significant figures, the percentage by mass of chlorine in titanium tetrachloride.

(*A*<sub>r</sub>:  Ti = 48   Cl = 35.5)
parts.solutionMd:
d) The percentage, by mass, of chlorine in titanium tetrachloride is:

- Relative molar mass of TiCl<sub>4</sub> = 48 + (4 x 35.5) = 190;** [1 mark]**
- Percentage by mass = $\frac{4\times35.5}{190}\times100$= 74.7%; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *Careful: **There are four chlorine in titanium tetrachloride, so you have to calculate the percentage by mass for all four chlorines*
- *You will not score the second mark if your answer is not to three significant figures *
- *In the actual exam, you might be given the atomic masses that you need to use but there is also the possibility that you will be expected to look them up on the Periodic Table*
- *If the formula of titanium tetrachloride is given as TiCl*<sub>*2*</sub>* in part (a), then error carried forward is allowed giving a final answer of 59.7% for 1 mark*
- *If the formula of titanium tetrachloride is given as TiCl in part (a), then error carried forward is allowed giving a final answer of 42.5% for 1 mark*

parts.problemMd:
#### Extended Only

Magnesium displaces copper from copper sulfate solution.

Write the balanced symbol equation for the reaction.

You should include state symbols.
parts.solutionMd:
a) The word equation for magnesium displacing copper from copper sulfate solution is:

Mg (s) +  CuSO<sub>4</sub> (aq) →  Cu (s) + MgSO<sub>4</sub> (aq)

- Correct reactants and products; **[1 mark] **
- Correct state symbols; **[1 mark] **

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *Remember:** Displacement reactions are where a more reactive metal displaces / swaps places with the less reactive metal that is in a compound*
- *This means that magnesium sulfate must be the other product formed*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Magnesium displaces copper from copper sulfate solution.
Mg (s) + CuSO4 (aq) → Cu (s) + MgSO4 (aq)

#### Extended Only

State **two **changes that would be observed during the displacement reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
b) **Two **changes that will be observed are:

Any **two** from:

- Solution changes from <u>blue</u> to colourless 
**OR **
Blue colour (in solution) fades / disappears; **[1 mark]**
- Magnesium dissolves / displaces into solution; **[1 mark]**
- Solid copper appears; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *It is likely that you would be told that copper sulfate solution is blue*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Mg (s) + CuSO4 (aq) → Cu (s) + MgSO4 (aq)

#### Extended Only

Write the ionic equation for the displacement of copper from copper sulfate by magnesium. You should include state symbols.
parts.solutionMd:
c) The ionic equation for the displacement of copper from copper sulfate by magnesium is:

Mg (s) + Cu<sup>2+</sup> (aq) → Mg<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + Cu (s)

- All chemical formulae correct; **[1 mark]**
- All state symbols correct;** [1 mark]**

**[2 marks]**

- *The balance symbol equation is *

  - *Mg (s) + CuSO*<sub>*4*</sub>* (aq) → MgSO*<sub>*4*</sub>* (aq) + Cu (s)*
- *Identify the ionic substances and write the ions out separately*

  - *Mg (s) + Cu*<sup>*2+*</sup>* (aq) +  SO*<sub>*4*</sub><sup>*2-*</sup>* (aq) → Mg*<sup>*2+*</sup>* (aq)  + SO*<sub>*4*</sub><sup>*2-*</sup>* (aq) + Cu (s)*
- *Eliminate the ions which appear on both sides of the equation*
- *These are known as spectator ions and in this case are the sulfate ions*

  - *Mg (s) + Cu*<sup>*2+*</sup>* (aq) +  **SO*<sub>*4*</sub><sup>*2-*</sup>* **(aq) → Mg*<sup>*2+*</sup>* (aq)  + **SO*<sub>*4*</sub><sup>*2-*</sup>* **(aq) + Cu (s)*
  - *Mg (s) + Cu*<sup>*2+*</sup>* (aq) → Mg*<sup>*2+*</sup>* (aq) + Cu (s)*
  - *Don't forget state symbols!*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Mg (s) + Cu^2+ (aq) → Mg^2+ (aq) + Cu (s)

#### Extended Only

Displacement reactions are examples of redox reactions.

Explain why the displacement reaction between magnesium and copper sulfate is both reduction and oxidation.
parts.solutionMd:
d) The displacement reaction between magnesium and copper sulfate is both reduction and oxidation because:

- The magnesium / Mg atom is oxidised **AND **it loses electrons **OR **
Mg → Mg<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> **AND** which is oxidation; **[1 mark]**
- The copper ion / Cu<sup>2+</sup> is reduced **AND i**t gains electrons 
**OR **
Cu<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> → Cu **AND** which is reduction; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *Remember:** OIL-RIG, oxidation is loss of electrons and reduction is gain of electrons*

parts.problemMd:
#### Extended Only

This question is about lead nitrate.

Lead nitrate is an ionic compound.

It consists of Pb<sup>2+</sup> and NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> ions.

What is the chemical formula of lead nitrate?
parts.solutionMd:
a) The chemical formula for lead nitrate is:

- Pb(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

- *The overall charge on the ionic compound should be 0 *
- *Therefore two nitrate ions are needed for every one lead ion *
- *To show that there are two lead ions, brackets need to be around the nitrate ion as the nitrate ion contains more than one element*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The chemical formula for lead nitrate is: Pb(NO3)2.

#### Separate: Chemistry and Extended Only

Calculate the percentage by mass of oxygen in lead nitrate, Pb(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>.
parts.solutionMd:
b) The percentage by mass of oxygen in lead nitrate, Pb(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> is:

- Relative formula mass of lead nitrate = 207 + (14 x 2) + (16 x 6) = <u>331</u>; **[1 mark]**
- Percentage by mass of oxygen = $\frac{16\times6}{331}\times100$= 29.0%;** [1 mark] **

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *Remember:**  *`% mass of an element = (A _ r x number of atoms of the element)/(M _ r of the compound) x 100`
- *In this question, you are being asked about the six oxygen atoms so make sure you include them all in your calculation*
- *In the actual exam, you might be given the atomic masses that you need to use but there is also the possibility that you will be expected to look them up on the Periodic Table*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

This question is about lead nitrate. Lead nitrate is an ionic compound. It consists of Pb^2+^ and NO~3~^-^ ions. The chemical formula for lead nitrate is Pb(NO~3~)~2~.

#### Extended Only

A displacement reaction occurs between solutions of lead nitrate and potassium iodide, KI, to form solid lead(II) iodide and aqueous potassium nitrate.

Write the balanced symbol equation, including state symbols, for this reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
c) The balanced symbol equation, including state symbols, for this reaction is:

Pb(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> (aq) + 2KI (aq) → PbI<sub>2</sub> (s) + 2KNO<sub>3</sub> (aq)

- Correct formula of lead(II) iodide = PbI<sub>2</sub> 
**AND **
Correct formula of potassium nitrate = KNO<sub>3</sub>; **[1 mark]**
- All reactant chemical formulae correct 
**AND **
Equation correctly balanced; **[1 mark]**
- All state symbols correct; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**** **

- *You are told (in this and previous questions) the chemical formula and physical state of both lead nitrate and potassium iodide*

parts.problemMd:
#### Separate: Chemistry and Extended Only

The element gallium has a relative atomic mass of 69.735 and only contains two isotopes. A sample of gallium contained the isotope <sup>69</sup>Ga, with a relative abundance of 63.25 %. Calculate the mass number of the other isotope. You **must** show all your working.
parts.solutionMd:
b) The mass number of the other isotope is:

- Relative abundance of unknown isotope: 100 – 63.25 = 36.75; **[1 mark]**
- Calculation of mass number of unknown isotope of gallium with suitable working: $\frac{( 69 \mathrm{x} 63.25 ) + ( \mathrm{M} \mathrm{x} 36.75 )}{100} = 69.735$ **OR** $43.64+\frac{36.75M}{100}=69.735$ **AND** M = 71; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *This question is asking you to manipulate the equation used to calculate RAM to find the abundance of one of the isotopes:*

  - *RAM = *$\frac{ ( \text{abundance} of \text{isotope} 1 \mathrm{x} \text{mass} \text{number} ) + ( \text{abundance} of \text{isotope} 2 \mathrm{x} \text{mass} \text{number} ) }{100}$
- *You only get one mark if you give an answer with no working out*
- *To calculate M:*

  - $\frac{(69x63.25)+(Mx36.75)}{100}=69.735$
  - *4364.25 + (M x 36.75) = 6973.5*
  - *(M x 36.75) = 2609.25*
  - *M = *$\frac{2609.25}{36.75}$
  - *M = 71*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Ethanol is manufactured from glucose, C~6~H~12~O~6~, by fermentation according to the following equation. C~6~H~12~O~6 ~→ 2C~2~H~5~OH + 2CO~2~

#### Extended Only

In an experiment, 30.0 g of glucose was fermented.

i) Calculate the number of moles of glucose in 30.0 g.

[2]

ii) Calculate the maximum mass of ethanol that could be obtained from 30.0 g of glucose.

[2]

iii) Calculate the volume of carbon dioxide at room temperature and pressure that can be obtained from 30.0 g of glucose.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
b)

i) The number of moles of glucose in 30.0 g is:

- *M*<sub>r</sub> = 180; **[1 mark]**
- (30/180) = 0.167 moles; **[1 mark]**

ii) The maximum mass of ethanol that could be obtained from 30.0 g of glucose is:

- 2 × 0.167 **OR **2 × 46 **OR **0.333 **OR **92 ; **[1 mark]**
- (2 × 0.167 × 46) = 15.3(33) (g); **[1 mark]**

iii)  The volume of carbon dioxide at room temperature and pressure that can be obtained from 30.0 g of glucose is:

- (2 × 0.167 × 24 ) = 8 (dm<sup>3</sup>); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

- *The** M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of glucose is calculated by adding the **A*<sub>*r*</sub>* of all the atoms present in the formula:*

  - *(6 x C) + (12 x H) + (12 x O)*
  - *(6 x 12) + (12 x 1) + (6 x 16) = 180*
- *The number of moles can be found from the equation moles = *$\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{\mathrm{molar} \mathrm{mass}}$* where the molar mass is the **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* in grams*

  - *moles = 30 ÷ 180 = 0.167 moles*
- *The balanced symbol equation shows you that 1 mole of glucose produces 2 moles of ethanol so the number of moles of ethanol produced will be double the number of moles of glucose that was calculated in (ii)*

  - *2 x 0.167 = 0.334 moles*
- *The** M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of ethanol is calculated by:*

  - *(2 x C) + (6 x H) + (1 x O) *
  - *(2 x 12) + (6 x 1) + (1 x 16) = 46*
- *To calculate the mass of ethanol, use the equation mass = moles x molar mass*

  - *mass = 0.334 x 46 = 15.3 g*
- *The number of moles of carbon dioxide produced will be the same as the number of moles of ethanol, as shown from the balanced symbol equation = 2 x 0.167 = 0.334 moles*
- *The mole of gas will occupy 24 dm*<sup>*3*</sup>* at r.t.p. so the volume of carbon dioxide produced is calculated by 0.334 x 24 = 8 dm*<sup>*3*</sup>

i) Complete the equation for the equilibrium present in the region **BC**. X(s) $\rightleftharpoons$ ....................

[1]

ii) What is the significance of temperature t°C?

[1]

iii) What is the physical state of compound X in the region **EF**?

[1]

iv) What would be the difference in the region **BC** if an impure sample of X had been used?

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
a)

i) The equation for the equilibrium present in the region **BC** is:

vapour; **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
#### Separate: Chemistry and Extended Only

Compound X is a hydrocarbon. It contains 85.7% of carbon. The mass of one mole of X is 84g.

i) What is the percentage of hydrogen in the compound?

[1]

ii) Calculate the empirical formula of X. Show your working.

[3]

iii) What is the molecular formula of compound X?

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
b)

i) The percentage of hydrogen in the compound is:

- 14.3 (%); **[1 mark]**

ii) The empirical formula of compound X is found by:

- (Moles of) C = 85.7/12 
**OR **
7.14 **AND** (Moles of) H = 14.3/1 
**OR **
14.3; **[1 mark]**
- Ratio of C:H is 1:2;** [1 mark]**
- Empirical formula: CH<sub>2</sub>; **[1 mark]**

**OR**

- 85.7 × 84 ÷ 100 
**OR** 
71.988/72 **AND **14.3 × 84 ÷ 100 
**OR **
12/12.012; **[1 mark]**
- 6:12 or ratio of C:H is 1:2; **[1 mark]**
- Empirical formula: CH<sub>2</sub>; **[1 mark]**

iii) The molecular formula of compound X is:

- C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

- *To calculate the empirical formula when given percentages, it is easiest to assume that you have 100 g of the sample, then you can workout the number of moles of each element in 100 g by using the **M*<sub>*r*</sub>*:*

|   | > *C* | > *H* |
|---|---|---|
| > *Calculate the number of moles of each element in 100g (%/**M*<sub>*r*</sub>*)* | $\frac{85.7}{12}\,=7.14$ | $\frac{14.3}{1}\,=14.3$ |
| > *Divide by the smallest number to find the smallest ratio* | > * 7.17/7.14 = 1* | > * 14.3/7.14 = 2* |

- *The **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of CH*<sub>*2*</sub>* is 12 + (2 x 1) = 14*
- *The **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of X is 84*

When calcium carbonate is heated strongly, it decomposes.

CaCO<sub>3</sub> → CaO + CO<sub>2</sub>

i) Calculate the relative formula mass of:    CaCO<sub>3</sub>

CaO

[2]

ii) 7.00 kg of calcium oxide was formed. What mass of calcium carbonate was heated?

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
b)

i) The relative formula masses are:

- CaCO<sub>3</sub> = 40 + 12 + (3 x 16) = 100; **[1 mark]**
- CaO = 40 + 16 = 56; **[1 mark]**

ii) The mass of calcium carbonate heated was:

- 7.00 kg is 1/8 of 56; **[1 mark]**
- 1/8 of 100 kg is 12.5 kg; **[1 mark]** 
*Give both marks for correct answer without explanation* *Ignore missing units but penalise wrong units*

**OR**

- Moles of calcium oxide = mass/molar mass = 7.0 x 1000/56 = 125 moles; **[1 mark]**
- Mass of calcium carbonate = moles x molar mass = 125 x 100 = 12500 g / 12.5 kg; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *You can either calculate the mass of calcium carbonate by calculating the number of moles of CaO, then using this to find the number of moles of CaCO*<sub>*3*</sub>* (it is a 1:1 reacting ratio so the number of moles of CaO = number of moles of CaCO*<sub>*3*</sub>*) and then finally calculating the mass of CaCO*<sub>*3*</sub>
- *An alternative way to think about it is:*

  - *1 mole of CaCO*<sub>*3*</sub>* has a mass of 100 g and 1 mole of CaO is 56 g*
  - *So, 100 g CaCO*<sub>*3 *</sub>*will decompose to form 56 g of CaO*
  - *Scaling up using this ratio, 100 kg CaCO*<sub>*3 *</sub>*will decompose to form 56 kg of CaO*
  - *Therefore, 100/8 = 12.5 kg CaCO*<sub>*3 *</sub>*will decompose to form 56/8 = 7 kg of CaO*

#### Separate: Chemistry and Extended Only

Two salts can be made from potassium hydroxide and sulfuric acid. They are potassium sulfate, K<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, and the acid salt potassium hydrogen sulfate, KHSO<sub>4</sub>. They are both made by titration.

![titration-h2so4-koh](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-chemistry-23/3-stoichiometry/3-2-the-mole-and-the-avogadro-constant/assets/012-titration-h2so4-koh.png)

25.0 cm<sup>3 </sup>of potassium hydroxide, concentration of 2.53 mol / dm<sup>3</sup>, was neutralised by 28.2 cm<sup>3</sup> of dilute sulfuric acid.

2KOH (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4 </sub>(aq) → K<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4 </sub>(aq) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

Calculate the concentration of the sulfuric acid. number of moles of KOH used = ............................ number of moles of H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> needed to neutralise the KOH = ............................ concentration of dilute sulfuric acid = ............................ mol / dm<sup>3</sup>
parts.solutionMd:
a) To calculate the concentration of sulfuric acid:

- Moles of KOH used ( = 2.53 x 0.025 =) 0.06325 / 0.063; **[1 mark]**
- Number of moles of H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> needed to neutralise the KOH = 0.031625 / 0.032;** [1 mark]**
- Concentration of dilute sulfuric acid = ( 0.031625 / 0.0282 =) 1.121 / 1.1 (mol / dm<sup>3</sup>); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *To calculate the moles of KOH, use the equation:*

  - *Amount of substance (mol) = concentration (mol / dm*<sup>*3*</sup>*) x volume (dm*<sup>*3*</sup>*)*
  - *Volume of KOH used = 25.0 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* = 0.025 dm*<sup>*3*</sup>
  - *Therefore, amount of KOH (mol) = 2.53 x 0.025 = 0.06325 mol*
- *Remember**: You must convert cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* to dm*<sup>*3*</sup>* before using this equation by dividing the volume in cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* by 1000*
- *Use the balanced symbol equation to find the reacting ratio, in this case it the ratio of KOH to H*<sub>*2*</sub>*SO*<sub>*4 *</sub>*is 2:1*<sub>* *</sub>*so half the number of moles of H*<sub>*2*</sub>*SO*<sub>*4*</sub>* are needed to neutralise KOH*

  - *0.06325 ÷ 2 = 0.031625 mol*
- *To calculate the concentration of H*<sub>*2*</sub>*SO*<sub>*4, *</sub>*use the following equation, remembering to convert cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* to dm*<sup>*3*</sup>*:*

  - *Concentration (mol / dm*<sup>*3*</sup>*) = *$\frac{\mathrm{amount} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{substance}(\mathrm{mol})}{\mathrm{volume}(\mathrm{dm}^{3})}$
  - *Volume of H*<sub>*2*</sub>*SO*<sub>*4 *</sub>*used = 28.2 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* = 0.0282 dm*<sup>*3*</sup>
  - *Therefore, concentration = *$\frac{0.031625}{0.0282}=1.121\mathrm{mol}/\mathrm{dm}^{3}$

Two salts can be made from potassium hydroxide and sulfuric acid. They are potassium sulfate, K~2~SO~4~, and the acid salt potassium hydrogen sulfate, KHSO~4~. They are both made by titration.

- And same volume / amount of (same) KOH; **[1 mark]**

ii) You could make a solution of potassium hydrogen sulfate without using an indicator by:

- Make solution of potassium sulfate as above; **[1 mark]**
- Add same volume / amount of acid from part (a) again; **[1 mark]**

**OR**

- Same volume / amount of KOH (from part (a)); **[1 mark]**
- Add double the volume / amount of H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4 </sub>(from part (a)); **[1 mark]** *25cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* KOH + 56.4 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* H*<sub>*2*</sub>*SO*<sub>*4*</sub>* = ***[2 marks]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *To prepare a soluble salt from an acid and an alkali (a soluble base), it is necessary to have the quantities of the acid and alkali present in the molar ratio given in the balanced equation*
- *Activated charcoal can be added to the mixture to remove the indicator, the charcoal would need to be filtered off to produce a solution of potassium sulfate without the indicator*

parts.problemMd:
#### Extended Only

4.8 g of calcium is added to 3.6 g of water. The following reaction occurs.

Ca + 2H<sub>2</sub>O → Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>

i) The number of moles of Ca = .................... The number of moles of H<sub>2</sub>O = ....................

[1]

ii) Which reagent is in excess? Explain your choice.

[2]

iii) Calculate the mass of the reagent named in (ii) which remained at the end of the experiment.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
c)

i) The number of moles of Ca and H<sub>2</sub>O are:

- (Mass / molar mass =) 4.8/40 = 0.12 moles of Ca 
**AND** 
(Mass / molar mass =) 3.6/18 = 0.2 moles of H<sub>2</sub>O; **[1 mark]**

ii) The reagent that is in excess, with a reason, is:

- Ca is in excess 
**AND** 
(because 0.12 moles of Ca need) 0.24 moles / 4.32 g of H<sub>2</sub>O to react; **[1 mark]**
- There is not enough / there are 0.2 moles / 3.6 g of H<sub>2</sub>O; **[1 mark] **

**OR**

- Ca is in excess 
**AND **
(because 0.2 moles / 3.6 g of water will react with) 0.1 moles /4 .0 g of Ca; **[1 mark]**
- There is more than that / there are 0.12 moles / 4.8 g of Ca; **[1 mark] **

**OR**

- Ca is in excess 
**AND** 
because the mole ratio Ca : H<sub>2</sub>O is 3:5 / mass ratio 4:3; **[1 mark]**
- Which is bigger than the required mole ratio of 1:2 / mass ratio 10:9; **[1 mark] **

**OR**

- Ca is in excess 
**AND** 
because the mole ratio H<sub>2</sub>O : Ca is 5:3 / mass ratio 3:4; **[1 mark]**
- Which is smaller than the required mole ratio of 2:1 / mass ratio 9:10; **[1 mark]**

iii) The mass of the reagent named in (ii) which remained at the end of the experiment is:

- 0.02 × 40 = 0.8 (g); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *There are no marks for just stating that Ca is in excess, you must give a reason why this is the case too*
- *The term limiting reagent means the same as limiting reactant and you may see either term used in past papers*
- *The limiting reactant / reagent is the reactant that is used up first in the reaction*
- *Careful:** You must use the reacting ratio from the balanced symbol equation when determining the limiting reactant*
- *If it is a 1:1 reacting ratio, then you can compare the number of moles of each reactant directly, the reactant with the least number of moles present will be the limiting reactant*
- *However, if it is not 1:1 as in this question, you must consider the reacting ratio*
- *Here, the reacting ratio of Ca to H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O is 1:2 so twice the number of moles of H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O are required compared with the number of moles of Ca*
- *There are 0.12 moles of Ca which will require 2 x 0.12 = 0.24 moles of H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
- *Only 0.2 moles of H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O are present so this is the limiting reactant, therefore Ca is in excess*
- *This means that all 0.2 moles of H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O will be used up leaving some Ca remaining*
- *The amount of Ca that is used in the equation will be half the number of moles of H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O (remember the reacting ratio of Ca : H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O of 1:2) so the number of moles of Ca used = 0.2 ÷ 2 = 0.1 moles*
- *The initial amount of Ca was 0.12 moles, therefore the amount remaining is 0.12 - 0.1 = 0.02 moles*
- *This value can then be multiplied by the **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of Ca (= 40) to give the mass of Ca remaining at the end of the experiment*

parts.problemMd:
A compound, Al<sub>4</sub>C<sub>3</sub>, contains only aluminium and carbon. 0.03 moles of this compound reacted with excess water to form 0.12 moles of Al(OH)<sub>3</sub> and 0.09 moles of CH<sub>4</sub>.

Write a balanced equation for this reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
b) A balanced equation for this reaction is:

- Al<sub>4</sub>C<sub>3</sub> + 12H<sub>2</sub>O = 4Al(OH)<sub>3</sub> + 3CH<sub>4</sub>;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

- *To balance the equation:*
- *Write the unbalanced equation with the formulae as given in the question, don't forget to include water as a reactant:*

  - *Al*<sub>*4*</sub>*C*<sub>*3*</sub>* + H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O → Al(OH)*<sub>*3*</sub>* + CH*<sub>*4*</sub>
- *To work out the balancing numbers of Al*<sub>*4*</sub>*C*<sub>*3*</sub>*, Al(OH)*<sub>*3*</sub>* and CH*<sub>*4*</sub>* divide the number of moles of each compound present by the smallest number of moles (= 0.03):*

  - *Al*<sub>*4*</sub>*C*<sub>*3*</sub>* = 0.03 ÷ 0.03 = 1*
  - *Al(OH)*<sub>*3 *</sub>*= 0.12 ÷ 0.03 = 4*
  - *CH*<sub>*4 *</sub>*= 0.09 ÷ 0.03 = 3*
- *Add these to your equation:*

  - *Al*<sub>*4*</sub>*C*<sub>*3*</sub>* + H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O → 4Al(OH)*<sub>*3*</sub>* + 3CH*<sub>*4*</sub>
- *Now work out how many H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O molecules are needed to balance the equation:*

  - *On the RHS, there are 24 H atoms and 12 oxygen atoms, therefore 12 molecules of water are needed*
- *The balanced symbol equation is therefore:*

  - *Al*<sub>*4*</sub>*C*<sub>*3*</sub>* + 12H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O → 4Al(OH)*<sub>*3*</sub>* + 3CH*<sub>*4*</sub>

parts.problemMd:
#### Extended Only

0.07 moles of silicon reacts with 25 g of bromine.

Si + 2Br<sub>2</sub> → SiBr<sub>4</sub>

i) Which one is the limiting reagent? Explain your choice.

[3]

ii) How many moles of SiBr<sub>4</sub> are formed?

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
c)

i) The limiting reagent, with a reason why, is:

- Silicon is limiting reagent; **[1 mark]**
- 0.07 moles of Si and (mass / molar mass = 25 / 160 =) 0.156 moles of Br<sub>2</sub>; **[1 mark]**
- Because 0.14 (2 × 0.07) < 0.156; **[1 mark]** *If 80 is used to find moles of Br*<sub>*2*</sub>* the mark 1 and 3 are still available, arguments based on masses can be used*

ii) The number of moles of SiBr<sub>4</sub> that are formed is:

- 0.07; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *To find the number of moles, use the equation mass ÷ molar mass*

  - *The molar mass of Br*<sub>*2*</sub>* is 2 x 80 = 160*
  - *The number of moles of Br*<sub>*2 *</sub>*= 25 ÷ 160 = 0.156 moles*
- *The balanced symbol equation shows that 1 mole of Si reacts with 2 moles of Br*<sub>*2*</sub>
- *So 0.07 moles of Si will need to react with 2 x 0.07 = 0.14 moles of Br*<sub>*2*</sub>
- *As 0.156 moles of Br*<sub>*2*</sub>* are present, there are more moles of Br*<sub>*2*</sub>* than are needed therefore Br*<sub>*2*</sub>* is in excess, and Si is the limiting reactant*
- *The limiting reactant will determine the amount of product formed as all of it will be used up in the reaction*
- *The balanced symbol equation shows that for every 1 mole of Si used, 1 mole of SiBr*<sub>*4*</sub>* is produced*
- *Therefore 0.07 moles of SiBr*<sub>*4*</sub>* are produced*

parts.problemMd:

[3]

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
b)

- Moles of SO<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> formed = 0.125; **[1 mark]**
- The mass of sulphuryl chloride formed (=  moles x molar mass = 0.125 x 135) = 16.9 g; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

- *Don't be put off with this equation because it forms a product that you are not familiar with, the principles behind calculating reacting masses and using limiting reactants are just the same*
- *The molar masses of SO*<sub>*2*</sub>* and Cl*<sub>*2*</sub>* are needed to calculate the number of moles present:*

  - *M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of SO*<sub>*2*</sub>* = 32 + (2 x 16) = 64*
  - *M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of Cl*<sub>*2*</sub>* = 2 x 35.5 = 71*
- *It is a 1:1 reacting ratio between SO*<sub>*2*</sub>* and Cl*<sub>*2*</sub>* so 0.125 moles of SO*<sub>*2*</sub>* would react with 0.125 moles of Cl*<sub>*2*</sub>* *
- *There is more Cl*<sub>*2*</sub>* than will react with SO*<sub>*2*</sub>* and therefore Cl*<sub>*2*</sub>* is in excess and SO*<sub>*2*</sub>* is the limiting reactant*
- *The moles of SO*<sub>*2*</sub>*Cl*<sub>*2 *</sub>*formed is determined by the limiting reactant*
- *It is a 1:1 reacting ratio between SO*<sub>*2*</sub>* and SO*<sub>*2*</sub>*Cl*<sub>*2 *</sub>*so an equal number of moles of SO*<sub>*2*</sub>*Cl*<sub>*2 *</sub>*will be formed*

parts.problemMd:
#### Separate: Chemistry and Extended Only

A compound, **X**, contains 55.85% carbon, 6.97% hydrogen and 37.18% oxygen.

i) How does this prove that compound **X** contains only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen?

[1]

ii) Use the above percentages to calculate the empirical formula of compound **X**.

[2]

iii) The* M*<sub>r</sub> of **X** is 86. What is its molecular formula?

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
a)

i) This proves that compound **X** contains only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen because:

- Percentages add up to 100%;** [1 mark]**

ii) To work out the empirical formula of compound **X**:

- Moles of C = 55.85/12 
**OR **
4.65 **AND **moles of H = 6.97/1 
**OR **
6.97 **AND **mole of O = 37.18/16 
**OR **
2.32; **[1 mark]**
- Empirical formula: C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>3</sub>O;** [1 mark]** 
*Award 2 marks for correct answer with no working*

iii) The molecular formula for compound **X** is found by:

- *M*<sub>r</sub> of C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>3</sub>O = 43;** [1 mark]**
- (86/43 = 2 therefore molecular formula is) C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O<sub>2</sub>;** [1 mark] ***Award 2 marks for correct answer with no working*

**[Total: 5 marks]**

- *To calculate the empirical formula when given percentages, it is easiest to assume that you have 100 g of the sample, then you can workout the number of moles of each element in 100 g by using the **M*<sub>*r*</sub>*:*

|   | > *C* | > *H* | > *O* |
|---|---|---|---|
| > *Calculate the number of moles of each element in 100g (%/**M*<sub>*r*</sub>*)* | $\frac{55.85}{12}\,=4.65$ | $\frac{6.97}{1}\,=6.97$ | $\frac{37.18}{16}\,=2.32$ |
| > *Divide by the smallest number to find the smallest ratio* | > * 4.65/2.32 = 2* | > * 6.97/2.32 = 3* | > * 2.32/2.32 = 1* |

- *The empirical formula is therefore C*<sub>*2*</sub>*H*<sub>*3*</sub>*O*
- *Compound **X** has twice the** M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of the empirical formula, therefore compound **X** must contain twice the number of atoms that appears in the empirical formula*

parts.problemMd:

[1]

iii) Calculate its empirical formula and then its molecular formula. The empirical formula of benzene is ................... The molecular formula of benzene is ...................

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
b)

i) The percentage of hydrogen in benzene is:

- 7.7%; **[1 mark]**

ii) The ratio of moles of C atoms: moles of H atoms in benzene is:

- For any number: equal number ratio; **[1 mark]** 
*For example 1:1 or 6:6*

iii) Its empirical formula and molecular formula are:

- Empirical formula is CH; **[1 mark]**
- Molecular formula is C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>; **[1 mark]** 
*Do not allow e.c.f.* *Award of marks is not dependent on (ii)*

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *The question tells you that benzene is a hydrocarbon, therefore it only contains carbon and hydrogen atoms*
- *92.3% is carbon, so the rest of the mass must be due to hydrogen*

  - *100 - 92.3 = 7.7%*
- *Calculate the molar ratio by dividing the percentage of each element by its **A*<sub>*r*</sub>*:*

  - *Carbon: *$\frac{92.3}{12}=7.69$
  - *Hydrogen: *$\frac{7.7}{1}=7.7$
- *So the molar ratio is 7.69 : 7.7, or, more simply, 1:1*
- *Therefore, its empirical formula is CH*
- *The **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of its empirical formula is 12 + 1 = 13*

#### Separate: Chemistry Only

[1]

[2]

parts.problemMd:
#### Extended Only

The complete combustion of hydrocarbons produces carbon dioxide and water only.

i) Write the equation for the complete combustion of nonane, C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>20</sub>.

[2]

ii) 20cm<sup>3</sup> of a gaseous hydrocarbon was mixed with an excess of oxygen, 200 cm<sup>3</sup>. The mixture was ignited. After cooling, 40 cm<sup>3</sup> of oxygen and 100 cm<sup>3</sup> of carbon dioxide remained.

Deduce the formula of the hydrocarbon and the equation for its combustion. All volumes were measured at r.t.p..

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
c)

i) The equation for the complete combustion of nonane, C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>20</sub> is:

C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>20</sub> + 14O<sub>2</sub> → 9CO<sub>2</sub> + 10H<sub>2</sub>O

- Correct reactants and products; **[1 mark]**
- Correct balancing; **[1 mark] **

ii) To deduce the formula of the hydrocarbon and the equation for its combustion:

| General equation | C<sub>x</sub>H<sub>y</sub> + | O<sub>2</sub> | → | CO<sub>2</sub> + | H<sub>2</sub>O |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Volume in cm<sup>3</sup> | 20 | 200 - 40 = 160 |   | 100 |   |
| Ratio | 1 | 8 |   | 5 |   |
| Unbalanced equation | C<sub>x</sub>H<sub>y</sub> + | 8O<sub>2</sub> | → | 5CO<sub>2</sub> + | H<sub>2</sub>O |
| Fully balanced equation | C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub> + | 8O<sub>2</sub> | → | 5CO<sub>2</sub> + | 6H<sub>2</sub>O |

- Evidence of 1 : 8 : 5 ratio; **[1 mark]**
- Unbalanced equation; **[1 mark]**
- Identification of C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>  **AND **Fully balanced equation; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

- *Balancing chemical equations is a skill that you are expected to have in exams*
- *Part (ii) is a more challenging question*

  - *First you have to calculate how much oxygen was used, 200 - 40 = 160 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* *
  - *Since the volumes are all in cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* and measured at room temperature, there is no need to calculate moles *
  - *You can use the volumes as a ratio of 20 : 160 : 100 which simplifies to 1 : 8 : 5*
  - *This tells you that 1 mole of the hydrocarbon reacted with 8 moles of oxygen to form 5 moles of carbon dioxide, e.g. C*<sub>*x*</sub>*H*<sub>*y*</sub>* + 8O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → 5CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
  - *The 5 moles of carbon dioxide gives you the number of carbons in the hydrocarbon,  e.g. C*<sub>*5*</sub>*H*<sub>*y*</sub>* + 8O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → 5CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
  - *There are 16 oxygen atoms on the reactant side*
  - *There are 10 oxygen atoms in the carbon dioxide product which means that there must be 6 waters to account for the remaining oxygen atoms,  e.g. C*<sub>*5*</sub>*H*<sub>*y*</sub>* + 8O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → 5CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + 6H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
  - *This now means that there are 12 hydrogen atoms and gives the final balanced equation of  C*<sub>*5*</sub>*H*<sub>*12*</sub>* + 8O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → 5CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + 6H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*

parts.problemMd:
#### Separate: Chemistry and Extended Only

Chlorine reacts with propane in a substitution reaction to form 1-chloropropane.

CH<sub>3</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>3</sub> + Cl<sub>2</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–Cl + HCl

i) What is the essential condition for the above reaction?

[1]

ii) There is more than one possible substitution reaction between chlorine and propane.

Suggest the structural formula of a different product.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
e)

i) The essential condition for the reaction is:

- UV light / sunlight; **[1 mark]** 
*Accept lead tetraethyl / catalyst / high temperature*

ii) The structural formula of a different product is:

- CH<sub>3</sub>–CHCl–CH<sub>3</sub>; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *The equation shows that one of the hydrogen atoms is being substituted by a chlorine atom*

parts.problemMd:
#### Separate: Chemistry and Extended Only

Ammonia, NH<sub>3</sub>, is used to produce nitric acid, HNO<sub>3</sub>. This happens in a three-stage process. Stage 1 is a redox reaction.

4NH<sub>3</sub> + 5O<sub>2</sub> → 4NO + 6H<sub>2</sub>O

percentage yield of NO = ................................ %
parts.solutionMd:
a)

The percentage yield of NO in this reaction is:

- 75 (%);** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

- *The percentage yield is calculated by:*

  - *percentage yield = *$\frac{\mathrm{actual} \mathrm{yield}}{\mathrm{theoretical} \mathrm{yield}}$*x 100*
- *Substituting the values given in the question:*

  - *percentage yield = *$\frac{384}{512}$* x 100 = 75%*
- *The most common mistake with calculating percentage yield is to divide the theoretical yield by the actual yield which would give a value of over 100%*
- *Remember**: Percentage yield cannot be greater than 100% - if your value is greater, check your calculations!*
- *The only other reason that you may obtain a value greater than 100% is if there is an error in the method used to obtain the product*

  - *For example, some impurities could remain in the product, which would cause the actual yield to be a greater value than it should be*

#### Separate: Chemistry and Extended Only

The following method is used to make crystals of hydrated nickel sulphate. An excess of nickel carbonate, 12.0 g, was added to 40 cm<sup>3</sup> of sulphuric acid, 2.0 mol/dm<sup>3</sup>. The unreacted nickel carbonate was filtered off and the filtrate evaporated to obtain the crystals.

NiCO<sub>3 </sub>+ H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>  → NiSO<sub>4</sub> + CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O

NiSO<sub>4</sub> + 7H<sub>2</sub>O  → NiSO<sub>4</sub>.7H<sub>2</sub>O

Mass of one mole of NiSO<sub>4</sub>.7H<sub>2</sub>O = 281 g Mass of one mole of NiCO<sub>3</sub> = 119 g

i) Calculate the mass of unreacted nickel carbonate.

Number of moles of H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> in 40 cm<sup>3</sup> of 2.0 mol/dm<sup>3</sup> acid = 0.08 Number of moles of NiCO<sub>3 </sub>reacted = ......................................  
Mass of nickel carbonate reacted = ...................................... g Mass of unreacted nickel carbonate =  ...................................... g

[3]

ii) The experiment produced 10.4 g of hydrated nickel sulphate. Calculate the percentage yield.

The maximum number of moles of NiSO<sub>4</sub>.7H<sub>2</sub>Othat could be formed = ...................................... 
The maximum mass of NiSO<sub>4</sub>.7H<sub>2</sub>O that could be formed = ...................................... g 
The percentage yield = ...................................... %

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
a)

i) The mass of unreacted nickel carbonate can be calculated by:

- Moles of NiCO<sub>3</sub> reacted = 0.08;** [1 mark]**
- Mass of nickel carbonate reacted = (0.08 x 119 =) 9.52 g;** [1 mark]**
- Mass of nickel carbonate unreacted = (12.0 - 9.52 =) 2.48 g;** [1 mark]**

ii) The percentage yield can be calculated by:

- Maximum number of moles of hydrated salt = 0.08;** [1 mark]**
- Maximum mass of salt = 0.08 x 281 = 22.48 g;** [1 mark]**
- Percentage yield 10.4/22.48 x 100 = 46 % / 46.3%;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

- *NiCO*<sub>*3*</sub>* is in excess so the number of moles of it that reacts will be determined by the limiting reactant, H*<sub>*2*</sub>*SO*<sub>*4*</sub>
- *The balanced symbol equation shows that the reacting ratio is 1:1 and the question tells you that 0.08 moles of H*<sub>*2*</sub>*SO*<sub>*4*</sub>* were used, therefore the same number of moles of NiCO*<sub>*3*</sub>* is used*
- *The mass can be determined by the equation mass = moles x molar mass*
- *The molar mass is given in the question = 119 g per 1 mole*
- *Mass of NiCO*<sub>*3 *</sub>*= 0.08 x 119 = 9.52 g*
- *12.0 g of nickel carbonate was initially so you can find the mass of the unreacted nickel carbonate by 12.0 - 9.52 = 2.48 g*
- *In the first equation, 0.08 moles of NiSO*<sub>*4*</sub>* must be produced according to the reacting ratio given in the balanced symbol equation*
- *In the second equation, 0.08 moles of NiSO*<sub>*4*</sub>* will produce the same number of moles of the hydrated NiSO*<sub>*4*</sub>* as per the reacting ratio (1:1)*
- *The percentage yield is calculated by the following equation:*

  - $\mathrm{percentage} \mathrm{yield}=\frac{\mathrm{actual} \mathrm{yield}}{\mathrm{theoretical} \mathrm{yield}}\times100$
- *Percentage yield must be less than 100% so if you get an answer greater than this, check you have not divided the theoretical yield by the actual yield - this is a common mistake to make!*

parts.solutionMd:
b) To calculate the percentage yield:

- Number of moles of NaOH used (= volume in dm<sup>3</sup> x concentration = 0.025 x 2.24) = 0.056; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *When calculating the number of moles from concentration, it is important to convert the units of volume to dm*<sup>*3*</sup>* from cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* by dividing by 1000:*
- *25 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* = 25/1000 = 0.025 dm*<sup>*3*</sup>
- *When finding the number of moles of Na*<sub>*2*</sub>*SO*<sub>*4*</sub>*.10H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O that could be formed, you must refer to the balanced symbol equations:*

  - *The first equation shows that 2 moles of NaOH produce 1 mole of Na*<sub>*2*</sub>*SO*<sub>*4*</sub>
  - *The second equation shows that 1 mole of Na*<sub>*2*</sub>*SO*<sub>*4 *</sub>*produces 1 mole of Na*<sub>*2*</sub>*SO*<sub>*4*</sub>*.10H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
  - *Therefore 2 moles of NaOH produce 1 mole of Na*<sub>*2*</sub>*SO*<sub>*4*</sub>*.10H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
  - *So 0.056 moles of NaOH produces 0.056 / 2 = 0.028 moles of Na*<sub>*2*</sub>*SO*<sub>*4*</sub>*.10H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
- *Percentage yield must be less than 100%,*

  - *If you get a value greater than 100%, ensure you have not divided the theoretical yield by the actual yield - a common mistake!*
  - *If your value is very small, ensure you remembered to times by 100 to convert it to a percentage*

Calculate the percentage yield, giving your answer to one decimal place.

Number of moles of LiOH used = .......................

Number of moles of Li<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>.H<sub>2</sub>O which could be formed = .......................

Mass of one mole of Li<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>.H<sub>2</sub>O = 128g

Maximum yield of Li<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>.H<sub>2</sub>O = ....................... g

Percentage yield = .......................%
parts.solutionMd:
b) The percentage yield can be calculated by:

- Number of moles of LiOH used (= concentration x volume in dm<sup>3</sup> = 2.48 x 0.025 ) = 0.062; **[1 mark]**
- Number of moles of Li<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>.H<sub>2</sub>O which could be formed = 0.031; **[1 mark]**
- Mass of one mole of Li<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>.H<sub>2</sub>O = 128g

  - *2 moles of LiOH forms 1 mole of Li*<sub>*2*</sub>*SO*<sub>*4*</sub>* *
  - *1 mole of Li*<sub>*2*</sub>*SO*<sub>*4 *</sub>*forms 1 mole*<sub>* *</sub>*Li*<sub>*2*</sub>*SO*<sub>*4*</sub>*.H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
  - *So 2 moles of LiOH form 1 mole of Li*<sub>*2*</sub>*SO*<sub>*4*</sub>*.H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
  - *Therefore 0.062 moles of LiOH form 0.062 / 2 = 0.031 moles of Li*<sub>*2*</sub>*SO*<sub>*4*</sub>*.H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
- *Percentage yield is calculated by the equation:*

$\mathrm{percentage} \mathrm{yield}=\frac{\mathrm{actual} \mathrm{yield}}{\mathrm{theoretical} \mathrm{yield}}\times100$

parts.solutionMd:
c) The mass of iron(III) oxide formed and the volume of sulfur trioxide, at r.t.p., formed can be calculated by:

- Mass of one mole of Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3 </sub>= (2 x 56) + (3 x 16) = 160 g; **[1 mark]**

- Number of moles of SO<sub>3</sub> formed = 0.03 moles; **[1 mark]**
- Volume of sulfur trioxide formed = moles x 24 = 0.03 x 24 = 0.72 dm<sup>3</sup>;  **[1 mark]** *Apply ecf to number of moles of Fe*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*<sub>*3*</sub>* when calculating volume of sulfur trioxide*

- *Therefore 0.06 moles FeSO*<sub>*4 *</sub>*produce 0.06/2 = 0.03 moles of Fe*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*<sub>*3*</sub>

The *M*<sub>r</sub> of  lead(II) chloride, PbCl<sub>2</sub>.

- *M*<sub>r</sub> =  207 + (2 × 35.5); **[1 mark]**
- *M*<sub>r</sub> = 278; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *Step 1:** Write the formula: **PbCl*<sub>*2*</sub>
- *Step 2:** Use the atomic masses from the Periodic Table:*

  - *Pb = **207*
  - *Cl = **35.5*
- *Step 3:** Multiply the number of each atom by its atomic mass:*

  - *1 × 207 = **207*
  - *2 × 35.5 = **71*
- *Step 4:** Add them together:*

  - *207 + 71 = **278*

[1]

parts.solutionMd:
Balanced half equation provided:

4OH⁻ → O<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O + 4e⁻

- Correct balancing of OH⁻, O<sub>2</sub>, and H<sub>2</sub>O; **[1 mark]**
- Correct balancing of electrons; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *It is worth taking your time when balancing ionic half equations as they must be balanced for atoms and charge*
- *This is one of the more challenging equations that you are required to balance as it contains two different elements and electrons*
- *To balance the equation:*

  - *To balance oxygen atoms*
  
    - *Left:** OH⁻ = 1 oxygen atom*
    - *Right:** O*<sub>*2*</sub>* (2 O atoms) + 2H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O (2 O atoms) = **4 oxygen atoms*
    - *Place a 4 in front of OH*<sup>*-*</sup>
    - *The O atoms are balanced*
  - *Balance hydrogen atoms*
  
    - *Left:** 4OH⁻ = 4 H atoms*
    - *Right:** 2H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O = 4 H atoms*
    - *The H atoms are balanced*
  - *Balance charges with electrons*
  
    - *Left:** 4OH⁻ = −4 charge*
    - *Right:** All products are neutral, so net charge = 0*
    - *You need **4 electrons on the right** to match −4 on the left:*
  - *4OH⁻ → O*<sub>*2 *</sub>*+ 2H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O + 4e⁻*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A student set up the following electrolysis of copper(II) sulfate using graphite electrodes.

A student swapped the graphite electrodes for copper electrodes.

After some time, the mass of the cathode has increased by 0.10 g and the mass of the anode has decreased by 0.10 g.

i) Explain why the mass of the cathode increases during electrolysis.

ii) Copper is transferred from the anode to the cathode during electrolysis. Explain why the concentration of Cu²⁺ ions in the solution does not change.
parts.solutionMd:
i) The mass of the cathode increases during electrolysis because:

- Copper(II) ions (Cu²⁺) gain electrons at the cathode and are deposited as solid copper
**OR**
Cu²⁺ ions are reduced to copper atoms at the cathode)

ii) The concentration of Cu²⁺ ions in the solution does not change because:

- Copper atoms at the anode lose electrons and form Cu²⁺ ions, replacing the Cu²⁺ ions removed at the cathode
**OR**
The number of Cu²⁺ ions entering the solution equals the number leaving it

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *For part i) *

  - *Examiners often comment that students do not make the distinction between atoms and ions*
  - *In the electrolyte copper ions are present and when they are attracted to cathode they gain electrons and become atoms*

> *Cu*<sup>*2+*</sup>* (aq) + 2e*<sup>*-*</sup>* → Cu (s)*

- *For part ii)*

  - *If **inert electrodes** (like platinum or graphite) are used, copper is **not added** back into the solution at the anode*
  - *This means:*
  
    - *Cu*<sup>*2+*</sup>* ions are **removed** at the cathode*
    - *But **not replaced** at the anode*
    - *So the concentration of Cu*<sup>*2+*</sup>* **decreases over time*
    - *The concentration of the solution does not change only when the electrodes are made of copper*
- *Only with copper electrodes** is copper removed and replaced at equal rates, keeping the solution’s concentration unchanged.*

Zinc metal is made by the reduction of zinc oxide. The major ore of zinc is zinc blende, ZnS. Zinc blende contains silver and lead compounds as well as zinc sulfide. Zinc blende is converted into impure

[1]

[2]

[4]

iv) Describe how zinc metal can be obtained from zinc sulfate solution by electrolysis.

A labelled diagram is acceptable. Include all the products of this electrolysis. The electrolysis is similar to that of copper(II) sulfate solution with inert electrodes.

[4]
parts.solutionMd:
b)

i) Zinc oxide is reduced to zinc by:

- Heating  with carbon or coke or carbon monoxide;** [1 mark]**

ii)  A balanced symbol equation for zinc oxide and sulfuric acid is:

ZnO + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → ZnSO<sub>4</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O

- Correct reactants; **[1 mark]**
- Correct products; **[1 mark]**

iii) The addition of zinc powder produces pure zinc sulfate solution by:

- Zinc (not: ions) more reactive than silver and lead; **[1 mark]**
- Zinc displaces both metals / silver and lead produced / ions become atoms / zinc reduces silver ions and lead ions; **[1 mark]**
- (Silver and lead) can be removed by filtering / centrifugation / decanting; **[1 mark]**
- Zn + 2 Ag<sup>+</sup>→  Zn<sup>2+</sup> + 2Ag 
**OR** Zn + Pb<sup>2+</sup>  → Zn<sup>2+</sup> + Pb;** [1 mark]**

iv) The labelled apparatus is:

- Cathode labelled as carbon/zinc/ platinum; **[1 mark]**
- Zinc deposited at the cathode; **[1 mark]**
- Oxygen formed at anode; **[1 mark]**
- Electrolyte has remaining H<sup>+</sup> and SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup>; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *For part i)*

- *Make sure you state that heat is required, the reaction you describe must be feasible *
- *Many students forgot to mention heat so missed out on the mark*
- *Using **carbon or carbon monoxide** to reduce zinc oxide is useful because the only other product is **carbon dioxide gas**, which is easy to separate from the zinc metal.*
- *If a **more reactive metal** were used instead, zinc would still be produced, but it would be harder to separate  because a **solid metal oxide** would also form, making the process more complicated.*

> *For part ii)*

- *Make sure both sides of the equation have the **same number of atoms*
- *Remember that metal oxides react with acids to form a **salt** and **water*

> *For part iii)*

- *This part tests your knowledge of the reactivity series*
- *Zinc is **more reactive** than silver and lead.*
- *This means zinc will **displace silver and lead ions** from the solution.*
- *Write at least one **ionic equation** to show this:*

  - *Zn + 2Ag*<sup>*+*</sup>* → Zn²*<sup>*+*</sup>* + 2Ag*
  - *or **Zn + Pb²*<sup>*+*</sup>* → Zn²*<sup>*+*</sup>* + Pb*
- * These are **redox reactions**:*

  - *Zinc **loses electrons** (oxidised)*
  - *Silver/lead ions **gain electrons** (reduced)*
- *The **silver and lead metals form as solids**, which can be **filtered out**, leaving behind a **pure zinc sulfate solution*

> *For part iv)*

- *The question tells you that the electrolysis of zinc sulfate is similar to that of copper(II) sulfate solution and obtains zinc*
- *Copper(II) sulfate solution produces copper at the cathode and oxygen at the anode *
- *Therefore, zinc sulfate produces zinc at the cathode and oxygen at the anode *
- *The ions present were Zn*<sup>*2+*</sup>*, H*<sup>*+*</sup>*, SO*<sub>*4*</sub><sup>*2–*</sup>*, and OH*<sup>*–*</sup>

  - *Zn*<sup>*2+*</sup>* forms Zn*
  - *OH*<sup>*-*</sup>* forms O*<sub>*2*</sub>
  - *Therefore, the remaining ions in solution are H*<sup>*+*</sup>* and SO*<sub>*4*</sub><sup>*2–*</sup>

![45910fc9-4aea-431a-b96c-738742faed3c](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-chemistry-23/4-electrochemistry/4-1-electrolysis/assets/032-45910fc9-4aea-431a-b96c-738742faed3c.jpeg)

parts.problemMd:
The diagram below shows a fuel cell.

![fuel-cell](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-chemistry-23/4-electrochemistry/4-2-applications-of-electrolysis/assets/011-fuel-cell.png)

Hydrogen can be used as the fuel.

Complete the balanced symbol equation for the reaction that occurs in a hydrogen fuel cell.

___ H<sub>2</sub>   +   O<sub>2</sub>   →   ___ H<sub>2</sub>O
parts.solutionMd:
a) The balanced symbol equation is:

2H<sub>2</sub>   +   O<sub>2</sub>   →   2H<sub>2</sub>O

- 2H<sub>2</sub>   
**AND**
2H<sub>2</sub>O; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

- *To balance the equation, the same number of atoms of each element must be the same either side of the reaction*
- *Balance the oxygen atoms first, there are 2 oxygen atoms on the left-hand side of the unbalanced equation, but 1 on the right-hand side, to balance put a 2 in front of H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O:*

  - *H*<sub>*2*</sub>*   +   O*<sub>*2*</sub>*   →   **2**H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
- *Now there are 4 H atoms on the right, so to balance, put a 2 in front of H*<sub>*2*</sub>*:*

  - *2**H*<sub>*2*</sub>*   +   O*<sub>*2*</sub>*   →   2H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
- *Both numbers must be correct to gain the mark*

Cu<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> → Cu

Explain how this equation shows that copper is reduced.
parts.solutionMd:

parts.problemMd:
A fuel cell produces electrical energy by the oxidation of a fuel by oxygen. The fuel is usually hydrogen but methane and methanol are two other fuels which may be used. A diagram of a hydrogen fuel cell is given below.

![hydrogen-fuel-cell](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-chemistry-23/4-electrochemistry/4-2-applications-of-electrolysis/assets/014-hydrogen-fuel-cell.png)

parts.solutionMd:

- Carbon dioxide / CO<sub>2</sub>;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

parts.solutionMd:
d) The mass of water vapour produced when 500 cm<sup>3</sup> of hydrogen combusts in excess oxygen is:

- Moles of hydrogen = $\frac{500}{24000}=0.02083$ (mol); **[1 mark]**
- *M*<sub>r</sub> of water = 18; **[1 mark]**
- Mass of water = $0.02083 \times 18 = 0.375 ( \mathrm{g} )$;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *When asked to find the mass of a species in a reaction, you will be given enough information to calculate the moles of one reactant or product in the reaction*
- *You then need to use the stoichiometry of the reaction to find out the number of moles of the species asked about*
- *Then you can use this to find the mass*
- *You should be familiar with all of the equations that can be used to calculate moles*
- *In this case, you are dealing with gases, so you will need to use the equation involving molar gas volume to calculate the moles of hydrogen:*

  - *Volume (cm*<sup>*3*</sup>*) = moles x 24 000*
- *You need to work out the stoichiometry of the reaction: *

  - *2H*<sub>*2*</sub>* + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → 2H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
- *2 moles of hydrogen produces 2 moles of water, so 0.02803 moles of hydrogen produces 0.02803 moles of water*
- *To calculate the mass of water, use the equation*

  - *Mass = moles x molar mass*
- *The molar mass is the same value as the **M*<sub>*r*</sub>*, but has the units g / mol, so you need to calculate the **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of water to find the mass:*

  - *M*<sub>*r*</sub>* = (2 x 1) + 16 = 18*
- *Remember**: Show your working so that you can pick up marks, even if you make an error*

![4-2-4b-h-ring-dimensions](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-chemistry-23/4-electrochemistry/4-2-applications-of-electrolysis/assets/028-4-2-4b-h-ring-dimensions.png)

With wedding rings, electroplating to a depth of 8 microns (0.008 mm) is considered thick plating.

i) Calculate the cross-sectional area of:

- an average female, flat profile wedding ring.
- an average female, flat profile wedding ring with thick plating.

[2]

ii) Calculate the percentage of the ring that is plating.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
b)

i) The cross-sectional areas are:

- Average female, flat profile wedding ring = 2.8 (mm<sup>2</sup>); **[1 mark]**
- Average female, flat profile wedding ring with thick plating = 2.827 (mm<sup>2</sup>); **[1 mark]**

ii) The percentage of the ring that is plating is:

- 0.955% 
**OR **
0.96%; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *The width of an average female, flat profile wedding ring is 2 mm*
- *The depth of an average female, flat profile wedding ring is 1.4 mm*

  - *Therefore, the cross-sectional area of an average female, flat profile wedding ring is 2 x 1.4 = 2.8 mm*<sup>*2*</sup>*  *
- *The width of an average female, flat profile wedding ring with thick plating is 2.008 mm*
- *The depth of an average female, flat profile wedding ring with thick plating is 1.408 mm*

  - *Therefore, the cross-sectional area of an average female, flat profile wedding ring is 2.008 x 1.408 = 2.827264 mm*<sup>*2*</sup>*  *
- *This means that the plating accounts for 2.827264 - 2.8 = 0.027264 of the total ring with thick plating*

  - *Therefore, the percentage of an average female, flat profile wedding ring that is the plating is* $\frac{0.027264}{2.827264}\times100$ *= 0.96%*
