ii) The percentage of the ring that is plating is: 0.955% OR 0.96%

#### Extended Only

Most wedding rings contain between 4 and 6 g of metal. Wedding rings that are 18-carat gold are plated with gold that contains 750 parts per 1000 of gold.

Using your answer to part (b), calculate the number of moles of gold that is required to plate an average wedding ring with 18-carat gold.
parts.solutionMd:
c) The number of moles required to gold plate an average wedding ring is:

Calculations using 0.955% from part (b):

- Average mass of a wedding ring = 5 (g) **AND **Mass of gold = 0.0358(125) (g); **[1 mark]**
- Moles of gold = 1.82 x 10<sup>-4</sup>  
**OR **
0.000182; **[1 mark]**

Calculations using 0.96% from part (b):

- Average mass of a wedding ring = 5 (g) **AND **Mass of gold = 0.036 (g); **[1 mark]**
- Moles of gold = 1.83 x 10<sup>-4</sup>  
**OR **
0.000183; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *The mass of an average wedding ring is *$\frac{4+6}{2}$* = 5 g*
- *The mass of gold in an average wedding ring, assuming that the plating is 100% gold, is 0.955% (or your answer from part (b))*

  - *This gives a mass of* $\frac{5}{100}\times0.955$ *= 0.04775 g *
- *But 750 parts per 1000 or 75% of this mass is actually gold*

  - *This means that the actual mass of gold is* $\frac{0.04775}{100}\times75$ *= 0.0358125 g*
- *Remember:** Moles = *$\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{A_{r}}$

  - *Therefore, the number of moles of gold required is* $\frac{0.0358125}{197}$* = 1.82 x 10*<sup>*-4*</sup>* rounded to 2 decimal places*

parts.problemMd:
#### Extended Only

Tin-coated steel food cans and electrolytic chromium coated steel food cans that contain acidic foods can bulge as shown. The bulging is a result of a redox reaction inside the can forming a gas.

![4-2-5b-h-bulging-food-can](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-chemistry-23/4-electrochemistry/4-2-applications-of-electrolysis/assets/020-4-2-5b-h-bulging-food-can.png)

i) Give the ionic equation forming the gaseous product during the reaction between the metal food can and the acidic food.

[1]

ii) Explain how this shows that there is a break in the tin coating or chromium plating.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
b)

i) The ionic equation forming the gaseous product during the reaction between the metal food can and the acidic food is:

- 2H<sup>+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> → H<sub>2</sub>;** [1 mark]**

ii) This shows that there is a break in the tin coating or chromium plating because:

- Tin and chromium are relatively unreactive / low in the reactivity series; **[1 mark]**
- A break in the tin coating or chromium plating exposes the steel to the acidic food 
**AND **
Steel contains iron which reacts with acids; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *The reaction that is taking place inside the food can is:*

  - *Metal + acid → (metal) salt + hydrogen*
  - *Therefore, the ionic equation forming the gaseous product uses the hydrogen ions / H*<sup>*+*</sup>* from the acidic food to form hydrogen gas*
  
    - *H*<sup>*+*</sup>* → H*<sub>*2*</sub>* *
  - *You need two hydrogen ions to form a molecule of hydrogen*
  
    - *2H*<sup>*+*</sup>* → H*<sub>*2*</sub>* *
  - *You need two electrons to balance the 2+ charge on the left-hand side of the equation*
  
    - *2H*<sup>*+*</sup>* + 2e*<sup>*–*</sup>* → H*<sub>*2*</sub>* *
- *Food cans are coated / plated in tin or chromium because they are relatively unreactive metals*

  - *This means that they should not react with any acids within the food that they contain*
  - *It is the iron / steel underneath the tin / chromium that provides the electrons for the reaction to form hydrogen*

#### Separate: Chemistry and Extended Only

Use the bond energies to show that the following reaction is exothermic.

Bond energy is the amount of energy (kJ / mol) which must be supplied to break one mole of the bond.

![7-1-displayed-chlorination-of-methane-m5c-](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-chemistry-23/5-chemical-energetics/5-1-exothermic-and-endothermic-reactions/assets/058-7-1-displayed-chlorination-of-methane-m5c.png)

|   | Bond energies in kJ /mol |
|---|---|
| Cl–Cl | +242 |
| C–Cl | +338 |
| C–H | +412 |
| H–Cl | +431 |

bonds broken   energy in kJ /mol

......................        .............................

......................        .............................

total energy = .............................

bonds formed    energy in kJ /mol

......................        .............................

......................        .............................

total energy = .............................
parts.solutionMd:
c) To show that the reaction is exothermic:

- Bonds broken: 4 x C-H = 4 x 412 = 1648 kJ / mol 
**AND **
1 x Cl-Cl = 242 kJ / mol 
**AND **Total energy = 1648 + 242 = <u>1890</u> kJ / mol; **[1 mark]**
- Bonds formed: 3 x C-H = 3 x 412 = 1236kJ / mol 
**AND **
1 x C-Cl = 338 kJ / mol 
**AND** 
1 x H-Cl = 431 
**AND **
Total energy = 1236 + 338 + 431 = <u>2005</u> kJ / mol; **[1 mark]**
- Energy change = 1890 - 2005 = <u>–115</u> kJ / mol; **[1 mark]**
- The negative sign shows that the reaction is exothermic; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *This question is a straightforward application of the energy change = energy in - energy out equation*

  - *This can also be shown as energy change = bonds broken - bonds formed*
- *The little twist of this question is that you are told that the reaction is exothermic and have to prove this is the case*

  - *This means that you should be getting a negative value for your final answer*
  - *The final mark for saying about the negative value showing that the reaction is exothermic is missed by many students, presumably because they assume it is known / obvious*
- *Careful: **Make sure that you include all of the bonds in your calculation*

  - *If it helps, you can tick them off as you add them up*

parts.problemMd:
#### Separate: Chemistry and Extended Only

Bond breaking is an endothermic change and bond forming is an exothermic change.

Bond energy is the amount of energy in kJ / mol needed to break one mole of the specified bond.

![7-1-displayed-reaction-of-chlorpropane-m2b-](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-chemistry-23/5-chemical-energetics/5-1-exothermic-and-endothermic-reactions/assets/061-7-1-displayed-reaction-of-chlorpropane-m2b.png)

Use the following bond energies to determine whether this reaction is exothermic or endothermic. You must show your reasoning.

| bond | bond energies in kJ / mol |
|---|---|
| C-Cl | 338 |
| C-H | 412 |
| Cl-Cl | 242 |
| H-Cl | 431 |
| C-C | 348 |
parts.solutionMd:
b) To determine if the reaction is exothermic or endothermic:

- Bonds broken: (8 x C-H) + (2 x C-C) + (Cl-Cl) = (8 x 412) + (2 x 348) + 242 = 4234 (kJ / mol); **[1 mark]**
- Bonds formed: (7 x C-H) + (2 x C-C) + (C-Cl) + (H-Cl) = (7 x 412) + (2 x 348) + 338 + 431 = 4349 (kJ / mol); **[1 mark]**
- 4234 - 4349 = -115 (kJ / mol) 
**AND **
The reaction is exothermic; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *Remember: **The overall energy / enthalpy change for the reaction is based on the calculation of energy in - energy out*

  - *This can sometimes be shown as bonds broken - bonds formed*
- *Careful: **The most common mistake in this type of calculation is to miss one of the bonds so it is worth ticking the bonds off on the equation to ensure you don't miss any*
- *When these questions are for 3 marks, you will find:*

  - *1 mark for the bonds broken / energy in*
  - *1 mark for the bonds formed / energy out*
  - *1 mark for the final answer and conclusion of exothermic or endothermic*
  - *Remember: **Exothermic reactions will have a negative value and endothermic reactions will have a positive value*

parts.problemMd:
#### Separate: Chemistry and Extended Only

i) Chloropropane can be hydrolysed to propanol, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH, by sodium hydroxide.

Write the equation for this reaction.

[2]

ii) Propanol can be dehydrated. It loses a water molecule to form a hydrocarbon.

Give the name and structural formula of this hydrocarbon.

name .................................................

structural formula

[2]

iii) Propanol is oxidised to a carboxylic acid by acidified potassium manganate(VII).

Deduce the name of this acid.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
c)

i) The equation for the hydrolysis of chloropropane to propanol, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH, by sodium hydroxide is:

CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Cl + NaOH → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH + NaCl

- Correct identification of NaCl as product; **[1 mark]**
- Remainder of chemical equation correct; **[1 mark]**

ii) The name and structural formula of this hydrocarbon are:

- Name: Propene; **[1 mark]**
- Structural formula: CH<sub>2</sub>=CHCH<sub>3</sub> **OR** CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CH<sub>2</sub>; **[1 mark]**

iii) The name of the acid formed when propanol is oxidised by acidified potassium manganate(VII) is:

- Propanoic acid; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

- *The question for part (i) gives you most of the information that you require to write the chemical equation*

  - *"chloropropane **(reactant)** to propanol, CH*<sub>*3*</sub>*CH*<sub>*2*</sub>*CH*<sub>*2*</sub>*OH **(product)**, by sodium hydroxide **(reactant)**"*
  - *Chloropropane + sodium hydroxide → propanol + ?*
  - *CH*<sub>*3*</sub>*CH*<sub>*2*</sub>*CH*<sub>*2*</sub>*Cl + NaOH → CH*<sub>*3*</sub>*CH*<sub>*2*</sub>*CH*<sub>*2*</sub>*OH + ?*
  - *By looking at the atoms on either side, you should be able to see that Na and Cl have not been used*
  - *This would make common salt*
  - *CH*<sub>*3*</sub>*CH*<sub>*2*</sub>*CH*<sub>*2*</sub>*Cl + NaOH → CH*<sub>*3*</sub>*CH*<sub>*2*</sub>*CH*<sub>*2*</sub>*OH + NaCl*
- *In part (ii) you are told that propanol is dehydrated / loses a water molecule*

  - *Propanol: CH*<sub>*3*</sub>*CH*<sub>*2*</sub>*CH*<sub>*2*</sub>*OH *
  - *Water: H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O or H-OH*
  - *Careful: **Do not remove the H and OH from the same carbon of propanol, they are removed from neighbouring carbons*
  - *Incomplete product: CH*<sub>*3*</sub>*CHCH*<sub>*2*</sub>* *
  - *The bonding is then adjusted to make the molecule complete with all hydrogens having one bond and all carbons having 4 bonds*
  - *Complete product: CH*<sub>*3*</sub>*-CH=CH*<sub>*2*</sub>* *
- *In part (iii), you are told that propanol is being oxidised to form a carboxylic acid*

  - *This means that the acid must be propane-based, just like propanol*
  - *Therefore, the carboxylic acid is propanoic acid*

parts.problemMd:
#### Extended Only

Propanol reacts with methanoic acid to form the ester propyl methanoate.

CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH + HCOOH → HCOOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O

4.0 g of methanoic acid was reacted with 6.0 g of propanol.

i) Calculate the *M*<sub>r</sub> of methanoic acid = ........................................

[1]

ii) Calculate the *M*<sub>r</sub> of propanol = ........................................

[1]

iii) Determine which one is the limiting reagent. Show your reasoning.

[2]

iv) Calculate the maximum yield in grams of propyl methanoate, *M*<sub>r</sub> = 88.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
d) CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH + HCOOH → HCOOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O

i) The *M*<sub>r</sub> of methanoic acid is:

- H + C + O + O + H = 1 + 12 + 16 + 16 + 1 = <u>46</u>; **[1 mark]**

ii) The *M*<sub>r</sub> of propanol is

- C + (3 x H) + C + (2 x H) + C + (2 x H) + O + H = 12 + 3 + 12 + 2 + 12 + 2 + 16 + 1 = <u>60</u>; **[1 mark]**

iii) To determine the limiting reagent:

- Moles of propanol = $=\frac{6.0}{60}=$0.1; **[1 mark]**
- Moles of methanoic acid $=\frac{4.0}{46}=$0.087 
**AND **
The limiting reagent is methanoic acid; **[1 mark]**

iv) The maximum yield in grams of propyl methanoate is:

- 88 x 0.087 = <u>7.65</u> (g); **[1 mark]** 
*Allow error carried forward from part (iii) using the lowest number of moles, i.e. 88 x lowest number of moles*

**[Total: 5 marks]**

- *To calculate the **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of a chemical, add up all of the atomic masses for **ALL** of the atoms in the chemical*

  - *Careful: **Make sure that you don't miss any atoms as this will lead to an incorrect answer*
- *Remember: **In this reaction, the limiting reagent is the reactant with the fewest number of moles involved in the reaction as the reactants react in a 1:1 ratio*

  - *For this question, you calculate the number of moles using the equation moles = *$\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{M_{r}}$
- *The limiting reagent will determine the maximum amount of a product that can be formed*

  - *This is because once the limiting reagent is used up, you cannot form any more product*
- *The **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of propyl methanoate, HCOOCH*<sub>*2*</sub>*CH*<sub>*2*</sub>*CH*<sub>*3*</sub>*, is 88 g / mol*

  - *The chemical equation shows that there is a 1 : 1 ratio between the either reactant and the propyl methanoate product*
  - *Therefore, the maximum yield will be the **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of propyl methanoate multiplied by the number of moles of limiting reagent, e.g. 88 x 0.087 = 7.65 g*

Iodine reacts with chlorine to form dark brown iodine monochloride. I~2~ + Cl~2~ → 2ICl. This reacts with more chlorine to give yellow iodine trichloride. An equilibrium forms between these iodine chlorides. ICl (l) + Cl~2~ (g) ⇌ ICl~3~ (s); ICl (l) is dark brown, ICl~3~ (s) is yellow.

reason ................................................

• number of moles of NaNO<sub>3</sub> used,

.................................. mol

• number of moles of O<sub>2</sub> formed,

parts.solutionMd:

- Number of moles of O<sub>2</sub> formed:

  - $\frac{0.04}{2}$ = 0.02 moles; **[1 mark]**
- Volume of O<sub>2</sub> formed, in dm<sup>3</sup>:

  - 0.02 x 24 = 0.48 dm<sup>3</sup>; **[1 mark]**

- *To calculate the number of moles of NaNO*<sub>*3*</sub>*, you first have to calculate the **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of NaNO*<sub>*3*</sub>

  - *23 + 14 + (16 x 3) = 85*

- *From the overall chemical equation, there is a ratio of 2 NaNO*<sub>*3*</sub>* to 1 O*<sub>*2*</sub>
- *Therefore, there are half the number of moles of oxygen, i.e.  *$\frac{0.04}{2}$*= 0.02 moles*
- *You then use the number of moles of oxygen to calculate the volume of oxygen, using the relationship that 1 mole of any gas occupies 24 dm*<sup>*3*</sup>* at room temperature and pressure*

parts.problemMd:
#### Separate: Chemistry and Extended Only

Sulfur tetrafluoride, SF<sub>4</sub>, can be made by combining gaseous sulfur with fluorine.

i) Complete the energy level diagram for this reaction. Include an arrow which clearly shows the energy change during the reaction.

![7-1-chemical-energetics-m1f-energy-profile](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-chemistry-23/5-chemical-energetics/5-1-exothermic-and-endothermic-reactions/assets/050-7-1-chemical-energetics-m1f-energy-profile.png)

[3]

ii) During the reaction the amount of energy given out is 780 kJ / mol.

The F–F bond energy is 160 kJ / mol.

Use this information to determine the bond energy, in kJ / mol, of one S–F bond in SF<sub>4</sub>

![7-1-chemical-energetics-m1f-bonds](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-chemistry-23/5-chemical-energetics/5-1-exothermic-and-endothermic-reactions/assets/051-7-1-chemical-energetics-m1f-bonds.png)

.................................. kJ / mol [3]
parts.solutionMd:
f)

i) The completed energy level diagram is:

![sf4-energy-profile](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-chemistry-23/5-chemical-energetics/5-1-exothermic-and-endothermic-reactions/assets/052-sf4-energy-profile.png)

- (Horizontal) energy level line for products <u>below</u> the level of the reactants; **[1 mark]**
- SF<sub>4</sub> (g) labelled on the energy level line for the products; **[1 mark]**
- Correct arrow pointing downwards from the reactants to the products; **[1 mark]**

ii) The bond energy of one S-F bond is:

- Bond energy of 2F<sub>2</sub> = 2 x 160 = 320 (kJ / mol); **[1 mark]**
- Bond energy of all bonds in SF<sub>4</sub> = 780 + 320 = 1100 (kJ / mol); **[1 mark]**
- Bond energy of one bond in SF<sub>4</sub> = $\frac{1100}{4}$ = 275; (kJ / mol); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

- *The question tells you that the reaction is exothermic*

  - *This means that heat energy is given out *
  - *Therefore, the products should be at a lower energy level than the reactants*
- *The question also gives you the formulae and states of the reactants in the chemical equation as well as the reactants including state symbols in the energy level diagram*

  - *Therefore, you should write the products with its state symbol on the products line*
- *The energy change that you are being asked to draw is from the reactants to the products*

  - *Many incorrect answers will include an activation energy "hump" going up from the reactants, reaching a peak and then dropping to the products - this is **not** what the question asks for *
- *The calculation is a little more complex than usual as the sulfur reactant does not have a bond energy associated with it because it is elemental with no bonds *

  - *You can work out the total bond energy for the 2 fluorine molecules*
  - *You then add this to the overall energy given out to calculate the total energy of the reactants*
  - *This is the value for all 4 S-F bonds, which means that you have to divide that answer by 4 to get the individual bond energy for an S-F bond*

parts.problemMd:
#### Extended Only

Chemical reactions are always accompanied by an energy change.

Aluminium is extracted by the electrolysis of a molten mixture which contains aluminium oxide, Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>. This decomposes to form aluminium at the negative electrode and oxygen at the positive electrode.

i) Write an ionic equation for the reaction at the negative electrode.

[2]

ii) Complete the ionic equation for the reaction at the positive electrode.

2O<sup>2–</sup> → ....... + .......

[2]

iii) Is the reaction exothermic or endothermic? Explain your answer.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
a)

i) The ionic equation for the reaction at the negative electrode is:

Al<sup>3+</sup> + 3e<sup>–</sup> → Al

- Al<sup>3+</sup>; **[1 mark]**
- Remainder of the ionic equation;** [1 mark]**

ii) The ionic equation for the reaction at the positive electrode is:

2O<sup>2–</sup> → O<sub>2</sub> + 4e<sup>–</sup>  **   **
**OR **   
2O<sup>2–</sup> - 4e<sup>–</sup> → O<sub>2</sub>

- Correct products, i.e. O<sub>2</sub> with / without e<sup>–</sup> dependent on the equation given; **[1 mark]**
- Correct balancing, i.e 4e<sup>–</sup>; **[1 mark]**

iii) The reaction is:

- Endothermic 
**AND **
Because (electrical) energy is supplied / given / taken in; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

- *The reaction at the negative electrode will involve the positive ion because opposites attract *

  - *The aluminium ion is 3+ since aluminium is in group 3*
  - *This means that it will gain 3 electrons to form aluminium*
- * At the positive electrode, the oxide ions will lose electrons to form oxygen gas, O*<sub>*2*</sub>* *

  - *Since there are two oxide ions with a 2- charge, there will be four electrons lost*
- *Although the terms exothermic and endothermic commonly talk about heat energy, the principle can be applied to electrical energy as well*

  - *Since electrical energy is being supplied, the reaction must be endothermic*

parts.problemMd:
#### Separate: Chemistry and Extended Only

The balanced equation for the combustion of ethene is

C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub> (g) + 3O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2CO<sub>2</sub> (g) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

| **Bond** | **Bond energy (kJ / mol) ** |
|---|---|
| C=C | 614 |
| C-H | 414 |
| O-H | 463 |
| C=O | 804 |
| O=O | 498 |

Use the information in the table to calculate the following:

i) Energy required to break the bonds

[1]

ii) Energy released when bonds are made

[1]

iii) Energy change for the reaction

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
a)

i) Energy required to break the bonds

4 x E (C-H) = 4 x 414 = 1656

1 x E (C=C) = 1 x 614 = 614

3 x E (O=O) = 3 x 498  = 1494

- Total = 3764 (kJ / mol); **[1 mark]**

ii) Energy released when bonds are made

4 x E (C=O) = 4 x 804  = 3216

4 x E (O-H) = 4 x 463  = 1852

- Total = 5068 (kJ / mol); **[1 mark]**

iii) Energy change:

- Energy change =  3764 - 5068 = -1304 (kJ / mol); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks] **

- *To work out the energy change you can use*
- *Energy change = sum of bonds broken - sum of bonds made*
- *You may find it easier to draw out the structures of the reactants and products so you can identify all the bonds broken and formed* ![076e1308-5483-4760-b837-bfa8ccbac2db](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-chemistry-23/5-chemical-energetics/5-1-exothermic-and-endothermic-reactions/assets/046-076e1308-5483-4760-b837-bfa8ccbac2db.jpeg)

parts.problemMd:
#### Separate: Chemistry and Extended Only

The forward reaction for the production of ethanol from ethene is shown below.

** C**<sub>**2**</sub>**H**<sub>**4**</sub>** (g) + H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O (g) **$\rightleftharpoons$** CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**CH**<sub>**2**</sub>**OH (g)   **$\Delta$*H* = -45 kJ / mol

In terms of temperature and pressure, explain which conditions would give an economically viable yield.
parts.solutionMd:
c) The conditions that would give an economically viable yield are:

- The forward reaction is exothermic so it is favoured by low temperatures; **[1 mark] **
- There are more molecules of gas on left-hand side so the forward reaction is favoured by high pressure; **[1 mark] **
- The rate is slowed by low temperature 
**AND **
So, the temperature is increased (to 300 °C); **[1 mark] **
- High pressure is unsafe / expensive / could result in polymerisation of ethene 
**AND **
So, the pressure is reduced; **[1 mark] **
- Addition of a catalyst;** [1 mark] **

**[Total: 5 marks]**

- *This question asks for the conditions to give an 'economically viable' yield which does not necessarily mean as high a yield as possible*
- *A high yield will be favoured by a low temperature and high pressure *
- *The issue with a low temperature is that the rate of reaction would be very slow, so even though there would be a high percentage yield formed it would take too long*
- *A manufacturer is trying to produce as much ethanol as possible per day*

  - *It makes no sense to try to achieve an equilibrium mixture which contains a very high proportion of ethanol if it takes several years for the reaction to reach that equilibrium*
- *The issue with high pressure is that it is expensive to maintain and also potentially unsafe*

  - *In this reaction, high pressure could also form poly(ethene) as well*
- *A catalyst will speed up the reaction in both directions*

  - *They are economic to use as they can be used again*

parts.problemMd:
#### Separate: Chemistry and Extended Only

The table below has some enthalpy data for a different chemical reaction. Hydrazine, N<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4 </sub>can react with hydrogen peroxide in an exothermic reaction, as shown below.

N<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> → N<sub>2</sub> + 4H<sub>2</sub>O   Δ*H* = -789 kJ / mol

| **Bond** | **Bond Energy kJ / mol** |
|---|---|
| N-N | +158 |
| N$\equiv$N | +945 |
| O-H | +463 |
| O-O | +144 |

The structures of the reactants and products are shown.

![5-1-5a-h-hydrazine-reaction-figure-5-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-chemistry-23/5-chemical-energetics/5-1-exothermic-and-endothermic-reactions/assets/037-5-1-5a-h-hydrazine-reaction-figure-5-1.png)

Using the reaction equation and the data in the table above, calculate the value of the N-H bond in hydrazine.

Bond energy of N-H bond = .......... kJ / mol
parts.solutionMd:
d) To calculate the bond enthalpy of the N-H bond:

- Energy change = sum of bonds broken - sum of bonds made; **[1 mark]**
- -789 = [(4 x N-H) + (1 x 158) + (4 x 463) + (2 x 144)] - [(1 x 945) + (8 x 463)]** **
**OR** 
4 x N-H = -789 - [(1 x 158) + (4 x 463) + (2 x 144)] + [(1 x 945) + (8 x 463)]; **[1 mark]**
- 4 x N-H = -789 - 2298 + 4649; **[1 mark]**
- N-H bond enthalpy = 1562 ÷ 4 = (+)391 (kJ / mol); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *This bond energy calculation is very challenging however if you set out the question step by step you can gain 3 out of 4 marks just by showing logical working*
- *Careful:** A lot of students lose the last mark in this question because they forget that there are 4 N-H bonds in hydrazine, so the final answer needs to be divided by 4 to get the individual bond enthalpy for each N-H bond *
- *Remember: **Always write out the equation - often you can gain a mark for this *

A student used this method to investigate the effect of changing the concentration of the sodium thiosulfate solution on the speed of the reaction. The student used different concentrations of sodium thiosulfate solution. All other variables were kept the same.

parts.problemMd:
A catalyst is a substance that speeds up the rate of a chemical reaction and remains unchanged at the end of the reaction. Hydrogen peroxide solution, H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, breaks down to form oxygen. This decomposition is very slow if a catalyst is not used.

Plan an investigation to show that copper(II) oxide is a suitable catalyst for this reaction.

You can use aqueous hydrogen peroxide and common laboratory apparatus.

Step 1 Show that copper(II) oxide catalyses the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide and measure the rate of the reaction.

Step 2 Show that the copper(II) oxide is unchanged at the end of the decomposition.
parts.solutionMd:
An investigation to show that copper(II) oxide is a suitable catalyst for this reaction is:

Step 1: Proving catalysis & measuring the rate

Any **five** from: (1 mark per point and 5 marks maximum)

- Measure a specific volume of hydrogen peroxide solution using a measuring cylinder / pipette / burette; **[1 mark]**
- Weigh a specific mass of copper(II) oxide using a balance / electronic balance; **[1 mark]**
- Place the hydrogen peroxide in a conical flask and connect it to a gas syringe / an inverted measuring cylinder over a trough of water; **[1 mark]**
- Start a stopwatch/timer and measure the volume of gas collected at regular intervals / measure the time taken to collect a specific volume of gas; **[1 mark]**
- Test the gas produced using a glowing splint which relights to confirm the gas is oxygen; **[1 mark]**
- Describe running a control experiment under identical conditions without copper(II) oxide to show that little or no gas is produced; **[1 mark]**

Step 2: Showing the catalyst is chemically unchanged

- Filter the mixture at the end of the reaction to collect the copper(II) oxide as the residue; **[1 mark]**
- Wash the residue with distilled water 
**AND **
Dry the solid to constant mass between filter papers / in a warm place / in a drying oven; **[1 mark]**
- Reweigh the dry residue to show that the final mass is identical to the starting mass (and remains a black powder; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 8 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Use precise measurement language: "volume" for liquids and "mass" for solids. Writing "amount" for either may lose you the mark.
> 
> You must include a control experiment (hydrogen peroxide without copper(II) oxide) to prove the catalyst made a difference. Without this comparison, you have not shown catalysis.
> 
> Measure the volume of gas produced at regular time intervals, not just the total time for the reaction to finish.
> 
> Do not forget the glowing splint test to confirm the gas is oxygen.
> 
> For Step 2, you must describe a practical method: filter, wash, dry, and reweigh. Simply stating the catalyst is "unchanged" or describing its appearance earns no marks.
> 
> Wash and dry the filtered copper(II) oxide before reweighing. Wet residue will weigh more than the original mass and will not prove the catalyst is unchanged.

parts.solutionMd:
i)

- The initial rate is the gradient from the tangent when t = 0 min

  - A tangent is a line that touches the curve at a single point
  
    - The tangent must be slightly above the second point of your graph to mimic the initial rate of change
  - The gradient of the tangent indicates the instantaneous rate of change at that exact point
- The first step is drawing the tangent at t = 0, as shown in the diagram below

![Graph of mass loss (g) against time (min), 0–10 min.

Points plotted: (0.0, 0.00), (0.5, 0.32), (1.0, 0.58), (1.5, 0.79), (2.0, 0.97), (2.5, 1.12), (3.0, 1.25), (3.5, 1.36), (4.0, 1.46), (4.5, 1.54), (5.0, 1.61), (5.5, 1.67), (6.0, 1.72), (6.5, 1.76), (7.0, 1.79), (7.5, 1.81), (8.0, 1.82), (8.5, 1.83), (9.0, 1.83), (9.5, 1.83), (10.0, 1.83).

 A straight tangent is drawn at the start of the curve, passing through (0, 0) and marked point (2, 1.25).](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-chemistry-23/6-chemical-reactions/6-1-chemical-change-and-rate-of-reaction/assets/003-graph-of-mass-loss-g-against-time-min-0-10-min-p.png)

$\text{gradient} = \frac{change \text{in} \mathrm{y} }{change \text{in} \mathrm{x} } = \frac{( 1.25 \mathrm{g} - 0.00 \mathrm{g} ) }{( 2 \min - 0 \min ) }$

$\mathrm{gradient}=0.63\frac{g}{\mathrm{min}}$

**[1 mark]**

- The initial rate of reaction is **0.63 g/min ****[1 mark]**

> 1 mark is awarded for drawing a correct tangent at t = 0
> 
> - The line must touch the curve at that point and not cut across it
> 
> 1 mark is awarded for correctly calculating the gradient of the tangent.
> 
> - Use: **gradient = change in y ÷ change in x**
> - Show clear working using two points on your tangent
> 
> 1 mark is awarded for giving the final answer with correct units
> 
> - Missing units will lose this mark
> - A negative answer will lose this mark** **
> 
> Accept values between 0.53 g/min and 0.73  g/min

> **[exam-tip]**
> Each step earns a separate mark, so clear method and correct units can still make you gain marks even if the final value is slightly inaccurate.

ii)

The rate of reaction of iron with sulfuric acid can be determined by measuring the time taken to produce 20cm^3 of hydrogen.

In each experiment the student used:
- 1g of iron powder
- the same temperature
- the same volume of sulfuric acid.

Describe the effect of each of the following on the rate of this reaction with 0.5 mol / dm<sup>3</sup> of sulfuric acid.

- Larger pieces of iron are used. All other conditions stay the same. ...................................................................................................................
- The temperature is increased. All other conditions stay the same. ...................................................................................................................
parts.solutionMd:
b) The effect of each of the following on the rate of this reaction with 0.5 mol / dm<sup>3</sup> of sulfuric acid is:

- Larger pieces: decreases rate; **[1 mark]**
- Increasing temperature: increases rate; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *Using larger pieces of iron means you are decreasing the surface area of the iron *

  - *A smaller surface area results in the frequency of successful collisions decreasing and as a result a slower rate of reaction *
- *Increasing the temperature increases the frequency of successful collisions as a greater proportion will have the activation energy*

parts.problemMd:
Sulfur dioxide is a pollutant in the air.

Sulfur dioxide is oxidised to sulfur trioxide in the air. Oxides of nitrogen act as catalysts for this reaction.

What is meant by the term catalyst?
parts.solutionMd:
A catalyst is a :

- Substance which speeds up a reaction / substance which increases the rate of reaction; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

- *This question can be 1 or 2 marks *
- *If the question is 1 mark the answer is that it speeds up the rate of reaction *
- *If the question is 2 marks your second point can be achieved by saying one of the following:*

  - *A catalyst is not used up *
  - *It provides an alternative pathway for the reaction*
  - *It lowers the activation energy *

parts.solutionMd:

parts.problemMd:
#### Separate: Chemistry and Extended Only

A length of magnesium ribbon was added to 50 cm<sup>3</sup> of sulfuric acid, concentration 1.0 mol/dm<sup>3</sup>. The time taken for the magnesium to react was measured. The experiment was repeated with the same volume of different acids. In all these experiments, the acid was in excess and the same length of magnesium ribbon was used.

| Experiment | Acid | Concentration in mol/dm<sup>3</sup> | Time / s |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | sulfuric acid | 1.0 | 20 |
| B | propanoic acid | 0.5 | 230 |
| C | hydrochloric acid | 1.0 | 40 |
| D | hydrochloric acid | 0.5 | 80 |

i) Write these experiments in order of reaction speed. Give the experiment with the fastest speed first.

[1]

ii) Give reasons for the order you have given in (i).

[5]
parts.solutionMd:
a)

i) The order of reaction speed is:

- A C D B; **[1 mark] **

ii) Reasons for the order are:

Any **five** of the following:

- Speed (or rate) increases as concentration increases / time decreases as concentration increases; **[1 mark]**
- Rate or speed or time depends on (concentration) of H<sup>+</sup> or hydrogen ions;** [1 mark]**
- B is slow because propanoic acid is weak or doesn’t dissociate or weakly ionises; 
**OR** 
B is slow because HCl and H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> are stronger or ionise or dissociate more than propanoic; **[1 mark]**
- D slower than C because C is more concentrated than D / OR A; **[1 mark]**
- A is fast because H<sup>+</sup> concentration high (note: this would also score second mark if not already awarded) / H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is diprotic or dibasic or 2H<sup>+</sup> ; **[1 mark]**
- Time is inversely proportional to rate / owtte / OR A; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks] **

- *The higher the concentration of hydrogen ions, the faster the rate of reaction*
- *This is why stronger acids such as hydrochloric acid react faster than weak acids, such as propanoic acid*
- *Strong acids fully ionise, weak acids only partially ionise *

  - *HCl → H*<sup>*+*</sup>* + Cl*<sup>*+*</sup>
  - *CH*<sub>*3*</sub>*CH*<sub>*2*</sub>*COOH  *$\rightleftharpoons$* CH*<sub>*3*</sub>*CH*<sub>*2*</sub>*COO*<sup>*– *</sup>*+ H*<sup>*+*</sup>

manganese(II) oxide + hydrochloric acid → .....................  ..................... + .....................

parts.solutionMd:

manganese(II) oxide + hydrochloric acid → **manganese chloride** + **water**

- Manganese chloride; **[1 mark]**
- Water;** [1 mark]**

- Manganese(III) oxide

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Aqueous hydrogen peroxide decomposes to form water and oxygen.

2H~2~O~2 ~(aq) → 2H~2~O (l) + O~2 ~(g)

This reaction is catalysed by manganese(IV) oxide. The following experiments were carried out to investigate the rate of this reaction. A 0.1 g sample of manganese(IV) oxide was added to 20 cm^3^ of 0.2 mol / dm^3^ hydrogen peroxide solution. The volume of oxygen produced was measured every minute. The results of this experiment are shown on the graph.

i) How does the rate of reaction vary with time? Explain why the rate varies.

ii) The following experiment was carried out at the same temperature. 0.1 g of manganese(IV) oxide and 20 cm^3^ of 0.4 mol / dm^3^ hydrogen peroxide. Sketch the curve for this experiment on the same grid.

iii) How would the shape of the graph differ if only half the mass of catalyst had been used in these experiments?

Aqueous hydrogen peroxide decomposes to form water and oxygen.

2H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2 </sub>(aq) → 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + O<sub>2 </sub>(g)

This reaction is catalysed by manganese(IV) oxide. The following experiments were carried out to investigate the rate of this reaction. A 0.1 g sample of manganese(IV) oxide was added to 20 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.2 mol / dm<sup>3</sup> hydrogen peroxide solution. The volume of oxygen produced was measured every minute. The results of this experiment are shown on the graph.

![graph-o2-vs-time](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-chemistry-23/6-chemical-reactions/6-1-chemical-change-and-rate-of-reaction/assets/134-graph-o2-vs-time.png)

i) How does the rate of reaction vary with time? Explain why the rate varies.

[3]

ii) The following experiment was carried out at the same temperature. 0.1 g of manganese(IV) oxide and 20 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.4 mol / dm<sup>3</sup> hydrogen peroxide. Sketch the curve for this experiment on the same grid.

[2]

iii) How would the shape of the graph differ if only half the mass of catalyst had been used in these experiments?

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
c)

i) The way the rate of reaction varies with time is:

- The rate decreases 
**OR **
Becomes zero; **[1 mark]** *Do NOT accept rate increases then decreases*
- (Because) the concentration decreases;** [1 mark]** *This mark is conditional on the 1st mark being awarded*
- Hydrogen peroxide used up ONLY; **[1 mark]**

ii) The curve for the experiment would be:

![graph-o2-vs-time-answer](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-chemistry-23/6-chemical-reactions/6-1-chemical-change-and-rate-of-reaction/assets/135-graph-o2-vs-time-answer.png)

- Steeper initial gradient; **[1 mark]**
- Double final volume; **[1 mark]**

iii) The shape of the graph would differ if only half the mass of catalyst had been used in these experiments by:

- The initial gradient is less; **[1 mark]**
- The final volume is the same; **[1 mark]** 
*Answer must relate to shape of graph*

**[Total: 7 marks]**

- *Part (i) asks you to describe the graph and then go into detail about why the shape of the graph changes*

  - *Description = As the reaction progresses, the rate (volume of oxygen produced over time) decreases until it reaches zero*
  - *Explanation = As the reaction progresses, there are less hydrogen peroxide particles to react, i.e. the concentration is decreasing*
- *Part (ii) uses a concentration of hydrogen perosixde that is double the original*

  - *Therefore, it contains twice the number of particles and will be able to produce twice the volume of oxygen*
- *Part (iii) is using the same volume / concentration of hydrogen peroxide so it will produce the same volume of oxygen*

  - *A catalyst speeds up the rate of reaction*
  - *Using less catalyst means that the reaction will continue to same final volume of oxygen but be slower*
  - *This would be shown by having a gradient that is shallower / less steep*

parts.problemMd:
The equation for the reaction between sodium thiosulfate and hydrochloric acid is given below.

Na<sub>2</sub>S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> (aq) + 2HCl (aq) → 2NaCl (aq) + S (s) + SO<sub>2</sub> (g) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

The speed of this reaction was investigated using the following experiment. A beaker containing 50 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.2 mol/dm<sup>3</sup> sodium thiosulfate was placed on a black cross.

5.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of 2.0 mol/dm<sup>3</sup> hydrochloric acid was added and the clock was started.

![cie-igcse-sq-6-1-cross-reaction](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-chemistry-23/6-chemical-reactions/6-1-chemical-change-and-rate-of-reaction/assets/154-cie-igcse-sq-6-1-cross-reaction.png)

Initially, the cross was clearly visible. When the solution became cloudy and the cross could no longer be seen, the clock was stopped and the time recorded.

The experiment was repeated with 25 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.2 mol/dm<sup>3</sup> sodium thiosulfate and 25 cm<sup>3</sup> of water. Typical results for this experiment and a further two experiments are given in the table.

![thiosulfate-table](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-chemistry-23/6-chemical-reactions/6-1-chemical-change-and-rate-of-reaction/assets/155-thiosulfate-table.png)

i) Explain why it is necessary to keep the total volume the same in all the experiments.

[2]

ii) Complete the table.

[1]

iii) How and why does the speed of the reaction vary from experiment 1 to 4?

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
a)

i) It is necessary to keep the total volume the same in all the experiments as:

- The concentration of thiosulfate is proportional to the volume of thiosulfate solution added; **[1 mark]**
- The concentration of acid is always the same as the total volume is the same in all experiments; **[1 mark] ***For comments based on amount / to make experiments fair / comparable allow 1 mark*

ii) The value needed to complete the table is:

- 240 s;** [1 mark]**

iii) The speed of the reaction varies from experiment 1 to 4 as:

- It decreases / the reaction gets slower; **[1 mark]**
- Because the concentration of thiosulfate decreases; **[1 mark]**
- Frequency / chances / rate of collisions decreases;** [1 mark] ***Allow one mark can be scored for less / smaller amount / smaller volume of thiosulfate / fewer collisions*

**[Total: 6 marks]**

- *This reaction is known as the disappearing cross, and the measurement of rate comes from the time it takes for the cross to disappear as solid sulfur forms and means that the solution gradually clouds over*
- *The reaction has not stopped at the point that the timer is stopped, but the same mass of sulfur should have formed in each experiment, meaning that the same number of moles should have reacted, making the results comparable*
- *All of the usual rules around concentration and frequency of collisions still apply*
- *Experiment 4 takes 240 seconds because the concentration of thiosulfate is four times less than in experiment 2, so it will take 4 times as long: 4 x 60 = 240 s*

parts.problemMd:
The rate of the reaction between iron and aqueous bromine can be investigated using the apparatus shown below.

![cie-igcse-sq-6-1-mass-reaction-diagram-](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-chemistry-23/6-chemical-reactions/6-1-chemical-change-and-rate-of-reaction/assets/152-cie-igcse-sq-6-1-mass-reaction-diagram.png)

A piece of iron was weighed and placed in the apparatus. It was removed at regular intervals and the clock was paused. The piece of iron was washed, dried, weighed and replaced. The clock was restarted. 
This was continued until the solution was colourless. 
The mass of iron was plotted against time. The graph shows the results obtained.

![cie-igcse-sq-6-1-mass-reaction-graph](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-chemistry-23/6-chemical-reactions/6-1-chemical-change-and-rate-of-reaction/assets/153-cie-igcse-sq-6-1-mass-reaction-graph.png)

i) Suggest an explanation for the shape of the graph.

[3]

ii) Predict the shape of the graph if a similar piece of iron with a much rougher surface had been used. Explain your answer.

[2]

iii) Describe how you could find out if the rate of this reaction depended on the speed of stirring.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
a)

i) An explanation for the shape of the graph is:

- The rate of reaction decreases / gradient decreases; **[1 mark]**
- Because the concentration of bromine decreases; **[1 mark]**
- The reaction stops because all bromine is used up; **[1 mark]**

ii)  If a similar piece of iron with a much rougher surface had been used:

- The initial rate would be greater / gradient greater; **[1 mark]**
- Because bigger surface area / more particles of iron exposed; **[1 mark]**

**OR**

- The final mass is the same;** [1 mark]**
- Because the mass of bromine is the same so the same mass of iron is used;** [1 mark]**

- Measure the new rate / compare results; **[1 mark]**

- *Most rate of reaction graphs are showing the volume of a product being made, so this is essentially an upside-down version that looks different from usual, but can be treated the same*

  - *The steepest part of the slope is downwards rather than upwards*
  - *The graph still levels out when the reaction has stopped*
- *A rougher surface means a larger surface area; the question is again centred on the graph, so the two points you can make reference to either the speed of the reaction or the extent of the reaction*

parts.problemMd:

Fe + Br<sub>2</sub> → Fe<sup>2+</sup> + 2Br<sup>–</sup> 2Fe + 3Br<sub>2</sub> → 2Fe<sup>3+</sup> + 6Br<sup>–</sup>

[2]

ii) Which substance in the first equation is the reductant (reducing agent)?

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
b)

i) The change which is oxidation is:

- Fe to Fe<sup>2+</sup>; **[1 mark]**
- Because oxidation is electron loss / increase in oxidation number; **[1 mark]**

- Fe; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *Whenever a metal is going from its elemental form to an ion then it is being oxidised (as metal ions are all cations and involve the loss of electrons*
- *The reducing agent is the species that gets oxidised, thereby allowing another species to be reduced by transferring electrons to it*

parts.problemMd:

The experiment was repeated at the same temperature, using pieces of calcium carbonate of the same size but with acid of a different concentration. In all the experiments an excess of acid was used.

| concentration of acid in mol / dm<sup>3</sup> | 4 | 2 | 2 | .......... |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| number of pieces of carbonate | 1 | 1 | 2 | 1 |
| time in s | .......... | 80 | .......... | 160 |

i) Complete the table (assume the rate is proportional to both the acid concentration and the number of pieces of calcium carbonate).

[3]

ii) Explain why the reaction rate would increase if the temperature was increased.

[2]

iii) Explain why the rate of this reaction increases if the piece of carbonate is crushed to a powder.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
a) i) The completed table is: | concentration of acid in mol / dm3 | 4 | 2 | 2 | **1**; **[1 mark]** | |---|---|---|---|---| | number of pieces of carbonate | 1 | 1 | 2 | 1 | | time in s | **40**; **[1 mark]** | 80 | **40**
** OR **
**80**; **[1 mark]** | 160 | ii) The reaction rate would increase if the temperature was increased because: - The particles have more (kinetic) energy / move faster; **[1 mark]** - The particles collide more frequently / more collisions per unit time;** [1 mark]** iii) The rate of this reaction increases if the piece of carbonate is crushed to a powder because: - It has a greater / larger surface area; **[1 mark]** **[Total: 6 marks]** - *In part (i):* - *When the concentration is doubled from 2 mol / dm**3** to 4 mol / dm**3**, there will be twice as many as acid particles which means that the reaction should be twice as fast / take half the time* - *There are two possible answers / arguments when the number of pieces increases from 1 to 2:* 1. *The amount / mass of carbonate is the same so the time for the reaction will be the same* 2. *Although the amount / mass of carbonate is the same, it has been split into 2 pieces and should therefore react twice as fast / take half the time* - *When the number of pieces of carbonate (mass / amount) remains the same but the time for the reaction doubles from 80 s to 160 s* - *This can only happen if the concentration of the acid has halved* - *In part (ii), when the temperature increases the particles have more kinetic energy which will lead to more frequent, successful collisions and, therefore, a faster rate / quicker reaction / lower time* - *Careful: **Make sure you talk about the frequency of collisions or number of collisions per unit time; just more collisions has not been sufficient for the mark for a while now* - *In part (iii) your mind should automatically be thinking about surface area as soon as the solid is being broken into smaller pieces / powder*

[1]

d)

parts.problemMd:
Ammonia is an important industrial chemical.

i) Give the electronic structure of an atom of nitrogen.

[1]

ii) Use this electronic structure, rather than the valency of nitrogen, to explain why the formula of ammonia is NH<sub>3</sub>, not NH<sub>4.</sub>

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
a)

i)  the electron structure of an atom of nitrogen is:

- 2, 5; **[1 mark]**

ii) The formula of ammonia is NH<sub>3</sub>, not NH<sub>4 </sub>because:

- Nitrogen needs three electrons; **[1 mark]**
- To complete the energy level; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *Nitrogen has an atomic number of 7 so has 7 electrons in total*
- *A maximum of 2 electrons can fit in the first shell and a maximum of 8 in the second*
- *The electronic configuration is therefore 2, 5, using up the 7 electrons*
- *This means that 3 more electrons are required to fill the second shell to make it a full valence shell of 8*
- *The three hydrogen atoms will share one electron each with nitrogen as follows:* ![ammonia-dot-and-cross](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-chemistry-23/6-chemical-reactions/6-2-reversible-reactions-and-equilibrium/assets/027-ammonia-dot-and-cross.png)

parts.problemMd:
#### Separate: Chemistry and Extended Only

Ammonia is made by the Haber Process.

N<sub>2</sub> (g) + 3H<sub>2</sub> (g)   $\rightleftharpoons$  2NH<sub>3</sub> (g)

The forward reaction is exothermic.

The percentage of ammonia in the equilibrium mixture varies with conditions.

| **Pressure/ atmospheres** | **100** | **200** | **300** | **400** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| % ammonia at 300 °C | 45 | 65 | 72 | 78 |
| % ammonia at 500 °C | 9 | 18 | 25 | 31 |

The conditions actually used are 200 atmospheres, 450 °C and an iron catalyst. Osmium was previously used as the catalyst for this process.

i) Suggest a reason why it was changed to iron.

[1]

ii) Explain why the highest pressure gives the highest percentage of ammonia in the equilibrium mixture.

[2]

iii) What happens to the unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen?

[1]

iv) State one advantage and one disadvantage of using a lower temperature. 
advantage ................................................................................................................. 
disadvantage ..........................................................................................................

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
b)

i) A reason why the catalyst was changed to iron is:

- Iron is cheaper; 
**OR** 
It is a better catalyst; **[1 mark]**

ii) The highest pressure gives the highest percentage of ammonia in the equilibrium mixture. because:

- High pressure favours the side with smaller volume / fewer moles; **[1 mark]**
- This is right-hand side / the product side / ammonia side; **[1 mark]**

iii) The unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are:

- Recycled / sent over catalyst again; **[1 mark]**

*Accept 'used again'*

iv) One advantage and one disadvantage of using a lower temperature is:

- Advantage - high yield; **[1 mark]**
- Disadvantage - slow reaction rate; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

- *Part i) is a 'suggest' question so you may not have covered this question specifically but should be able to come up with a sensible reason *
- *Remember: according to Le Chatelier's principle, the change made to the system will cause the system to shift the equilibrium to oppose the change*
- *So higher pressures will cause the system to try and decrease the pressure by favouring the reaction that produces few molecules of gas, in this case, the forward reaction *
- *The equilibrium shifts to the right producing more product/ ammonia *
- *Similarly, low temperatures will cause the system to oppose the change and increase the temperature by favouring the exothermic reaction, in this case, the forward reaction *
- *At low temperatures the rate of reaction is slow due to the decreased frequency of successful collisions between particles, so a compromise between yield and rate is often made*
- *As the unreacted gases in the Haber process are recycled, there is no loss of unreacted reactants so the % yield is less of an important factor than it otherwise would be, and a good rate to maintain a high daily yield is more important for profits*

parts.problemMd:
#### Separate: Chemistry and Extended Only

The following graph shows how the percentage of ammonia in the equilibrium mixture changes with temperature.

![temp-equilbrium-graph-](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-chemistry-23/6-chemical-reactions/6-2-reversible-reactions-and-equilibrium/assets/012-temp-equilbrium-graph.png)

i) Explain the term equilibrium.

[2]

ii) How does the percentage of ammonia vary with temperature?

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
b)

i) Equilibrium means:

- Rate of the forward and back reactions is equal;** [1 mark]**
- So concentrations of reactant and products do not change; ** [1 mark]**

*Accept amounts stay the same* *Do NOT accept 'no change'*

ii) The percentage of ammonia varies with temperature because:

- It <u>decreases</u> with <u>increased</u> temperature **OR** It <u>increases</u> with <u>decreased</u> temperature; ** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *Remember:** According to Le Chateliers principle, the change made to the system will cause the system to shift the equilibrium to oppose the change*
- *High temperatures will cause the system to oppose the change and decrease the temperature by favouring the endothermic reaction, in this case, the reverse reaction *
- *The equilibrium would shift to the left, thereby reducing the percentage yield of ammonia*
- *Equilibrium cannot be described as 'no change' as this is a dynamic equilibrium where there is always change, but the rate of that change in both directions is equal*

dark brown              yellow

- The second reaction (forward) reaction is exothermic; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *Le Chatelier's principle states that when a change is made to the conditions of a system at equilibrium, the system will automatically move to oppose the change*
- *If there are the same number of reactant and product molecules, no reaction (forward or reverse) will be favoured if a change in pressure is imposed on the system*

  - *If no reaction is favoured, then the yield of reactant and product will not change*
- *If a high temperature is imposed on the system, it will move to oppose the change and attempt to decrease the temperature*
- *It will do this by favouring the endothermic reaction *

  - *In the first reaction, this is the forward reaction and so a higher yield of product is obtained *
  - *In the second reaction, the forward reaction is exothermic and so the reverse reaction is favoured, lowering the yield of product*

| N<sub>2</sub> (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) | 2NO (g)       **equilibrium 1** |
|---|---|
|   | nitric oxide |

| 2NO (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) | 2NO<sub>2</sub> (g)       **equilibrium 2** |

Nitric acid is now made by the oxidation of ammonia. It used to be made from air and water. This process used very large amounts of electricity.

Air was blown through an electric arc and heated to 3000 °C.

| N<sub>2</sub> (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) | $\rightleftharpoons$ 2NO (g)       **equilibrium 1** |
|---|---|
|   | nitric oxide |

The equilibrium mixture leaving the arc contained 5% of nitric oxide. This mixture was cooled rapidly. At lower temperatures, nitric oxide will react with oxygen to form nitrogen dioxide.

| 2NO (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) | $\rightleftharpoons$ 2NO<sub>2</sub> (g)       **equilibrium 2** |
|---|---|

Nitrogen dioxide reacts with oxygen and water to form nitric acid.

i) Suggest a reason why the yield of nitric oxide in **equilibrium 1** increases with temperature.

[1]

ii) What effect, if any, would increasing the pressure have on the percentage of nitric oxide in **equilibrium 1**? Explain your answer.

[2]

iii) Deduce why **equilibrium 2 **is only carried out at lower temperatures.

[2]

iv) Complete the equation for the reaction between nitrogen dioxide, water and oxygen to form nitric acid.

........NO<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub> + ............ → ............HNO<sub>3</sub>

[2]

v) Ammonia is more expensive than water and air. Suggest a reason why the ammonia-based process is preferred to the electric arc process.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
a)

i) The yield of nitric oxide in **equilibrium 1** increases with temperature because:

- The (forward) reaction is <u>endothermic</u>; **[1 mark]**

ii) Increasing the pressure will cause the percentage of nitric oxide in **equilibrium 1** to:

- Not change / have no effect; **[1 mark]**
- (Because,) the volume / number of moles / number of molecules of reactants and products are the same; **[1 mark]**

iii) **Equilibrium 2 **is only carried out at lower temperatures because:

- The reaction is <u>exothermic</u>; **[1 mark]**
- High temperatures push the equilibrium to the left / reactants 
**OR **
High temperatures decrease the yield of the products 
**OR **
Low temperatures favour the forward reaction / products; **[1 mark]**

iv) The equation for the reaction between nitrogen dioxide, water and oxygen to form nitric acid is:

4NO<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O → 4HNO<sub>3</sub>

- H<sub>2</sub>O identified as the missing reactant; **[1 mark]**
- Correct balancing of the equation; **[1 mark]**

v) The ammonia-based process is preferred to the electric arc process because:

- A high / large amount of electricity / energy is used;** [1 mark] ***References to cost are ignored*

**[Total: 8 marks]**

- *Remember: **Increasing temperature favours the endothermic reaction and increasing pressure favours the side with fewest moles*

  - *For **equilibrium 1*
  
    - *Using a higher temperature (3000 *<sup>*o*</sup>*C) suggests that the forward reaction is endothermic*
    - *There are 2 moles of reactant and 2 moles of product, therefore changing the pressure will have no effect on the equilibrium*
  - *For **equilibrium 2*
  
    - *Using a lower temperature (cooled rapidly) suggests that the forward reaction is exothermic*
    - *There are 3 moles of reactant and 2 moles of product, therefore an increase in pressure will favour the forward reaction, increasing the yield of nitrogen dioxide*
- *To balance the equation*

  - *You are told that the reactants are nitrogen dioxide, water and oxygen, which gives the unbalanced equation NO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* + H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O → HNO*<sub>*3*</sub>* *
  - *One mole of water would form 2 moles of nitric acid and require 2 moles of nitrogen dioxide, i.e. 2NO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* + 2H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O → 2HNO*<sub>*3*</sub>
  
    - *This has 6 atoms of oxygen on the product side and 7 atoms of oxygen and is unbalanced*
  - *Two moles of water would form 4 moles of nitric acid and require 4 moles of nitrogen dioxide, i.e. 4NO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* + 2H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O → 4HNO*<sub>*3*</sub>
  
    - * This has 12 atoms of oxygen on the product side and 12 atoms of oxygen and is therefore balanced*
- *Part (v) mentions expense and the use of electricity*

  - *You are warned that the ammonia-based process is expensive due to the use of ammonia*
  - *The only reason to use the ammonia-based process would be if it was less expensive than the electric arc process*
  - *Therefore, you can assume that there must be a large amount of electricity / energy used in the electric arc process which will have a high associated cost*

**Extract:**

| **bond** | **bond energy kJ / mol** | **energy change kJ** | **exothermic ** **or endothermic** |
|---|---|---|---|

| H–H | 436 | 3 x 436 = +1308 |   |
| N–H | 388 |   |   |

parts.solutionMd:
d)

- Endothermic reactions take in / absorb / use / need / gain (heat) energy 
**AND **

ii) The forward reaction is exothermic because:

| **bond** | **bond energy kJ / mol** | **energy change kJ** | **exothermic ** **or endothermic** |
|---|---|---|---|
| N$\equiv$N | 944 | +944 | endothermic |
| H–H | 436 | 3 x 436 = +1308 | **endothermic** |
| N–H | 388 | **6 x 388 = (-)2328** | **exothermic** |

- H-H identified as endothermic 
**AND **
N-H identified as exothermic; **[1 mark]**
- N-H energy change = 6 x 388 
**OR **
(-)2328 
**AND **
Indication of calculating energy in / bonds broken, i.e. 944 + 1308 
**OR **
2252; **[1 mark]**
- 2252 - 2328 = -76 (kJ) 
**OR **
(Total) Energy in / bonds broken is less than the (total) energy out / bonds formed 
**OR **
The (total) energy of the reactants / right-hand side is less than the (total) energy of the products / left-hand side 
**OR **
2252 < 2328; **[1 mark]** *Accept reverse arguments*

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *Remember: **To prove that the reaction is exothermic, you need to calculate the total energy change using  energy change = energy in - energy out*

i) What is the formula of vanadium(V) oxide?

[1]

ii) Vanadium(V) oxide is an efficient catalyst at any temperature in the range 400 to 450 °C. Scientists are looking for an alternative catalyst which is efficient at 300°C. What would be the advantage of using a lower temperature?

[2]

iii) The process does not use a high pressure because of the extra expense. Suggest two advantages of using a high pressure? Explain your suggestions.

[4]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The formula of vanadium(V) oxide? is:

- V<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub>; **[1 mark]**

ii) The advantage of using a lower temperature is:

- The position of equilibrium shifts right / yield increases; **[1 mark]**
- To save energy;** [1 mark]**

iii) Advantages of using a high pressure are:

- A faster reaction / rate;** [1 mark]**
- (Because) there are more collisions per second / higher collision frequency; **[1 mark]**
- The position of equilibrium shifts right / yield increases; **[1 mark]**
- (Because) there are fewer moles / molecules (of gas) on right; **[1 mark]**

- *The charge on an ion is indicated by the Roman numeral in its name:*

  - *2 x (2+) + 5 x (2-) = 0*
- *Therefore, vanadium(V) oxide contains 2 vanadium ions for every 5 oxide ions*
- *Lower temperatures will favour the exothermic reaction, which is the forward reaction in this case*

**Extract:**

In 1909, Haber discovered that nitrogen and hydrogen would react to form ammonia. N~2~ (g) + 3H~2~ (g) ⇌ 2NH~3~ (g). The forward reaction is exothermic

i) Complete the following table that describes the bond breaking and forming in the reaction between nitrogen and hydrogen to form ammonia.

| **Bonds** | **Energy Change** | **Exothermic or Endothermic?** |
|---|---|---|
| 1 mole of N$\equiv$N broken | +945 | ....................................... |
| 3 moles of ............ broken | +1308 | ....................................... |
| 6 moles of N – H formed | -2328 | ....................................... |

[4]

ii) Explain, using the above data, why the forward reaction is exothermic.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
c)

i) The completed table is:

| **Bonds** | **Energy Change** | **Exothermic or Endothermic?** |
|---|---|---|
| 1 mole of N$\equiv$N broken | +945 | Endothermic; **[1 mark]** |
| 3 moles of H-H; **[1 mark]** broken | +1308 | Endothermic; **[1 mark]** |
| 6 moles of N – H formed | -2328 | Exothermic; **[1 mark]** |

ii) The forward reaction is exothermic because:

Alternative 1

- More heat is given out than taken in; **[1 mark]**
- –2328 -( 945 + 1308) = –75 (kJ); **[1 mark]**

Alternative 2:

- More heat is given out when bonds form than is taken in to break the bonds; **[2 marks] **
*Must mention bond breaking and forming*

**[Total: 6 marks]**

- *Energy is taken in to break bonds so bond breaking is endothermic*
- *Energy is released when new bonds are formed so forming bonds is exothermic *
- *Be very careful with your answer, a common mistake is to write 'More heat is used to form bonds than to break bonds'*

  - *You must say that the heat is **released/given out** when new bonds are formed, not that it is used to form bonds*
- *To calculate the overall energy change for the reaction: Energy to break bonds- Energy released when bonds are made*

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
b)

i) The percentage of ammonia increases as the pressure increases because:

- There are fewer moles of gas on the product side  
**OR** 
The volume decreases in the forward reaction; **[1 mark]**
- (Increase in pressure) causes equilibrium shifts to the right; **[1 mark]**

ii) The percentage of ammonia will change if the measurements had been made at a lower temperature by:

- Increasing; **[1 mark]**
- Exothermic reaction favoured by lower temperature; **[1 mark]**

iii) Two of the reaction conditions used in the Haber Process are;

The simplest alcohol is methanol.

It is manufactured by the following reversible reaction.

300 <sup>o</sup>C             
30 atm 
CO (g) + 2H<sub>2</sub> (g)  CH<sub>3</sub>OH (g)

The simplest alcohol is methanol.

It is manufactured by the following reversible reaction.

300 <sup>o</sup>C             
30 atm 
CO (g) + 2H<sub>2</sub> (g) $\rightleftharpoons$ CH<sub>3</sub>OH (g)

i) Reversible reactions can come to equilibrium. Explain the term *equilibrium*.

[1]

ii) At 400 <sup>o</sup>C, the percentage of methanol in the equilibrium mixture is lower than at 300 <sup>o</sup>C. Suggest an explanation.

[2]

iii) Suggest **two **advantages of using high pressure for this reaction. Give a reason for each advantage.

[5]
parts.solutionMd:
a)

i) The term *equilibrium means:*

- No change in concentration of reactants / products 
**OR **
Rates ( of the forward and reverse reaction are) equal; **[1 mark]** 
*Accept no change in amounts or it is as if the reaction has stopped*

ii) The percentage of methanol in the equilibrium mixture is lower than at 300 <sup>o</sup>C because:

- Backwards reaction is endothermic 
**OR **
the forward reaction is exothermic; **[1 mark]**
- An increase in temperature favours the endothermic reaction which is the back reaction 
**OR **
vice versa; **[1 mark]**

iii) Two advantages, with reasons, of using high pressure for this reaction are:

- Increased rate; **[1 mark]**
- (Because) molecules collide more frequently 
**OR **
concentration of molecules is increased 
**OR **
molecules are closer: **[1 mark]** *Do NOT accept they have more KE*
- Increased yield; **[1 mark]**
- (Because) high pressure favours side with few molecules 
**OR **
smaller volume 
**OR **
moves to reduce the pressure; **[1 mark]**
- (which) is the product side; **[1 mark]** *This can be implied*

**[Total: 8 marks]**

- *Remember**:  The industrial conditions used are usually a compromise between yield and rate (for temperature) and yield and expense/safety (for pressure)*

parts.problemMd:
i) Complete the equation for the combustion of methanol in an excess of oxygen.

.......... CH<sub>3</sub>OH + .......... O<sub>2</sub> → .............................. + ..............................

[2]

ii) Complete the word equation.

methanol + ethanoic acid → .......................  ..................... + ....................

[2]

iii) Methanol can be oxidised to an acid. Name this acid.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
b)

i) The equation for the combustion of methanol in an excess of oxygen is:

**2**CH<sub>3</sub>OH + **3**O<sub>2</sub> → **2CO**<sub>**2**</sub> + **4H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O**

- CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O as products; **[1 mark]**
- Correct balancing; **[1 mark]**

ii) The word equation is:

methanol + ethanoic acid → **methyl ethanoate **+ **water**

- Methyl ethanoate; **[1 mark]**
- Water; **[1 mark]**

iii) The acid that can oxidise methanol to an acid is:

- Methanoic acid; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

- *The products of combustion of alcohols are CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* and H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O, so the unbalanced equation for the combustion of methanol is:*

  - *CH*<sub>*3*</sub>*OH + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
- *When balancing combustion equations, balance the carbon atoms first, in this case, they are already balanced:*

  - *CH*<sub>*3*</sub>*OH + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
- *Then balance the hydrogen atoms:*

  - *CH*<sub>*3*</sub>*OH + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + 2H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
- *Then the oxygen atoms:*

  - *CH*<sub>*3*</sub>*OH + 1½O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + 2H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
- *If you end up with a fraction, multiply all balancing numbers by 2:*

  - *2CH*<sub>*3*</sub>*OH + 3O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → 2CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + 4H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
- *When a carboxylic acid and alcohol react, an ester and water are formed*
- *The first part of the name of an ester indicates the length of the carbon chain in the alcohol, and it ends with the letters ‘- yl’*
- *The second part of the name indicates the length of the carbon chain in the carboxylic acid, and it ends with the letters ‘- oate’*

  - *So the ester formed from methanol and ethanoic acid is called methyl ethanoate*
- *Alcohols can be oxidised to carboxylic acids which have the same number of carbon atoms in their chain, therefore **meth**anol will oxidise to** meth**anoic acid*

**Extract:**

Carbonyl chloride, COCl<sub>2</sub>, is widely used in industry to make polymers, dyes and pharmaceuticals.

Carbonyl chloride was first made in 1812 by exposing a mixture of carbon monoxide and chlorine to bright sunlight.

This is a photochemical reaction.

CO (g) + Cl<sub>2</sub> (g) → COCl<sub>2</sub> (g)

Carbonyl chloride is now made by the reversible reaction given below.

CO (g) + Cl<sub>2</sub> (g) $\rightleftharpoons$ COCl<sub>2</sub> (g)

[2]

- Increasing pressure moves the position of equilibrium to the right-hand side / increases the yield of COCl<sub>2</sub>; **[1 mark]**

ii) Very little carbonyl chloride forms above 200 °C because:

- Increasing temperature favours the endothermic reaction;** [1 mark]**

- It keeps the rate high 
**OR **
It increases the rate at lower temperatures; **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
Reversible reactions can come to equilibrium. The following are three examples of types of gaseous equilibria.

A<sub>2</sub> (g) + B<sub>2</sub> (g)$\rightleftharpoons$2AB (g)    **reaction 1**

A<sub>2</sub> (g) + 3B<sub>2</sub> (g)$\rightleftharpoons$ 2AB<sub>3</sub> (g)    **reaction 2**

2AB<sub>2</sub> (g) $\rightleftharpoons$2AB(g) + B<sub>2</sub> (g)    **reaction 3**

Explain the term *equilibrium*.
parts.solutionMd:
a) The term *equilibrium* means:

- The rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the backwards / reverse reaction; **[1 mark]**
- Concentrations do not change / macroscopic properties remain constant (with time); **[1 mark]** 
*Accept: amounts*

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *Definitions are easy marks to pick up in exams - if you have taken the time to learnt them!*
- *Careful**: Do not say that the reaction has stopped*

  - *Whilst it may look like it has, equilibrium is said to be dynamic as reactants are still forming products and vice versa, so reactions are still occurring*
  - *However, the amount of reactant / product remains constant as the reactions are happening at the same rate*

- *If pressure increases, the equilibrium will favour the reaction which produces the fewest number of molecules as this will reduce the pressure to oppose the change*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Reversible reactions can come to equilibrium. They have both a forward and a backward reaction.

When water is added to an acidic solution of bismuth(III) chloride, a white precipitate forms and the mixture slowly goes cloudy.

BiCl<sub>3</sub> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l)       BiOCl (s) + 2HCl (aq)

colourless             white

Reversible reactions can come to equilibrium. They have both a forward and a backward reaction.

When water is added to an acidic solution of bismuth(III) chloride, a white precipitate forms and the mixture slowly goes cloudy.

BiCl<sub>3</sub> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l)   `rightwards harpoon over leftwards harpoon from backward to forward of`    BiOCl (s) + 2HCl (aq)

colourless             white

i) Explain why the rate of the forward reaction decreases with time.

[2]

ii) Why does the rate of the backward reaction increase with time?

[1]

iii) After some time why does the appearance of the mixture remain unchanged?

[2]

iv) When a few drops of concentrated hydrochloric acid are added to the cloudy mixture, it changes to a colourless solution. Suggest an explanation.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
a)

i) The rate of the forward reaction decreases with time because:

- The concentration of BiCl<sub>3</sub>; **[1 mark]**
- Decreases; **[1 mark]** 
Allow bismuth chloride is used up for **[1 mark]**

ii) The rate of the backward reaction increases with time because:

- Products are being formed 
**OR** 
The concentration of products increases; **[1 mark]** 
*The use of the term concentration can be awarded in either (i) or (ii)*

iii) After some time the appearance of the mixture remains unchanged because:

- The reaction has come to equilibrium; **[1 mark]**
- The (forward and backward) rates are equal **OR** There is no change in concentration; **[1 mark]**

iv) The cloudy mixture changes to a colourless solution when a few drops of concentrated hydrochloric acid are added because:

- The equilibrium to left / favours backward reaction / equilibrium moves to use up hydrochloric acid; **[1 mark]**
- BiOCl is used up 
**OR **
BiCl<sub>3</sub> is formed; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 7 marks]**

- *When dynamic equilibrium is established, even though both the forward and reverse reaction are still occurring but as this happens at the same rate, there is no difference in the macroscopic properties - i.e. there are no visible changes*
- *When hydrochloric acid is added, the concentration of HCl increases*
- *The equilibrium will shift to oppose this change by favouring the reaction which uses HCl as a reactant which is the reverse reaction*
- *This uses up the white, solid BiOCl and produces more BiCl3 which is a colourless liquid - you can tell this from the (aq) state symbol*

![Energy vs progress diagram for N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3. Reactants (N2 + 3H2) at higher level; curve rises to peak then falls to lower product (2NH3) level. Ea one way arrow to peak starting same height as reactants; ΔH arrow downward from reactants to products.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-chemistry-23/6-chemical-reactions/6-2-reversible-reactions-and-equilibrium/assets/008-energy-vs-progress-diagram-for-n2-3h2-2nh3-react.png)

**Extract:**

Ammonia is manufactured by the Haber process. The forward reaction is exothermic. N~2~(g) + 3 H~2~(g) ⇌ 2 NH~3~(g)      ΔH < 0

The engineer changes the conditions of the reactor.

Complete Table 2.1 to show the effect of changing the conditions on the equilibrium yield of ammonia and on the rate of the forward reaction. Use only the words **increases**, **decreases**, or **no change**.

**Table 2.1**

| **change in condition** | **effect on the equilibrium yield of ammonia** | **effect on the rate of the forward reaction** |
|---|---|---|
| increasing the temperature |   |   |
| increasing the pressure |   |   |
| adding a catalyst |   | increases |
parts.solutionMd:
| **change in condition** | **effect on the equilibrium yield of ammonia** | **effect on the rate of the forward reaction** |
|---|---|---|
| increasing the temperature | **decreases** **[1]** | **increases** **[1]** |
| increasing the pressure | **increases** **[1]** | **increases** **[1]** |
| adding a catalyst | **no change** **[1]** | increases |

> **[exam-tip]**
> Remember that **Haber Process is a frequent problem for exams**. You must know how changes in temperature, pressure, volume or adding a catalyst affect the equilibrium and the rate of reaction.
> 
> - **Increasing temperature**
> 
>   - The Haber process forward reactions is **exothermic**, so higher temperature shifts equilibrium **away from ammonia **favouring the endothermic reaction, decreasing the **yield.**
>   - However, particles move faster, so the **rate of the forward reaction increases.**
> - **Increasing pressure**
> 
>   - There are **4 moles of gas on the left (N**<sub>**2**</sub>**+ 3H**<sub>**2**</sub>**)** and **2 moles on the right (2NH**<sub>**3**</sub>**).**
>   - Higher pressure favours the side with **fewer gas molecules**, so the **yield of ammonia increases**, and collisions happen more often so the **rate also increases.**
> - **Adding a catalyst**
> 
>   - A catalyst **does not change equilibrium**, so the **yield stays the same.**
>   - It only **increases the rate** by lowering the activation energy.

a) **Two **advantages, with reasons, of using a high pressure are:

- Advantage 1: Faster reaction rate; **[1 mark]**
- Reason 1: Higher collision rate; **[1 mark]**
- Advantage 2: Greater yield; **[1 mark]**
- Reason 2: Pressure favours products / the right hand side of the reaction because it has a lower volume / there are fewer product molecules; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *Increasing the pressure will increase the rate of reaction*

  - *This is because the particles are closer together (same number of particles in a smaller unit volume)*
  - *This results in the particles colliding more frequently and successfully (more successful collisions per unit time / more frequent successful collisions)*
- *Increasing the pressure will increase the yield*

  - *This is because all of the chemicals involved in the reaction are gaseous*
  - *Therefore, one mole of any chemical will occupy the same volume*
  - *As a consequence, increasing the pressure will move the reaction towards the side that occupies the least space / has the fewest number of moles*
  - *In this case, there are 4 moles of reactant and 2 moles of product *
  - *Since there are less moles of product, the product side will take up the least space and increasing the pressure will move the reaction to make more product*

  - *3 N-F bonds are formed in one molecule of nitrogen trifluoride*
  - *3 H-F bonds are formed in three molecules of hydrogen fluoride*
  - *This information can then be used to complete the table*
- *The information in the table can be used to determine if the reaction is endothermic or exothermic using:*

  - *Energy change = total energy in - total energy out  OR Energy change = total bonds broken - total bonds formed*
- *Placing the appropriate numbers in this equation gives an answer with a negative value, meaning that energy is given out*

i) Explain the term *equilibrium mixture*.
