- *Lighter gas particles can travel faster and hence further, therefore the lower its relative mass the faster a gas will diffuse*

parts.problemMd:
Rubidium and strontium are very reactive metals at the top of the reactivity series. Because their ions have different charges, their compounds behave differently when heated.

The formulae of the ions of these two elements are Rb<sup>+</sup> and Sr<sup>2+</sup>.

Explain why these metals, which are in different groups, form ions which have different charges.
parts.solutionMd:
a) The metals form different ions because:

- Rb loses 1 electron / 1 electron in outer shell / 1 valency or valence electron; **[1 mark] **
- Sr loses 2 electrons / 2 electrons in outer shell / 2 valency or valence electrons; **[1 mark] **

**Final answer:** **[Total: 2 marks] **

- *In order for a metal to become an ion, it will lose electrons*
- *You must state how many electrons are lost*
- *If a 1+ ion is formed then 1 electron has been lost*
- *If a 2+ ion is formed then 2 electrons have been lost and so on*

parts.problemMd:
Strontium carbonate is similar to calcium carbonate. It is insoluble in water and it decomposes when heated. Rubidium carbonate is soluble in water and does not decompose when heated.

i) Describe a method to prepare a pure sample of the insoluble salt, strontium carbonate, by precipitation.

[4]

ii) Complete the equation for the decomposition of strontium carbonate.

SrCO<sub>3</sub> → ............ + ............

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
b)

i) A method to prepare a pure sample of the insoluble salt, strontium carbonate, by precipitation is:

- (Mix solutions of) rubidium carbonate / Rb<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>; **[1 mark] **
- Strontium chloride / SrCl<sub>2</sub> 
**OR **
Strontium nitrate / Sr(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> 
**OR **
Strontium sulfate / SrSO<sub>4</sub> 
**OR **
Strontium hydroxide / Sr(OH)<sub>2</sub>; **[1 mark] **
- Filter / centrifuge / decant (the residue); **[1 mark] **
- Wash with water and dry/ press between filter paper / put in (low) oven / put on a (sunny) windowsill / put in sun / heat; **[1 mark] **

- SrCO<sub>3</sub> → SrO + CO<sub>2</sub>; **[1 mark] **

- *Insoluble salts must be made from the precipitation reaction between two soluble salts *
- *Nitrate salts and group 1 salts are soluble, so these are always good options when having to name appropriate reactants*

- *A more familiar example is the thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate - this occurs in the blast furnace*

parts.problemMd:
Strontium and zinc are both metals with a valency of 2. Strontium is more reactive than zinc. Its chemistry is similar to that of calcium.

i) Complete the following table that shows the number of protons, electrons and neutrons in each particle.

| particle | protons | electrons | neutrons |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Sr presubscript blank presuperscript 88` |   |   |   |
| $\text{Sr} pre_{ } pre^{90}$ |   |   |   |
| $\text{Zn} pre_{ } pre^{65^{2} +}$ |   |   |   |

[3]

ii) Explain why `Sr presubscript blank presuperscript 88` and `Sr presubscript blank presuperscript 90` are isotopes.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
a)

i) The completed table should look as follows:

| particle | protons | electrons | neutrons |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Sr presubscript blank presuperscript 88` | 38 | 38 | 50 |
| $\text{Sr} pre_{ } pre^{90}$ | 38 | 38 | 52 |
| $\text{Zn} pre_{ } pre^{65^{2} +}$ | 30 | 28 | 35 |

- Each correct row; **[1 mark]**

ii) `Sr presubscript blank presuperscript 90` and $\text{Sr} pre_{ } pre^{88}$ are isotopes because:

- (They have the) same number of protons and different number of neutrons; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *You can determine the number of protons by looking at which element it is*

  - *Strontium, Sr, has 38 protons*
  - *Zinc, Zn, has 30 protons*
- *Mass number (larger number) = number of protons + number of neutrons*

  - *Sr-88*
  
    - *88 = 38 + neutrons*
    - *neutrons = 88 - 38*
  - *Sr-90*
  
    - *90 = 38 + neutrons*
    - *neutrons = 90 - 38*
  - *Zinc*
  
    - *65 = 30 + neutrons*
    - *neutrons = 65 - 30*
- *Both isotopes of Sr have no charge*

  - *Therefore number of protons = number of electrons*
- *Zn has a 2+ charge*

  - *Therefore Zn must have two more protons than electrons*

parts.problemMd:
#### Extended Only

The major ore of strontium is its carbonate, SrCO<sub>3</sub>. Strontium is extracted by the electrolysis of its molten chloride.

i) Name the reagent that will react with the carbonate to form the chloride.

[1]

ii) The electrolysis of molten strontium chloride produces strontium metal and chlorine. Write ionic equations for the reactions at the electrodes.

negative electrode (cathode) .............. positive electrode (anode) ................

[2]

iii) One of the products of the electrolysis of concentrated aqueous strontium chloride is chlorine. Name the other two.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
b)

i) The reagent that will react with the carbonate to form the chloride is:

- Hydrochloric acid; **[1 mark]**

ii)The ionic equations at the electrodes for the electrolysis of molten strontium chloride are:

Negative electrode (cathode)

- Sr<sup>2+</sup> + 2e → Sr; **[1 mark]**

Positive electrode (anode)

- 2Cl<sup>-</sup> – 2e → Cl<sub>2 </sub>**OR **2Cl<sup>–</sup> → Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2e; **[1 mark]**

iii) The other two products of the electrolysis of concentrated aqueous strontium chloride are:

- Hydrogen; **[1 mark]**
- Strontium hydroxide; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

- *For the electrolysis of **molten** strontium chloride*
- *At the **anode**, negatively charged ions **lose** **electrons** and are thus oxidised*

  - *Chloride is the negatively charged ion so will lose electrons to form chlorine*
- *At the **cathode,** the positively charged ions **gain electrons** and are thus reduced*

  - *Strontium is a Group II metal so forms a positively charged 2+ ion*
  - *Strontium ions will gain electrons to form strontium atoms*
- *For the electrolysis of** aqueous** strontium chloride*

  - *Negative electrode (cathode) *
  
    - *From the reactivity series we know that both potassium and sodium are more reactive than hydrogen*
    - *Both of these are Group I metals*
    - *As strontium is also a Group I metal we can assume it has similar chemical properties and will also be more reactive than hydrogen*
    - *This means that hydrogen will be produced at the negative electrode (cathode)*
  - *Positive electrode (anode)*
  
    - *We are told one of the products is chlorine so this must be produced at the positive electrode*
  - *This means there are both strontium ions (from the strontium chloride) and hydroxide ions (from the water) present in the solution*
  - *Hence the other product will be strontium hydroxide*

#### Extended Only

In an experiment to investigate the rate of rusting of steel, three pieces of steel were used. One piece of steel was completely coated with copper, one piece was completely coated with zinc and the third piece was left uncoated. All three pieces were left exposed to the atmosphere.

i) Explain why the uncoated piece started to rust.

[1]

ii) The coating on both of the other two pieces was scratched, exposing the steel.

![screen-shot-2022-09-14-at-11-14-25](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-chemistry-23/9-metals/9-1-properties-uses-and-alloys-of-metals/assets/019-screen-shot-2022-09-14-at-11-14-25.png)

The piece of steel coated with zinc still did not rust but the copper-coated piece of steel rusted very rapidly.

Explain these observations in terms of the formation of ions and the transfer of electrons.

[4]
parts.solutionMd:
b)

i) The uncoated piece started to rust because:

- Steel (or iron) is exposed to oxygen and water;** [1 mark] **

ii) The piece of steel coated with zinc still did not rust but the copper-coated piece of steel rusted very rapidly because:

- Zn more reactive than Fe (allow steel);** [1 mark] **
- Zn loses / transfers electrons (more readily) and forms (+ve) ions (in preference to Fe);** [1 mark] **

- *There are now 3 oxygen atoms on each side of the equation, but 6 hydrogen atoms on the right-hand side and 2 on the left-hand side, so balance the hydrogen atoms:*
- *WO*<sub>*3*</sub>* + **3**H*<sub>*2*</sub>* → W + **3**H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O *

parts.problemMd:
#### Separate: Chemistry and Extended Only

Acid digestion is a method used to dissolve metals into a solution which can then be analysed to determine the composition of the metal.

A 3.00 g sample of an aluminium alloy was reacted with an excess of concentrated nitric acid. The resulting mixture was made up to 250 cm<sup>3</sup> with distilled water and analysed. The concentration of aluminium ions in the 250 cm<sup>3 </sup>solution was found to be 0.36 mol/dm<sup>3</sup>.

Calculate the percentage composition by mass of aluminum in the 3.00 g sample of aluminum alloy.

[*A*<sub>r</sub> (Al) = 27]
parts.solutionMd:
d) The percentage composition by mass of aluminium in the 3.00 g sample of aluminium alloy is:

- Number of moles of aluminium ions in 250 cm<sup>3</sup> solution = 0.36 x $\frac{250}{1000}$ = 0.09 moles; **[1 mark]**
- Mass of aluminium = 0.09 x 27 = 2.43 (g); **[1 mark]**
- Percentage composition of aluminium in alloy = $\frac{2.43}{3.00}$ x 100 = 81%; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *Don't be put off this question by the unfamiliar method of acid digestion*
- *If you know the concentration and volume of aluminium ions, then you can calculate the number of moles using the equation:*

  - *moles = concentration x volume in dm*<sup>*3*</sup>
  - *To convert from cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* to dm*<sup>*3*</sup>*, divide by 1000*
- *The aluminium ions that are in this 250 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* solution all came from the aluminium alloy that underwent acid digestion*

  - *Therefore, the number of moles of aluminium ions = the number of moles of aluminium in the alloy*
- *You can then work out the mass of the aluminium in the alloy using the equation:*

  - *mass = moles x **A*<sub>*r*</sub>
- *As you need to calculate the percentage composition by mass, you can work out what this mass is as a percentage of the 3.00 g mass of the alloy*

Some metals react with cold water. Give the balanced symbol equation for the reaction of calcium reacting with water. Ca (s) + 2H~2~O (l) → Ca(OH)~2~ (aq) + H~2~ (g)

#### Separate: Chemistry and Extended Only

Using oxidation numbers, show that calcium is oxidised during the reaction with water.
parts.solutionMd:
b) To show that calcium is oxidised during the reaction with water:

- The oxidation number of Ca increases; **[1 mark]**
- From 0 (in Ca); **[1 mark]**
- To +2 (in Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub>); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *Remember**: Oxidation number increases when oxidation occurs and decreases when reduction occurs*
- *The oxidation number of an uncombined element, such as Ca, is zero*
- *The oxidation number of an element in a mono-atomic ion is always the same as its charge*

  - *The charge on the calcium ion in Ca(OH)*<sub>*2*</sub>* is +2, therefore its oxidation number is +2*

parts.problemMd:
A student added 20 cm<sup>3</sup> of dilute hydrochloric acid to two boiling tubes. To one of the boiling tubes they added a small piece of calcium and to the other they added a small piece of magnesium.

State **two **observations that the student would make and how the observations would differ between the two boiling tubes.
parts.solutionMd:
c) Comparing the reaction of calcium with HCl and magnesium with HCl:

- The student would see effervescence / bubbles / fizzing in both boiling tubes 
**OR** 
The student would see effervescence / bubbles / fizzing with calcium and magnesium; **[1 mark]**
- The solid would dissolve / disappear in both boiling tubes; **[1 mark]**
- The reaction would be more vigorous / violent with calcium
**OR** 
The solid would dissolve / disappear faster with calcium; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *You must be able to describe the reactions of different metals with acid, comparing them to each other and must be able to provide reaction equations *
- *When acids react with metals, a salt and hydrogen are formed:*

  - *M**etal + **A**cid → **S**alt + **H**ydrogen (think **MASH**)*
- *When giving observations, think about the states of the reactants and prdocuts*
- *The metal is a solid, so as it reacts, it will be used up and you will see it disappear*
- *Hydrogen is a gas, so as it is produced you will see bubbles of gas*

  - *Careful**: When asked for observations, do not state that 'a gas / hydrogen is produced', as this is not an observation, you need to explain what you see, i.e. the bubbles*
- *Calcium is further up the reactivity series than magnesium, so the reaction of calcium with acid is more vigorous than of magnesium with acid*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A student added 20 cm^3^ of dilute hydrochloric acid to two boiling tubes. To one of the boiling tubes they added a small piece of calcium and to the other they added a small piece of magnesium.

The student had added the exact amount of magnesium required to react with the hydrochloric acid used. After carrying out the experiment, the student accidentally added some more magnesium. The student was surprised that the extra magnesium still reacted although the reaction was a lot slower.

Explain these observations. Include an equation in your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
d) The reason for this observation is:

- Magnesium reacts with water producing hydrogen / H<sub>2</sub>;** [1 mark]**
- The reaction between magnesium and water is a lot slower (than the reaction between magnesium and acid); [1 mark]
- Mg + 2H<sub>2</sub>O → Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub>  + H<sub>2</sub> ; [1 mark]

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *Water is present in the aqueous solution of hydrochloric acid*
- *Once the hydrochloric acid has been used up, magnesium will continue to react with the water*
- *The reaction between water and magnesium is very slow, magnesium will react readily with steam*

What type of chemical process occurs when zinc and iron react with aqueous copper(II) sulfate?
parts.solutionMd:
e) The type of chemical process that occurs when zinc and iron react with aqueous copper(II) sulfate is:

- Exothermic 
**OR **
Redox 
**OR **
Displacement; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

- *Since the temperature in the results is increasing, you can deduce that the reaction is exothermic*
- *Zinc and iron are both more reactive than copper, so they will displace copper out of solution*

  - *This displacement involves the copper(II) ions gaining electrons while the zinc / iron ions lose electrons, so this is also a redox reaction*

parts.problemMd:
#### Separate: Chemistry and Extended Only

Aluminium is an important metal with a wide range of uses.

Aluminium is obtained by the electrolysis of aluminium oxide dissolved in molten cryolite.

![electrolysis-of-aluminium-oxide](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-chemistry-23/9-metals/9-3-extraction-of-metals/assets/026-electrolysis-of-aluminium-oxide.png)

i) Solid aluminium oxide is a poor conductor of electricity. It conducts either when molten or when dissolved in molten cryolite. Explain why.

[2]

ii) Why is a solution of aluminium oxide in molten cryolite used rather than molten aluminium oxide?

[1]

iii) Explain why the carbon anodes need to be replaced periodically.

[1]

iv) One reason why graphite is used for the electrodes is that it is a good conductor of electricity. Give another reason.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
a)

i) Aluminium oxide is a poor conductor of electricity and conducts either when molten or when dissolved in molten cryolite because:

- Ions cannot move / no free ions in the solid state; **[1 mark]**
- Ions can move / free ions in the liquid state; **[1 mark]**

ii) A solution of aluminium oxide in molten cryolite is used rather than molten aluminium oxide because:

- Reduce melting point 
**OR **
Reduce energy costs 
**OR **
Better conductor when dissolved in cryolite; **[1 mark] **

iii) The carbon anodes need to be replaced periodically because they:

- Burn in / react with oxygen 
**OR **
Are oxidised by oxygen 
**OR **
Form carbon dioxide / carbon monoxide; **[1 mark]**

iv) Another reason why graphite is used for the electrodes is:

- High melting point 
**OR** 
Inert / unreactive; **[1 mark]**

**Final answer:** **[Total; 5 marks]**

- *Aluminium oxide is an ionic compound so it can only conduct electricity when the **ions **are able to move*

  - *The ions are only able to move when the aluminium oxide is aqueous or molten *
- *Aluminium oxide has a high melting point so cryolite is used to lower this thereby reducing energy requirements and costs*
- *The oxygen formed at the anode reacts with the carbon of the anode / electrode to form carbon dioxide so the anode wears aware and therefore needs replacing *

[2]

ii) Complete the ionic equation for the reaction at the anode.

.......... O<sup>2–</sup> → O<sub>2 </sub>+ ......... e<sup>-</sup>

[2]

iii) Why do the carbon anodes need to be replaced frequently?

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
b)

i)  **Two **reasons why the oxide is dissolved in cryolite are:

- Reduce the melting point of aluminium oxide; **[1 mark]**
- Enable aluminium oxide to conduct; **[1 mark]**

ii) The ionic equation for the reaction at the anode is:

2O<sup>2–</sup> → O<sub>2</sub> + 4e<sup>- </sup>

- Correct number of electrons on right-hand side; **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
Aluminium reacts with iron(III) oxide in the thermite reaction.

2Al + Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> → 2Fe + Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>

10.0 g of aluminium is reacted with 15.0 g of iron(III) oxide.

i) Calculate the number of moles of aluminium and iron(III) oxide used.

[Relative atomic masses, *A*<sub>r</sub>: Al = 27; Fe = 56; O = 16]

moles of Al = .............mol

moles of Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> = ............. mol

[2]

ii) Determine which reactant is the limiting reactant. Show your reasoning.

limiting reactant:

reasoning:

[1]

iii) Calculate the maximum mass of iron that can be produced in this reaction.

moles of iron produced = ........... mol

mass of iron produced = ............... g

[2]

iv) In an experiment, the actual mass of iron produced is 8.40 g. Calculate the percentage yield of iron.

percentage yield = ....................%

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) To calculate the number of moles of aluminium and iron(III) oxide used, the following equation must be used:

$\mathrm{moles}=\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{M_{r}}$

- For Al,

  - Use the relative atomic mass, as the M<sub>r</sub> since aluminium is an element

$n=\frac{10.0}{27}$

n = 0.370 mol **[1 mark]**

- For Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>, *M*<sub>r</sub> = 2 × Fe + 3 × O *M*<sub>r</sub> = 2 × 56 + 3 × 16 *M*<sub>r</sub> = 160

  - Calculate the *M*<sub>r</sub>

  - Using the calculated  *M*<sub>r </sub>, calculate the amount of moles of iron (III) oxide

$n=\frac{15.0}{160}$

n = 0.09375 mol **[1 mark]**

ii) To determine which reactant is the limiting reactant, you must use the ratio from the chemical equation to calculate the expected amount of reactants that will react together in a complete ratio** **(1:2 ratio shown in the equation), and compare with the answer obtained in (i)

- Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> is limiting 
**AND **
0.09375 moles of Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> only requires 0.1875 moles of Al However, 0.370 moles of Al are available, meaning Al is in excess **[1 mark]**

iii) To calculate the maximum mass of iron produced you must follow these steps:

- Using the moles of the limiting reactant, determine the moles of iron produced using the ratio from the chemical equation

  - The ratio of Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3 </sub>to Fe, is **1:2**

moles of Fe produced = 0.09375 × 2

moles of Fe produced = 0.1875 mol **[1 mark]**

- Rearrange the equation used in (i) to obtain the mass

$\mathrm{moles}=\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{M_{r}}$

mass of Fe = moles of Fe ×* M*<sub>r</sub>

mass of Fe = 0.1875 × 56

mass of Fe = 10.5 g **[1 mark]**

iv) To calculate the percentage yield, you must apply the formula :

$\text{percentage} \text{yield} = \frac{actual yield}{theoretical yield} \times 100 \%$

- The actual yield is the mass obtained experimentally in the lab, the theoretical yield is the mass obtained under practical conditions, and it is calculated from the balanced equation and reacting masses

$\text{percentage} \text{yield} = \frac{8.40}{10.5} \times 100 \%$

percentage yield  = **80.0 % ****[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In reacting masses questions, marks are often **independent**, so do not give up if one step feels difficult.
> 
> Show **every stage of your working clearly**. For example moles, ratios, and final calculation  because you can still gain method marks even if an earlier answer is wrong.
> 
> Clear working gives the examiner places to award marks.

#### Extended Only

The equation for the decomposition of copper(II) nitrate is given below.

2Cu(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> → 2CuO + 4NO<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub>

Copper(II) nitrate forms a series of hydrates with the formula Cu(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>.xH<sub>2</sub>O.

All these hydrates decompose to form copper(II) oxide.

1 mole of Cu(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>.xH<sub>2</sub>O forms 1 mole of CuO.

i) What is meant by 1 mole of a substance?

[1]

ii) 7.26 g of a hydrate, Cu(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>.xH<sub>2</sub>O, formed 2.4 g copper(II) oxide.

number of moles of CuO formed = ...................... number of moles of Cu(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>.xH<sub>2</sub>O in 7.26 g = ...................... mass of 1 mole of Cu(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>.xH<sub>2</sub>O = ...................... g mass of 1 mole of Cu(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> is 188 g the value of x in this hydrate = ......................

[4]
parts.solutionMd:
b)

i) One mole of a substance is:

- (The number of particles which is equal to the number of atoms in) 12 g of carbon 12 
**OR** 
The mass in grams which contains the Avogadro’s constant number of particles 
**OR** 
Avogadro’s constant or 6 to 6.02 × 10<sup>23 </sup>of atoms / ions / molecules / electrons / particles 
**OR**
(The amount of substance which has a mass equal to) its relative formula mass / relative atomic mass / relative molecular mass in grams 
**OR** 
(The amount of substance which has a volume equal to) 24 dm<sup>3</sup> of a gas at r.t.p.;** [1 mark]**

ii) To calculate the value of x:

- Number of moles of CuO formed = 0.03 mol; **[1 mark]**
- Number of moles of Cu(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>.xH<sub>2</sub>O in 7.26g = 0.03; **[1 mark]**
- Mass of 1 mole of Cu(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>.xH<sub>2</sub>O = 7.26 ÷ 0.03 = 242 (g) 
**AND** 
Mass of 1 mole of Cu(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> is 188 g; **[1 mark]**
- The value of x = 3; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

- *The concept of the mole is one that causes difficulties for many Chemistry students*

  - *The mole is simply a word that is used to represent a number (6.02 x 10*<sup>*23*</sup>*) in a similar way to the way that we use the word dozen to represent the number 12*
  - *If you wanted 3 dozen eggs, you would know to multiply 12 by 3 to give you 36 eggs*
  - *In a similar way, if you want 3 moles of atoms, you multiply 6.02 x 10*<sup>*23*</sup>* by 3 to give you 1.806 x 10*<sup>*24*</sup>* atoms*
  - *The numbers are larger but the concept is exactly the same!*
- *For part (ii)*

  - *To calculate the moles of CuO formed use: *
  
    - *moles = mass ÷ molar mass*
    - *The molar mass of CuO is its **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* in grams = 64 + 16 = 80 *
    - *So moles of CuO = 2. 4 ÷ 80 = **0.03 mol*
  - *From the equation we can see that the molar ratio of Cu(NO*<sub>*3*</sub>*)*<sub>*2*</sub>* to CuO is equal, there are 2 moles of each*
  
    - *So the number of moles of Cu(NO*<sub>*3*</sub>*)*<sub>*2 *</sub>*in 7.26g =  **0.03 mol*
  - *The mass of 1 mole of Cu(NO*<sub>*3*</sub>*)*<sub>*2*</sub>*.xH*<sub>*2*</sub>*O =  mass ÷ moles = 7.26 ÷ 0.03 = **242 g*
  - *You are told the mass of 1 mole of Cu(NO*<sub>*3*</sub>*)*<sub>*2*</sub>* is **188 g*
  - *So the mass of H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O within Cu(NO*<sub>*3*</sub>*)*<sub>*2*</sub>*.xH*<sub>*2*</sub>*O = 242 - 188 = 54 g*
  - *The molar mass of H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O is its **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* in grams = (2 x 1) + 16 = **18*
  - *So the moles of H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O (the value of x):*
  
    - *= mass ÷ molar mass *
    - *= 54 ÷ 18 = **3 *

parts.problemMd:
#### Separate: Chemistry and Extended Only

When chlorine is added to water it undergoes a reaction which forms hydrogen chloride and chloric(I) acid. The chloric(I) acid is the compound that kills the bacteria.

parts.solutionMd:
d) Chlorine is both oxidised and reduced because:

- Reduced to -1 in HCl; **[1 mark] **

  - *This is a bit unusual considering you are used to chlorine being -1 in a compound*

6.25 - 4.00 = 2.25 g | | Divide each mass by the relative formula mass to find the number of moles | $\frac{4.00}{160}=0.025$ | $\frac{2.25}{18}=0.125$ | | Find the molar ratio by dividing by the smallest number | $\frac{0.025}{0.025}=1$ | $\frac{0.125}{0.039}=5$ | - Mass of CuSO4 = 4.00 g **AND ** Mass of water = 2.25 g; **[1 mark]** - Moles of CuSO4 = 0.025 **AND ** Moles of water = 0.125; **[1 mark]** - Molar ratio = 1 : 5 **AND ** Therefore, x = 5; **[1 mark]** **[Total: 3 marks]** - *Use the table to work through the problem and treat water of crystallisation questions like empirical formula calculations* - *Instead of using **A**r**'s for the elements, you need to use them to work out the **M**r**'s of the compounds CuSO**4** and H**2**O* - *CuSO**4** = 64 + 32 + (4 x 16) = 160* - *H**2**O = (2 x 1) + 16 = 18*

parts.problemMd:
The burning of fossil fuels is largely responsible for the formation of acid rain. Two of the acids in acid rain are sulfuric acid and nitric acid.

i) Explain how the combustion of coal can form sulfuric acid.

[3]

ii) High temperatures generated by the combustion of fossil fuels can lead to the formation of nitric acid. Explain.

[3]

iii) Nitric acid contains nitrate ions.

Describe a test for nitrate ions.

[2]

iv) Explain how you could determine which one of two samples of acid rain had the higher concentration of hydrogen ions.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
b)

i) The combustion of coal can form sulfuric acid by:

- Oxygen / air and sulfur (from fuel) react; **[1 mark] **
- (Forms) sulfur (di)oxide;** [1 mark] **
- (Sulfur dioxide) reacts with oxygen / air and water (to form sulfuric acid) 
**OR **
Sulfur trioxide reacts with water (to form sulfuric acid) 
**OR** 
Sulfurous acid reacts with oxygen (to form sulfuric acid); **[1 mark] **

ii) High temperatures generated by the combustion of fossil fuels can lead to the formation of nitric acid by:

- Oxygen and nitrogen react; **[1 mark] **
- Making oxides of nitrogen; **[1 mark] **
- (Oxides of nitrogen) react with water (making nitric acid); **[1 mark] **

iii) A test for nitrate ions is:

- Add sodium hydroxide (solution) and aluminium; [**1 mark] **
- (Warm) and ammonia made; **[1 mark] **

iv) You could determine which one of two samples of acid rain had the higher concentration of hydrogen ions by:

Alternative 1

- Measure pH/ describe how to measure pH (such as using universal indicator); **[1 mark] **

Alternative 2

- Add Ca, Mg, Zn, Fe; **[1 mark] **
- Faster reaction / more bubbles (during the same time) / more hydrogen (during the same time) = greater concentration of H<sup>+</sup>; **[1 mark] **

Alternative 3

- Rate of reaction with (metal) carbonate; **[1 mark] **
- Faster reaction / more bubbles (during the same time) / more carbon dioxide (during the same time) = greater concentration of H<sup>+</sup>; **[1 mark] **

Alternative 4

- Electrical conductivity; **[1 mark] **
- Greater conductivity greater concentration of H<sup>+</sup>; **[1 mark] **

Alternative 5

- Titrate with (named) alkali; **[1 mark]**
- Correct result; **[1 mark] **

**[Total: 10 marks] **

- *All of the above questions in part b) are very common and also give an insight of how different topics can cover one question*
- *The testing for the higher concentration of hydrogen ions is a very common question and you only need to be able to state one method*
- *Make sure you learn at least two, in case one is given in the question and you are asked to provide an alternative method *

parts.problemMd:
#### Extended Only

The alcohols form a homologous series. The first five members are given in the table below.

| alcohol | formula | heat of combustion in kJ / mol |
|---|---|---|
| methanol | CH<sub>3</sub>OH | 730 |
| ethanol | CH<sub>3</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–OH | 1380 |
| propan-1-ol |   |   |
| butan-1-ol | CH<sub>3</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–OH | 2680 |
| pentan-1-ol | CH<sub>3</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–OH | 3350 |

i) Complete the table.

[2]

ii) Complete the equation for the combustion of pentan-1-ol in excess oxygen.

C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>11</sub>OH + .......O<sub>2</sub> → ..................... + .....................

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
a)

i) The completed table is:

| alcohol | formula | heat of combustion in kJ / mol |
|---|---|---|
| methanol | CH<sub>3</sub>OH | 730 |
| ethanol | CH<sub>3</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–OH | 1380 |
| propan-1-ol | **CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**–CH**<sub>**2**</sub>**–CH**<sub>**2**</sub>**–OH**; **[1 mark]** | **Value in the range of 2030 - 2050**; **[1 mark]** |
| butan-1-ol | CH<sub>3</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–OH | 2680 |
| pentan-1-ol | CH<sub>3</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–OH | 3350 |

ii) The completed equation for the combustion of pentan-1-ol in excess oxygen is:

- C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>11</sub>OH + 7.5O<sub>2</sub> → 5CO<sub>2</sub> + 6H<sub>2</sub>O;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *The mark for the missing formula can be achieved by spotting the pattern in the formula, which is gaining a CH*<sub>*2*</sub>* as you move down the alcohols*
- *The heat of combustion should be a value in between the values for ethanol and butan-1-ol, e.g. *$\frac{(1380+2680)}{2}$* = 2030 kJ / mol*
- *To balance the equation:*

  - *You are told that it is excess oxygen, which means that you are looking at complete combustion*
  - *5 carbons on the reactants side will form 5 carbon dioxide*
  
    - *C*<sub>*5*</sub>*H*<sub>*11*</sub>*OH + .......O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → 5CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + ..........*
  - *12 hydrogens on the reactants side will form 6 waters*
  
    - *C*<sub>*5*</sub>*H*<sub>*11*</sub>*OH + .......O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → 5CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + 6H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
  - *This means that you now have 16 oxygen atoms on the product side There is one oxygen atom in the alcohol, which means that 15 more oxygen atoms need to be accounted for The "missing" oxygen atoms come from the O*<sub>*2*</sub>* / oxygen molecule, which means that you need *$\frac{15}{2}$* or 7.5 oxygen molecules*
  
    - *C*<sub>*5*</sub>*H*<sub>*11*</sub>*OH + 7.5O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → 5CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + 6H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*

#### Extended Only

i) Ethanol is made from sugars by fermentation.

C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub> → 2C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH + 2CO<sub>2</sub>

Calculate the maximum mass of ethanol which could be obtained from 72 g of glucose.

**petroleum (alkanes) → ethene → ethanol**

** **[3]
parts.solutionMd:
d)

i) The maximum mass of ethanol that can be obtained from 72 g of glucose is:

Option 1:

- Moles of glucose: $\frac{72}{180}$ = 0.4; **[1 mark]**
- Maximum number of moles ethanol: 0.8; **[1 mark]**
- Maximum mass of ethanol *M*<sub>r</sub> = 46 g 
**AND ** 0.8 × 46 = 36.8 g; **[1 mark]**

Option 2:

- 180 (g) produces 2 × 46 = 92 (g); **[1 mark]**
- (72 (g) produces) $\frac{72}{180}$ × 92; **[1 mark]**
- 36.8 (g); **[1 mark]**

ii) Ethanol is made from petroleum by:

- Cracking (petroleum or alkane); **[1 mark]**
- Then reacting the ethene formed with water / hydrate (ethene to make ethanol); **[1 mark]**

Conditions:

**   One **of the following conditions for cracking:

- Temperature of 450 <sup>o</sup>C - 800 <sup>o</sup>C; **[1 mark]**

  - (Catalyst) zeolites / aluminosilicates / silica / aluminium oxide / alumina / china / broken pot / chromium oxide; **[1 mark]**

**One** of the following conditions for hydration:

- Temperature of 300 <sup>o</sup>C; **[1 mark] **

  - Pressure of 60 atmospheres; **[1 mark]**
  - Phosphoric acid (catalyst); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

- *To calculate the maximum mass of ethanol that can be produced, you need to determine the number of moles of ethanol that can be produced by 72 g of glucose*

  - *This can be done by working out the number of moles in 72 g of glucose *
  - *Then you use the equation to see that 1 glucose reacts to form 2 ethanol*
  - *Therefrore, the number of moles of ethanol will be double the number of moles of glucose*
  - *Finally, you multiply the number of moles of ethanol by the **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of ethanol*
- *Part (ii) requires you to recognise that the first reaction is cracking to form ethene and the second step is hydration of ethene*

  - *Since this question is for 3 marks, you need to add some more information so the conditions for cracking or hydration would be a sensible idea*

parts.solutionMd:
b)

- Catalyst / named catalyst, e.g. zeolites, alumina, aluminium oxide, aluminosilicate, silica or oxides of chromium; **[1 mark]**
- High pressure/ pressure in the range of 2 – 70 atm; **[1 mark]**
- Steam; **[1 mark]**
- Absence of air/ oxygen; **[1 mark]**

ii) An equation for the cracking of heptane into an alkane and an alkene is:

- C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>16</sub> → CH<sub>4</sub> + C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub> 
**OR **

**OR **

**OR **

- C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>16</sub> → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub> + C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub> + H<sub>2 </sub>
**OR **
C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>16</sub> → C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub> + C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>; **[1 mark]**

iv) **One **reason why cracking is important is:

Any **one **of the following:

- Alkenes are used to make chemicals / petrochemicals; **[1 mark]**
- Shorter alkanes / smaller molecules are used as fuels; **[1 mark]**
- Cracking produces more petrol (fraction) or hydrogen; **[1 mark]**
- Cracking produces lighter fractions from heavier fractions or suitable example, e.g. naphtha to gasoline; **[1 mark]**
- Cracking produces more useful smaller molecules; **[1 mark]**
- There is more demand for smaller molecules / fractions; **[1 mark]**
- Hydrogen produced from cracking is used to make ammonia / in Haber process / to hydrogenate vegetable oils / to make HCl; **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
A compound X contains carbon, hydrogen and oxygen only.

X contains 54.54% of carbon by mass, 9.09% of hydrogen by mass and 36.37% of oxygen by mass.

i) Calculate the empirical formula of compound X.

[2]

ii) Compound X has a relative molecular mass of 88.

Deduce the molecular formula of compound X.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
b)

i) The empirical formula of compound X is found by:

- (Moles of) C = 54.54/12 **OR **4.5 
**AND** 
(Moles of) H = 9.09/1 **OR **9.09 
**AND** 
(Moles of) O = 36.37/16 **OR **2.27; **[1 mark]**
- Empirical formula: C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O; **[1 mark]**

ii) The molecular formula of compound X is found by:

- *M*<sub>r</sub> of C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O = 44;** [1 mark]**
- (88/44 = 2 therefore molecular formula is) C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>2</sub>;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *To calculate the empirical formula when given percentages, it is easiest to assume that you have 100 g of the sample, then you can work out the number of moles of each element in 100 g by using the **M*<sub>*r*</sub>*:*

|   | > *C* | > *H* | > *O* |
|---|---|---|---|
| > *Calculate the number of moles of each element in 100g (%/**M*<sub>*r*</sub>*)* | $\frac{54.54}{12}\,=4.5$ | $\frac{9.09}{1}\,=9.09$ | $\frac{36.37}{16}\,=2.27$ |
| > *Divide by the smallest number to find the smallest ratio* | > * 4.5/2.27 = 2* | > * 9.09/2.27 = 4* | > * 2.27/2.27 = 1* |

- *The empirical formula is therefore C*<sub>*2*</sub>*H*<sub>*4*</sub>*O*
- *Compound X has twice the** M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of the empirical formula, therefore compound X must contain twice the number of atoms that appears in the empirical formula*

parts.problemMd:
A piece of magnesium was added to 100 cm<sup>3</sup> of an aqueous acid. The time taken for the metal to react completely was measured. This experiment was repeated using different aqueous acids. The same volume of acid was used in each experiment and the pieces of magnesium used were identical. In one experiment the reaction was carried out at a different temperature.

| experiment | acid | concentration in mol / dm<sup>3</sup> | temperature / <sup>o</sup>C | time / minutes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | propanoic | 1.0 | 20 | 5 |
| B | propanoic | 1.0 | 30 | 3 |
| C | propanoic | 0.5 | 20 | 8 |
| D | hydrochloric | 1.0 | 20 | 1 |

Explain the following in terms of collision rate between reacting particles.

i) Why is the rate in experiment **C** slower than the rate in experiment **A**?

[2]

ii) Why is the rate in experiment **B** faster than the rate in experiment **A**?

[2]

iii) Why is the rate in experiment **D** faster than the rate in experiment **A**?

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
d)

i) The rate in experiment **C** is slower than the rate in experiment **A** because:

- The concentration (of acid in **C**) is less / halved 
**OR **
The concentration of **A** is more / doubled; **[1 mark]**
- Therefore, there are less <u>frequent</u> (successful) collisions in **C**
**OR **
Therefore, there are more <u>frequent</u> (successful) collisions in **A**; **[1 mark]**

ii) The rate in experiment **B** is faster than the rate in experiment **A** because:

- The particles in **B** move faster / have more energy / more have *E*<sub>a</sub> 
**OR **
The particles in **A** move slower / have less energy / less have *E*<sub>a</sub>; **[1 mark]** 
*Accept molecules or atoms in place of the word particles*
- Therefore, there are less <u>frequent</u> (successful) collisions in **A OR **
Therefore, there are more <u>frequent</u> (successful) collisions in **B**; **[1 mark] **

iii) The rate in experiment **D** is faster than the rate in experiment **A** because:

- **D** is a strong acid **AND **A is a weak acid 
**OR **
**D** is a stronger acid / **A **is a weaker acid 
**OR **
**D** ionises / dissociates more 
**OR **
**A** ionises / dissociates less;** [1 mark]**
- **D **has a higher concentration of hydrogen ions 
**OR **
**A** has a lower concentration of hydrogen ions; **[1 mark]**
- Therefore, there are less <u>frequent</u> (successful) collisions in **A OR **
Therefore, there are more <u>frequent</u> (successful) collisions in **D**; **[1 mark] **

**[Total: 7 marks]**

- *The key to this question is recognising what each row of information is actually telling you and then linking that change to the appropriate collision theory explanation*

  - *Rows **A **and **B** have different temperatures*
  
    - *This should lead you to ideas about the energy of the particles and the frequency of collisions*
  - *Rows **A** and **C** have different acid concentrations*
  
    - *This should lead you to ideas about the number of particles and the frequency of collisions*
  - *Rows **A **and **D **have different acid strengths*
  
    - *This is more subtle than rows **A **and **C **because it is still about the concentration of the particles but this is changing due to the strength of the acid and how much it dissociates into its ions*

name ..........................................................................................................

[3]

What is meant by the term *weak acid*?

[3]
parts.solutionMd:

;** [1 mark]**

ii) **Three **characteristics of a homologous series are:

Any **three **of the following:

- Same general formula; **[1 mark]**
- Same functional group; **[1 mark]**
- Successive / consecutive members differ by CH<sub>2</sub>; **[1 mark]**
- Same or similar chemical properties; **[1 mark]**
- A gradual change / trend in physical properties
**OR**
An example of a gradual change / trend in a physical property i.e. melting point / boiling point / volatility; **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part (i), the carbon in the -COOH group counts as one of the four carbons in butanoic acid. A common mistake is drawing five carbons by adding four carbons to the functional group carbon.
> 
> When asked for a structural formula, draw every bond line explicitly. It is good practice as sometimes writing -OH instead of -O-H will lose you a mark.
> 
> For part (ii), write "similar chemical properties," not "same." Members undergo the same types of reactions but rates vary with molecular size. Write "gradual change" or "trend" for physical properties, not just "different physical properties."

> For part (iii), "partially dissociates" scores 2 of the 3 marks on its own. To get the third, you must state that it is a proton / H⁺ donor. Do not confuse "weak" with "dilute" — dilute refers to concentration, weak refers to incomplete ionisation.

- Contains only single bonds
**OR**

parts.problemMd:
#### Separate: Chemistry and Extended Only

A compound **X** contains 82.76% of carbon by mass and 17.24% of hydrogen by mass.

i) Calculate the empirical formula of compound **X**.

[2]

ii) Compound **X** has a relative molecular mass of 58.

Deduce the molecular formula of compound **X**.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
a)

i) The empirical formula can be found by:

- 82.76 / 12 **AND **17.2(4) (/1) 
**OR** 
Evaluation: 6.897 / 6.9(0) **AND **17.2(4); **[1 mark]**
- Empirical formula: C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>;** [1 mark]**

**OR**

- 82.76 / 100 x 58 = 48 **AND **17.24 / 100 x 58 = 10 
**OR** 
Evaluation i.e. 48 **AND **10; **[1 mark]**
- Empirical formula: C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>;** [1 mark]**

ii) The molecular formula of compound **X** can be found by:

- (*M*<sub>r</sub> of C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub> =) 29; **[1 mark]**
- (58 / 29 = 2) C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>;** [1 mark]**

**OR**

- 82.76 / 100 × 58 = 48 **AND **17.24 / 100 × 58 = 10 
**OR** 
Evaluation i.e. 48 **AND **10; **[1 mark]**
- 48 / 12 = 4 **AND** 10 / 1 = 10 (therefore) C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *To calculate the empirical formula when given percentages, it is easiest to assume that you have 100 g of the sample, then you can work out the number of moles of each element in 100 g by using the **M*<sub>*r*</sub>*:*

|   | > *C* | > *H* |
|---|---|---|
| > *Calculate the number of moles of each element in 100g (% / **M*<sub>*r*</sub>*)* | $\frac{82.76}{12}\,=6.897$ | $\frac{17.24}{1}\,=17.24$ |
| > *Divide by the smallest number to find the smallest ratio* | > *6.897/6.897 = 1* | > * 17.24/6.897 = 2.5* |
| > *Multiply both by the same number to give a whole number ratio* | > *1 x 2 = 2* | > *2.5 x 2 = 5* |

- *The empirical formula is therefore C*<sub>*2*</sub>*H*<sub>*5*</sub>
- *M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of compound X  = (2 x 12) + (5 x 1) = 29*
- *M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of compound X = 59*
- *59 / 29 = 2*
- *Therefore the molecular formula is 2 x C*<sub>*2*</sub>*H*<sub>*5 *</sub>*= C*<sub>*4*</sub>*H*<sub>*10*</sub>

parts.problemMd:
#### Separate: Chemistry and Extended Only

Esters, polyesters and fats all contain the ester linkage.

Esters can be made from alcohols and carboxylic acids. For example, the ester ethyl ethanoate can be made by the following reaction.

CH<sub>3</sub>COOH + CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH → CH<sub>3</sub>COOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3 </sub>+ H<sub>2</sub>O

i) Name the carboxylic acid and the alcohol from which the following ester could be made.

![ethyl-ethanoate](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-chemistry-23/11-organic-chemistry/11-2-organic-families/assets/090-ethyl-ethanoate.png)

[2]

ii) 6.0 g of ethanoic acid, *M*<sub>r </sub>= 60, was reacted with 5.5 g of ethanol, *M*<sub>r </sub>= 46.  Determine which is the limiting reagent and the maximum yield of ethyl ethanoate, *M*<sub>r </sub>= 88.

Number of moles of ethanoic acid =

[1]

Number of moles of ethanol =

[1]

The limiting reagent is

[1]

Number of moles of ethyl ethanoate formed =

[1]

Maximum yield of ethyl ethanoate =

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
a)

i) The carboxylic acid and the alcohol from which the ester could be made are:

- Butanoic acid; **[1 mark]**
- Methanol; **[1 mark]**

ii) The limiting reagent and the maximum yield of ethyl ethanoate can be found by:

- Number of moles of ethanoic acid = mass/molar mass = 6.0/60 = 0.1 moles; **[1 mark]**
- Number of moles of ethanol = mass/molar mass = 5.5/46 = 0.12 moles; **[1 mark]**
- The limiting reagent is ethanoic acid; **[1 mark]**
- Number of moles of ethyl ethanoate formed = 0.1 moles; **[1 mark]**
- Maximum yield of ethyl ethanoate = moles x molar mass = 0.1 x 88 = 8.8 g; **[1 mark]**

Bond breaking is an endothermic change and bond forming is an exothermic change.  Bond energy is the amount of energy in kJ / mol needed to break one mole of the specified bond.

![propane--cl2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-chemistry-23/11-organic-chemistry/11-2-organic-families/assets/065-propane-cl2.png)

Use the following bond energies to determine whether this reaction is exothermic or endothermic. You must show your reasoning.

| **Bond** | **Bond energies in kJ / mol** |
|---|---|
| C-Cl | 338 |
| C-H | 412 |
| Cl-Cl | 242 |
| H-Cl | 431 |
| C-C | 348 |
parts.solutionMd:
b) To determine whether this reaction is exothermic or endothermic:

- Bonds breaking = (8 × 412) + (2 × 348) + 242 = 4234;** [1 mark]**
- Bonds forming = (7 × 412) + (2 × 348) + 338 + 431 = 4349; **[1 mark]**
- 4234 – 4349 = –115 **AND **exothermic;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *It is very easy make errors in these types of calculations by not accounting for all of the bonds in the reactants and prodcuts*
- *It is a good idea to draw the displayed formula, if not provided, then as you include the bond in your calculation, cross the bond out*
- *In this case, the bonds being broken in the reactants are:*

  - *8 x C-H, 2 x C-C, 1 x Cl-Cl*
- *These are used to work out the energy taken in by the reaction in breaking these bonds*
- *The bonds being formed are:*

  - *7 x C-H, 2 x C-C, 1 x C-Cl and 1 x H-Cl*
- *These are used to work out the energy given out in the reaction when new bonds are formed*
- *The following equation** **is then used to calculate the overall enthalpy change *

  - *enthalpy change (Δ**H**)  = energy taken in - energy given out is then used to calculate the overall enthalpy change*
  - *If this value is positive, the reaction is endothermic*
  - *If it is negative as it is in this question, it is exothermic*

parts.problemMd:
Propanol reacts with methanoic acid to form the ester propyl methanoate.

CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH + HCOOH → HCOOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O

4.0 g of methanoic acid was reacted with 6.0 g of propanol.

i) Calculate the *M*<sub>r</sub> of methanoic acid.

[1]

ii) Calculate the* M*<sub>r </sub>of propanol.

[1]

iii) Determine which one is the limiting reagent. Show your reasoning.

[2]

iv) Calculate the maximum yield in grams of propyl methanoate, *M*<sub>r </sub>= 88.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
d)

i) The *M*<sub>r</sub> of methanoic acid is:

- 46;** [1 mark]**

ii) The* M*<sub>r </sub>of propanol is:

- 60; **[1 mark]**

iii) The limiting reagent and reason why is:

- Moles of CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH (= $\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{\mathrm{molar} \mathrm{mass}}=\frac{6.0}{60}$) = 0.1 moles; **[1 mark]**
- Moles of HCOOH (= $\frac{4.0}{46}$) = 0.087 (0.09) and limiting reagent is methanoic acid;** [1 mark]**

iv) The maximum yield in grams of propyl methanoate is:

- (= mass x molar mass =) 88 x (mol of limiting reagent in 4(d)(iii)); **[1 mark]** *Expected answer: 88 × 0.087 = 7.65 g*

**[Total: 5 marks]**

- *M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of methanoic acid: (1 X C) + (2 x H) + (2 x O) = (1 x 12) + (2 x 1) + (2 x 16) = 46*
- *M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of propanol: (3 X C) + (8 x H) + (1 x O) = (3 x 12) + (8 x 1) + (1 x 16) = 60*
- *M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of propyl methanoate: (4 X C) + (8 x H) + (2 x O) = (4 x 12) + (8 x 1) + (2 x 16) = 88*
- *The balanced symbol equation shows equal number of moles of methanoic acid and propanol will react*
- *There are more moles present of propanol, therefore this is in excess and the limiting reagent is methanoic acid*

parts.problemMd:
The alcohols form a homologous series.

i) Give **three **characteristics which all members of a homologous series share.

[3]

ii) Give the name of the third member of this series.

[1]

iii) Deduce the molecular formula of the alcohol whose *M*<sub>r</sub> = 158. Show your working.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
a)

i)** Three **characteristics of a homologous series are:

Any **three **of the following:

- Same general formula; **[1 mark]**
- Consecutive members differ by CH<sub>2</sub>; **[1 mark]**
- Similar / same chemical properties; **[1 mark]**
- Same functional group; **[1 mark]**
- Physical properties vary in a predictable way / give trends such as mp increases with n; **[1 mark]**

ii) The name of the third member of this series is:

- Propanol / propan-1-ol / propan-2-ol; **[1 mark]**

iii) The molecular formula of the alcohol whose *M*<sub>r</sub> = 158 is:

- If molecular formula is given as C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>22</sub>O / C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>21</sub>OH award **[2 marks]**
- If not, look for evidence of some correct working for one mark 158 – 17 = 141 
**OR** 
12n + 2n + 1 = 141 
**OR** 
n = 10; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

- *You need to know what a homologous series is and how this affects the properties of the chemicals within  a homologous series*
- *To work out the molecular formula of the alcohol whose **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* is 158:*

  - *It must have an -OH group, whose **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* is 16 + 1 = 17*
  - *The carbon chain must have an **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of 158 - 17 = 141*
  - *The carbon chain will have one CH*<sub>*3*</sub>* group and some CH*<sub>*2*</sub>* groups*
  - *M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of CH*<sub>*3*</sub>* = 12 + (3 x 1) = 15*
  - *141 - 15 = 126*
  - *Therefore the **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of the CH*<sub>*2*</sub>* groups must = 126*
  - *M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of one CH*<sub>*2*</sub>* group = 12 + (2 x 1) = 14*
  - *126/14 = 9 so there are 9 CH*<sub>*2*</sub>* groups*
  - *Therefore the formula is C*<sub>*10*</sub>*H*<sub>*21*</sub>*OH*

parts.problemMd:
The alcohols form a homologous series. The first member of this series is methanol, CH<sub>3</sub>OH.

i) Give the general formula of the alcohols.

[1]

ii) The mass of one mole of an alcohol is 116 g. What is its formula? Show your reasoning.

[2]

ii) Draw a diagram showing the arrangement of the outer (valency) electrons in one molecule of methanol.

Use x to represent an electron from a carbon atom. 
Use o to represent an electron from a hydrogen atom. 
Use ● to represent an electron from an oxygen atom.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
a)

i) The general formula of the alcohols is:

- C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+1</sub>OH; **[1 mark]**

ii) The formula of the alcohol is:

- 116 - 17 = 99, 12n + (2n + 1) = 99, n = 7; **[1 mark]** *For any evidence of valid working out award 1 mark*
- C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>15</sub>OH; **[1 mark]**

iii) A diagram showing the arrangement of the outer (valency) electrons in one molecule of methanol is:

![methanol-dot-and-cross](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-chemistry-23/11-organic-chemistry/11-2-organic-families/assets/032-methanol-dot-and-cross.png)

- 8 bonded electrons around C; **[1 mark]**
- 2 bonded electrons on each hydrogen; **[1 mark]**
- 4 bonded electrons and 4 non-bonded electrons on oxygen; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

- *The **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* due to OH = 16 + 1 = 17*
- *So the **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* due to C*<sub>*n*</sub>*H*<sub>*2n+1*</sub>* = 116 - 17 = 99*
- *The mass due to carbon is 12 x n = 12n*
- *The mass due to hydrogen is 1 x (2n + 1) = 2n + 1*
- *So, the mass due to carbon and hydrogen is 99:*

  - *12n + (2n+1) = 99*
  - *Simplifying gives 14n + 1 = 99*
  - *Rearranging: 14n = 98*
  - *n = 98/14 = 7*
- *Giving the formula C*<sub>*7*</sub>*H*<sub>*15*</sub>*OH*
- *When drawing the dot and cross diagram, check that all the electron shells are complete*

  - *Carbon and oxygen should have 8 electrons in their shell*
  - *Hydrogen should have 2 electrons*

parts.problemMd:
20 cm<sup>3 </sup>of a hydrocarbon was burnt in 175 cm<sup>3</sup> of oxygen. After cooling, the volume of the remaining gases was

125 cm<sup>3</sup>. The addition of aqueous sodium hydroxide removed carbon dioxide leaving 25 cm<sup>3</sup> of unreacted oxygen.

Volume of oxygen used = .......... cm<sup>3</sup>

[1]

Volume of carbon dioxide formed = .......... cm<sup>3</sup>

[1]

Deduce the formula of the hydrocarbon and the balanced equation for the reaction.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
d) To determine the formula of the hydrocarbon and write a balanced equation:

- Volume of oxygen used = 150 cm<sup>3</sup>; **[1 mark]**
- Volume of carbon dioxide formed: 100 cm<sup>3</sup>; **[1 mark]**
- Correct equation of the combustion of an pentene; **[2 marks]** e.g. 2C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub> + 15O<sub>2</sub> → 10CO<sub>2</sub> + 10H<sub>2</sub>O 
*Accept multiples *
*Accept 1 mark for correct equation for a different alkene*

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *The general equation for complete combustion is:*

  - *hydrocarbon + oxygen → carbon dioxide + oxygen*
- *After addition of sodium hydroxide, you are told that 25 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* of unreacted oxygen remains, meaning that oxygen must be in excess and the hydrocarbon is the limiting reactant*
- *To calculate the volume of oxygen that reacted:*

  - *Initial volume = 175 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>
  - *The total amount of gas produced after cooling is 25 cm*<sup>*3 *</sup>*which would include oxygen and carbon dioxide*
  - *Carbon dioxide was removed by the sodium hydroxide leaving 25 cm*<sup>*3 *</sup>*of unreacted oxygen *
  - *Therefore the volume of oxygen that reacted = 175 - 25 = 150 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>
- *To calculate the volume of carbon dioxide that was produced:*

  - *The total volume of gases produced was 125 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* but 25 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* was oxygen*
  - *Therefore, the volume of carbon dioxide produced = 125 - 25 = 100 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>
- *Once you know these volumes, you can use the fact that equal amounts of gases occupy the same volume of space*
- *So, the volume of gases produced tells you the molar ratio that reacts:*

  - *The ratio of hydrocarbon:oxygen:carbon dioxide is 20:150:100 *
  - *Or simplified: 2:15:10*
- *We can substitute this to give an unbalanced equation, using CxHy to represent the hydrocarbon:*

  - *2C*<sub>*x*</sub>*H*<sub>*y*</sub>* + 15O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O + 10CO*<sub>*2*</sub>
- *Now you need to work out the formula of the hydrocarbon and the number of moles of H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O present:*

  - *2C*<sub>*5*</sub>*H*<sub>*y*</sub>* + 15O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O + 10CO*<sub>*2*</sub>

  - *2C*<sub>*5*</sub>*H*<sub>*y*</sub>* + 15O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → 10H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O + 10CO*<sub>*2*</sub>

  - *2C*<sub>*5*</sub>*H*<sub>*10*</sub>* + 15O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → 10H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O + 10CO*<sub>*2*</sub>

  - *There are 10 C atoms on the RHS, so there must be 10 C atoms in the hydrocarbon:*
  - *There are 30 O atoms on the LHS and 20 already on the RHS, so 10 more are needed on the RHS:*
  - *There are now 20 H atoms on the RHS, so there must be 10 within the hydrocarbon:*
- *The formula of the hydrocarbon obeys the general equation C*<sub>*n*</sub>*H*<sub>*2n*</sub>* therefore it is the alkene, pentene*

parts.solutionMd:
a) The completed table is:

| ethanol | CH<sub>3</sub> –CH<sub>2</sub> –OH | 46 | 78 |
| propan-1-ol | CH<sub>3</sub> –CH<sub>2 </sub>–CH<sub>2</sub> –OH | 60 | 98 |

- *The mass of one mole can be found by adding up the Ar of all of the atoms in pentan-1-ol:*

  - *(5 x 12) + (12 x 1) + (1 x 16) = 88*

parts.problemMd:
Propene reacts with hydrogen iodide to form 2-iodopropane.

CH<sub>3</sub>−CH=CH<sub>2</sub> + HI →  CH<sub>3</sub>−CHI−CH<sub>3</sub>

1.4 g of propene produced 4.0 g of 2-iodopropane. Calculate the percentage yield.

moles of CH<sub>3</sub>–CH=CH<sub>2</sub> reacted = .........................................

maximum moles of CH<sub>3</sub>–CHI–CH<sub>3</sub> that could be formed = .........................................

mass of one mole of CH<sub>3</sub>–CHI–CH<sub>3</sub> = 170 g

maximum mass of 2- iodopropane that could be formed = .........................................

percentage yield ......................................... %
parts.solutionMd:
d) To calculate the percentage yield:

- Moles of CH<sub>3</sub>-CH = CH<sub>2</sub> reacted = $\frac{1.4}{42}$ = 0.033 mol; **[1 mark]**
- Maximum moles of CH<sub>3</sub>-CH(I)-CH<sub>3</sub> that could be formed = 0.033 mol; **[1 mark]**
- Maximum mass of 2-iodopropane that could be formed = 5.61 g; **[1 mark]** 
*Accept 170 x 0.033 = 5.61 and 170 x 0.033333 = 5.67*
- Percentage yield $\frac{4.0}{5.61}$ x 100 = 70.5%; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *To calculate percentage yield we use: *$\frac{\mathrm{actual} \mathrm{yield}}{\mathrm{theoretical} \mathrm{yield}}\times100$
- *We therefore need to calculate first the theoretical yield of 2-iodopropane *
- *The moles of CH*<sub>*3*</sub>*–CH=CH*<sub>*2*</sub>* reacted are determined by using: *$\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{\mathrm{molar} \mathrm{mass}}\mathrm{so}\frac{1.4}{4.2}=0.033\mathrm{mol}$
- *Using the equation, we can see the molar ratio of CH*<sub>*3*</sub>*–CH=CH*<sub>*2*</sub>* to CH*<sub>*3*</sub>*−CHI−CH*<sub>*3 *</sub>*is 1:1 and so the number of moles are the same= 0.033 mol*
- *The maximum (theoretical) mass of 2-iodopropane that could be formed = number of moles x molar mass = 0.033 x 170 = 5.61 g*
- *Then calculate percentage yield: *$\frac{4.0}{5.61} = 70.5 \%$

**Extract:**

0.01 moles of an alkene needed 2.4 g of oxygen for complete combustion. 2.2 g of carbon dioxide were formed.

0.01 moles of an alkene needed 2.4 g of oxygen for complete combustion. 2.2 g of carbon dioxide were formed.

Determine the following mole ratio.

moles of alkene : moles of O<sub>2</sub> : moles of CO<sub>2</sub>

From this ratio determine the formula of the alkene.

[3]

Write an equation for the complete combustion of this alkene.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
e)

i) The formula of the alkene and an equation for the complete combustion of this alkene are:

- Moles of O<sub>2 </sub>(= 2.4/32 =) 0.075 mol 
**AND** 
moles of CO<sub>2</sub> (= 2.2/44 =) 0.05 mol; **[1 mark]**
- Molar ratio: 1:7.5:5 
**OR** 
2:15:10; **[1 mark]**
- Formula of the alkene is C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>

ii) Equation for complete combustion of the alkene:

- Accept any correct equation for the complete combustion of C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>; **[1 mark]** 
*E.g 2C*<sub>*5*</sub>*H*<sub>*10 *</sub>*+ 15O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → 10CO*<sub>*2 *</sub>*+ 10H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O *
*Accept multiples including fractions *
*Allow: ecf for correct equation from any correct alkene including*

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *Complete combustion occurs when a fuel reacts with oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water *
- *The word equation would be:*

  - *Alkene + oxygen →    carbon dioxide + water *
- *You are given the number of moles of the alkene = **0.01 mol*
- *You are given the mass of oxygen and carbon dioxide so can use these to find the moles of the oxygen and carbon dioxide (as shown in the mark scheme) *

  - *Oxygen 2.4    32 = **0.075 mol*
  - *Carbon dioxide = 2.2    44=** 0.05 mol*
- *You therefore have:  0.01   :   0.075    :   0.05 *
- *To calculate the ratio divide each of these by the smallest number which is 0.01*

  - *This gives you the ratio of 1     :      7.5     :     5 or if you double it 2     :     15     :     10*
- *From this you know that you have five moles of carbon dioxide so you therefore have an alkene with five carbons*
- *The general formula for alkenes is C*<sub>*n*</sub>*H*<sub>*2n*</sub>* so if you have 5 carbons you have 10 hydrogen atoms *
- *Put this information into the equation  *

  - *C*<sub>*5*</sub>*H*<sub>*10*</sub>*      +     7.5O*<sub>*2 *</sub>*    →     5CO*<sub>*2*</sub>*    +     H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
- *Balance the rest of the equation*

  - *C*<sub>*5*</sub>*H*<sub>*10*</sub>*      +     7.5O*<sub>*2 *</sub>*    →     5CO*<sub>*2*</sub>*    +     **5**H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
- *This answer is accepted or you could double the 7.5 to achieve a whole number 15, but remember to double the other substances too*

parts.problemMd:
Maleic acid is an unsaturated acid. 5.8 g of this acid contained 2.4 g of carbon, 0.2 g of hydrogen and 3.2 g of oxygen.

i) How do you know that the acid contained only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen?

[1]

ii) Calculate the empirical formula of maleic acid.

Number of moles of carbon atoms = ................................

Number of moles of hydrogen atoms = ................................

Number of moles of oxygen atoms = ................................

The empirical formula is .................................................

[3]

iii) The mass of one mole of maleic acid is 116 g. What is its molecular formula?

[2]

iv) Maleic acid is dibasic. One mole of acid produces two moles of H<sup>+</sup>. Deduce its structural formula.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
b)

i) You know that the acid contained only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen because:

- Their masses add up to 5.8 g ; **[1 mark]**

ii) The empirical formula of maleic acid is calculated by:

Number of moles of carbon atoms = 2.4/12 = 0.2

Number of moles of hydrogen atoms = 0.2/1 = 0.2

Number of moles of oxygen atoms = 3.2/16 = 0.2

- All three correct = **[2 marks]** 
Two correct = **[1 mark]**
- The empirical formula is CHO; **[1 mark]**

iii) The molecular formula of maleic acid is:

- 116/29 = 4; **[1 mark]**
- C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O<sub>4</sub>; **[1 mark]** 
*Correct formula with no working scores both marks.*

iv) The structural formula of maleic acid is:

HOOCCH=CHCOOH / CH<sub>2</sub>=C(COOH)<sub>2</sub>

- Double bond present;** [1 mark]**
- Correct number of C, H and O atoms and rest of structural formula correct;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 8 marks]**

- *To calculate the empirical formula:*

|   | > *C* | > *H* | > *O* |
|---|---|---|---|
| > *Calculate the number of moles of each element (mass/**M*<sub>*r*</sub>*)* | $\frac{2.4}{12}\,=0.2$ | $\frac{0.2}{1}\,=0.2$ | $\frac{3.2}{16}\,=0.2$ |
| > *Divide by the smallest number to find the smallest ratio* | > * 0.2/0.2 = 1* | > *0.2/0.2 = 1 * | > *0.2/0.2 = 1 * |

- *The empirical formula is therefore CHO*
- *The **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of the empirical formula is 12 + 1 + 16 = 29*
- *The** M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of the compound is 116/29 = 4 times greater than the **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of the empirical formula therefore the molecular formula of maliec acid must contain 4 times the number of atoms than appears in the empirical formula*
- *As maliec acid is dibasic, it must contain 2 -COOH groups so that it can donate 2 moles of H*<sup>*+*</sup>* ions for every 1 mole of acid*
- *The **M*<sub>*r *</sub>* of the two  -COOH groups is 2 x (12 + (2 x 16) + 1 = ) = 90*
- *This leaves 116 - 90 = 26 which must come from C and H atoms*
- *This must be from 2 C atoms and 2 H atoms: (2 x 12) + (2 x 1) = 26*
- *This means that maliec acid must contain a double bond, otherwise there would be 2 more hydrogen atoms present*

parts.problemMd:
The alkanes are generally unreactive. Their reactions include combustion, substitution and cracking.

The complete combustion of an alkane gives carbon dioxide and water.

i) 10 cm<sup>3</sup> of butane is mixed with 100 cm<sup>3</sup> of oxygen, which is an excess. The mixture is ignited. What is the volume of unreacted oxygen left and what is the volume of carbon dioxide formed?

C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub> (g) + 6.5O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 4CO<sub>2</sub> (g) + 5H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

Volume of oxygen left = .................................................. cm<sup>3</sup>

Volume of carbon dioxide formed = ................................. cm<sup>3</sup>

[2]

ii) Why is the incomplete combustion of any alkane dangerous, particularly in an enclosed space?

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
a)

i) The volumes are:

- Volume of oxygen left = 35 cm<sup>3</sup>;** [1 mark]**
- Volume of carbon dioxide formed = 40 cm<sup>3</sup>; **[1 mark]**

ii) Incomplete combustion of any alkane, particularly in an enclosed space, is dangerous because:

- It forms carbon monoxide;** [1 mark]**
- Which is poisonous / toxic / lethal 
**OR **
Which prevents blood carrying oxygen / effect(s) on haemoglobin; **[1 mark]** 
*Harmful is not an accepted answer*

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *There are two ways of calculating the volume of oxygen and carbon dioxide, one is more complicated than the other*
- *Method 1:*

  - *This uses the concept that equal volumes of gases will occupy the same volume, regardless of what type of gaseous species it is*
  - *So, 10 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* of butane contains the same number of moles as 10 cm*<sup>*3 *</sup>*of carbon dioxide or 10 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* of oxygen*
  - *Using the balanced symbol equation, you can see that 1 mole of butane will react with 6.5 moles of oxygen, therefore 10cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* of butane will react with 10 x 6.5 = 65 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* of oxygen*
  - *Initially, there was 100 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* of oxygen, therefore the volume of oxygen remaining = 100 - 65 = 35 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>
  - *Also, 1 mole of butane will form 4 moles of carbon dioxide, therefore 10 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* of butane forms 10 x 4 = 40 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* of carbon dioxide*
- *Method 2:*

  - *This involves calculating the number of moles of butane*
  - *In both cases, you have to determine the number of moles of butane and then apply that to determine the volumes of oxygen remaining and carbon dioxide formed*
  - *Moles of butane =  = 0.000417 mol*
  - *Oxygen remaining*
  
    - *There are 6.5 times more moles of oxygen used in the reaction = 0.0027803 moles*
    - *This corresponds to 0.0027803 x 24 000 = 65 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* of oxygen that are consumed in the reaction*
    - *Therefore, there are 100 - 65 = 35 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* of oxygen remaining*
  - *Carbon dioxide formed*
  
    - *There are 4 times more moles of carbon dioxide formed in the reaction = 0.00167 moles*
    - *This corresponds to 0.00167 x 24 000 = 40 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* of carbon dioxide are formed in the reaction*
- *Incomplete combustion of hydrocarbons releases carbon dioxide (and carbon particulates) *

  - *Carbon monoxide is harmful to the human body but, nowadays, the word harmful is insufficient for any marks, so you have to be more specific by saying that it is poisonous / toxic / lethal or describe the effects that it has on haemoglobin and the blood's ability to transport oxygen*

parts.problemMd:
An unknown alcohol, **A**, has the following composition by mass: C = 37.5%;  H = 12.5%;  O = 50.0%

Determine the empirical formula of compound **A**. Show all your working.

empirical formula = .......................
parts.solutionMd:
For determining the empirical formula, you must follow these simple steps:

**Step 1: **Calculate the amount of moles using the percentages as the amount of grams in the sample

$\mathrm{moles}=\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{M_{r}}$

Carbon (C):

$n=\frac{37.5}{12}=3.125$

Hydrogen (H):

$n=\frac{12.5}{1}=12.5$

Oxygen (O):

$n=\frac{50}{16}=3.125$

**[1 mark]**

**Step 2: **Divide each number of moles by the smallest number among them

- In this case, the smallest number of moles is **3.125**

Carbon (C):

$n=\frac{3.125}{3.125}=1$

Hydrogen (H):

$n=\frac{12.5}{3.125}=4$

Oxygen (O):

$n=\frac{3.125}{3.125}=1$

**[1 mark]**

**Step 3: **Use the calculated whole numbers as the subscripts for each element, indicating the amount of atoms in the empirical formula

The empirical formula of **A** is **CH**<sub>**4**</sub>**O ****[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for calculating the amount of moles correctly
> 
> 1 mark for dividing the number of moles by the smallest among them
> 
> 1 mark for reporting the correct answer

> **[exam-tip]**
> In empirical formula calculations, keep **up to three decimal places in intermediate steps** (such as when calculating moles). Only round at the end. If the final ratios end in **0.5**, multiply all values by **2**; if they end in **0.33 or 0.67**, multiply all values by **3** to obtain whole-number ratios.

parts.solutionMd:
To determine the molecular formula from the empirical formula, follow these steps:

**Step 1: **Add the relative atomic masses of the atoms in the empirical formula.

For **CH**<sub>**2**</sub>**O**:

*M*<sub>r</sub> empirical formula = C + 2 ×  H + O

*M*<sub>r</sub> empirical formula  = 12 + 2 + 16

*M*<sub>r</sub> empirical formula  =** 30** **[1 mark]**

**Step 2: **Divide the molecular mass by the empirical formula mass to obtain a whole number

Molecular mass =** **60

whole number = 60 ÷ 30 = 2

**Step 3: **Multiply all atoms in the empirical formula times the calculated whole number

(CH<sub>2</sub>O) × 2

The molecular formula is **C**<sub>**2**</sub>**H**<sub>**4**</sub>**O**<sub>**2 **</sub>**[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
#### Separate: Chemistry and Extended Only

A compound **X** contains 82.76% of carbon by mass and 17.24% of hydrogen by mass.

i) Calculate the empirical formula of compound **X**.

[2]

ii) Compound **X **has a relative molecular mass of 58.

Deduce the molecular formula of compound **X**.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
a)

i) The empirical formula of compound **X** is:

- Moles of carbon $=\frac{82.76}{12}=$ 6.897 
**AND **
Moles of hydrogen $=\frac{17.24}{1}=$ 17.24;** [1 mark]**
- Empirical formula = C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>; **[1 mark]**

ii) The molecular formula of compound X is:

- *M*<sub>r</sub> of C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub> = 29; **[1 mark]**
- $\frac{58}{29}$ = 2, therefore the molecular formula is C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *You can lay empirical formula calculations out in one templated style (EVADRA) that works for all empirical formula calculations:*
- *Instruction* |   | > * * | > * * |
|---|---|---|
| > *Elements - write them* | > *C* | > *H* |
| > *Values - taken from the question as % or g* | > *82.76* | > *17.24* |
| > *Atomic mass* | > *12* | > *1* |
| > *Divide - the calculation is already laid out correctly * | > $\frac{82.76}{12}$* = 6.897* | > $\frac{17.24}{1}$* = 17.24* |
| > *Ratio - divide by the smallest answer* | > $\frac{6.897}{6.897}$* = 1* | > $\frac{17.24}{6.897}$* = 2.50* |
| > *Answer - write the final empirical formula **Remember: **An empirical formula had to have whole numbers* | > *C*<sub>*2*</sub>* * | > *H*<sub>*5*</sub>* * |
- *To calculate the molecular formula using an empirical formula and a relative molecular mass:*

  - *Find the mass of the empirical formula*
  
    - *C*<sub>*2*</sub>*H*<sub>*5*</sub>* = (2 x 12) + (5 x 1) = 29*
  - *Divide the relative molecular mass by the mass of the empirical formula*
  
    - $\frac{58}{29}$* = 2*
  - *Apply the answer to the empirical formula*
  
    - *C*<sub>*2*</sub>*H*<sub>*5*</sub>* x 2 = C*<sub>*4*</sub>*H*<sub>*10*</sub>* *

| > *C*<sub>*x*</sub>*H*<sub>*y*</sub>* + * | > *O*<sub>*2*</sub>* →* | > *CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + * | > *H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O* |

parts.problemMd:
A compound X contains carbon, hydrogen and oxygen only.

X contains 54.54% of carbon by mass, 9.09% of hydrogen by mass and 36.37% of oxygen by mass.

i) Calculate the empirical formula of compound X.

[2]

ii) Compound X has a relative molecular mass of 88.

Deduce the molecular formula of compound X.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
b)

i) The empirical formula of compound X is:

- Moles of carbon $=\frac{54.54}{12}=$ 4.5(45) 
**AND **
Moles of hydrogen $=\frac{9.09}{1}=$ 9.09 
**AND **
Moles of oxygen $=\frac{36.37}{16}=$2.27;** [1 mark]**
- Empirical formula = C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O; **[1 mark]**

ii) The molecular formula of compound X is:

- *M*<sub>r</sub> of C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O = 44; **[1 mark]**
- $\frac{88}{44}$ = 2, therefore the molecular formula is C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>2</sub>;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *You can lay empirical formula calculations out in one templated style (EVADRA) that works for all empirical formula calculations:*
- *Instruction* |   | > * * | > * * | > * * |
|---|---|---|---|
| > *Elements - write them* | > *C* | > *H* | > *O* |
| > *Values - taken from the question as % or g* | > *54.54* | > *9.09* | > *36.37* |
| > *Atomic mass* | > *12* | > *1* | > *16* |
| > *Divide - the calculation is already laid out correctly * | > $\frac{54.54}{12}$* = 4.545* | > $\frac{9.09}{1}$* = 9.09* | > $\frac{36.37}{16}$* = 2.27* |
| > *Ratio - divide by the smallest answer* | > $\frac{4.545}{2.27}$* = 2.00* | > $\frac{9.09}{2.27}$* = 4.00* | > $\frac{2.27}{2.27}$* = 1* |
| > *Answer - write the final empirical formula* | > *C*<sub>*2*</sub>* * | > *H*<sub>*4*</sub>* * | > *O* |
- *To calculate the molecular formula using an empirical formula and a relative molecular mass:*

  - *Find the mass of the empirical formula*
  
    - *C*<sub>*2*</sub>*H*<sub>*4*</sub>*O = (2 x 12) + (4 x 1) + 16 = 44*
  - *Divide the relative molecular mass by the mass of the empirical formula*
  
    - $\frac{88}{44}$* = 2*
  - *Apply the answer to the empirical formula*
  
    - *C*<sub>*2*</sub>*H*<sub>*4*</sub>*O x 2 = C*<sub>*4*</sub>*H*<sub>*8*</sub>*O*<sub>*2*</sub>* *

parts.problemMd:
A student investigated the reaction between aqueous sodium carbonate and two different solutions of dilute hydrochloric acid, **A** and **B**.

The reaction is:

Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3 </sub>(aq) + 2HCl (aq) → 2NaCl (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + CO<sub>2 </sub>(g)

Three experiments were carried out.

*Experiment 1 *

Using a measuring cylinder, 25 cm<sup>3 </sup>of aqueous sodium carbonate were poured into a conical flask.

Thymolphthalein indicator was added to the conical flask. A burette was filled up to the 0.0 cm<sup>3</sup> mark with solution **A**. Dilute hydrochloric acid **A** was added to the flask, until the solution just changed colour. Use the burette diagram to record the reading in the table.

![experiment-1-final-reading](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-chemistry-23/12-experimental-techniques-and-chemical-analysis/12-1-experimental-techniques/assets/027-experiment-1-final-reading.png)

*Experiment 2*

Experiment 1 was repeated using methyl orange indicator instead of thymolphthalein.

Methyl orange is red-orange in acidic solutions and yellow in alkaline solutions. Use the burette diagrams to record the readings in the table and complete the table.

![experiment-2-initial-and-final-reading](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-chemistry-23/12-experimental-techniques-and-chemical-analysis/12-1-experimental-techniques/assets/028-experiment-2-initial-and-final-reading.png)

|   | experiment 1 | experiment 2 |
|---|---|---|
| final burette reading / cm<sup>3</sup> |   |   |
| initial burette reading / cm<sup>3</sup> |   |   |
| difference / cm<sup>3</sup> |   |   |
parts.solutionMd:
a) The completed table is:

|   | experiment 1 | experiment 2 |
|---|---|---|
| final burette reading / cm<sup>3</sup> | 13.2 | 39.2 |
| initial burette reading / cm<sup>3</sup> | 0.0 | 12.8 |
| difference / cm<sup>3</sup> | 13.2 | 26.4 |

- Final readings completed correctly: 13.2, 39.2; **[1 mark]**
- Initial readings completed correctly: 0.0, 12.8; **[1 mark]**
- Differences completed correctly: 13.2, 26.4; **[1 mark]**
- All readings and differences to 1 decimal place; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *The information to complete the table is all given in the question*
- *Experiment 1*

  - *You are told that a burette was filled up to the 0.0 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* mark- this is your initial volume *
  - *The final reading can be read from the diagram of the burette, each division represents a volume of 0.1 cm*<sup>*3 *</sup>*so the final volume is 13. 2 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>
  - *The volumes are also read from the bottom of the meniscus*
  - *The difference between these: 13.2 - 0.0 = 13. 2 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>
- *Experiment 2*

  - *You can read both initial and final volumes from the burette diagrams *
  - *The difference between these is: 39.2 - 12. 8 = 26.4 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>
- *You can either give the burette readings to 1 decimal place or to 2 decimal places but you must be consistent*
- *As the burette has an analogue graduated scale, the uncertainty is assumed to be ± half the smallest graduation*
- *The smallest graduation is 0.1 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* so the uncertainty is ±0.05 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>
- *This means that if you give readings to 2 decimal places, the final figure must be either 0 or 5*
- *At this level, giving burette readings to the nearest 0.1 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* is acceptable*

A chemist used a volumetric pipette to add 25.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of a solution of sodium hydroxide of unknown concentration to a conical flask.

parts.solutionMd:
a) To complete the titration:

- A suitable indicator (phenolphthalein / methyl orange / thymolphthalein) is added to the sodium hydroxide in the conical flask; **[1 mark]**
- The acid is added from the burette to the conical flask; **[1 mark]**
- The acid is added with swirling / dropwise towards the endpoint 
**OR** 
The acid is added with swirling / dropwise until the indicator just changes colour; **[1 mark]**
- The indicator changes colour at the endpoint 
**OR **
The indicator changes from pink to colourless (for phenolphthalein) 
**OR **
The indicator changes from yellow to red (for methyl orange) 
**OR** 
The indicator changes from blue to colourless ( for thymolphthalein); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *You should be able to describe how to carry out a titration *
- *You cannot score the mark for giving Universal indicator or litmus as an indicator*

  - *This is because they do not have a sharp colour change when the endpoint is reached *
- *Your colour change must also be the right way around*

  - *The question tells you that sodium hydroxide, an alkali, has been added to the conical flask *
  - *The indicator is therefore added to the alkali*
