A student investigated the effect of the size of calcium carbonate lumps, CaCO3, on the rate of reaction with hydrochloric acid, HCl, using the following method: 1. Put 50 cm3 of hydrochloric acid into a conical flask 2. Add 12 g of large calcium carbonate lumps into the flask 3. Attach the gas syringe 4. Measure the volume of gas produced every 30 seconds for 180 seconds 5. Repeat steps 1 - 4 using 12 g of small calcium carbonate lumps. 6. The number of moles of gas for each volume was calculated. The student had already plotted the data for small calcium carbonate lumps. [Graph: Number of moles of gas against Time in seconds - for small calcium carbonate lumps, at 35 seconds the moles of gas is 0.0022 and at 90 seconds the moles of gas is 0.0036]

Determine the mean rate of reaction for **small** calcium carbonate lumps between 35 seconds and 90 seconds.

Give the unit.

Use the graph in part (a)
parts.solutionMd:
b) To determine the mean rate of reaction for small calcium carbonate lumps between 35 seconds and 90 seconds:

- 0.0036  
**AND** 
0.0022; **[1 mark]**
- $\frac{0.0036-0.0022}{90-35}$ ; **[1 mark] ***allow correct use of incorrectly determined values*
- 0.000025** **
**OR**** **
2.5 x 10<sup>-5 </sup>; **[1 mark]**
- mol/s; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *To determine the moles of gas produced between 35 and 90 seconds: *

![dfeeed72-ece3-4adc-80df-be10b53c6a0f](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-chemistry-23/12-experimental-techniques-and-chemical-analysis/12-1-experimental-techniques/assets/049-dfeeed72-ece3-4adc-80df-be10b53c6a0f.jpeg)

- *Find the difference between the two times, 90-35= 55 seconds*
- *Find the difference between the moles of gas at these times, 0.0036- 0.0022= 0.0014*
- *To calculate the rate of reaction the equation is used:*

$\frac{\mathrm{moles} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{gas} \mathrm{formed}}{\mathrm{time} \mathrm{taken}}$

- *So 0.0014 / 55= 0.000025*
- *To determine the units, look at the units used for moles and time from the y and x axis *

final volume: 29.00; **[1 mark]**

[2]

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
e)

i) The effects of adding 0.3 g of powdered calcium carbonate to acid **K** were:

- It reacts with the acid / neutralised; **[1 mark]**
- Less sodium hydroxide was needed; **[1 mark]**

ii) The difference between the volume of sodium hydroxide needed to completely react with 50 cm<sup>3</sup> of acid **K** and the volume of sodium hydroxide used in Experiment 2 is:

- Correct value; **[1 mark]** e.g. 57 cm<sup>3</sup>

iii) The mass of calcium carbonate that would be needed to be added to 50 cm<sup>3</sup> of acid **K** to require 0.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of sodium hydroxide is:

- Answer to (ii) / 3 divided into 19 × 0.1 + 0.3 = 0.4 g;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

- *Part (ii) is challenging - from the previous questions you know that:*
- *50 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* of acid **K** required 76 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* of NaOH to be neutralised **OR** 50 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* of acid **K** required 0.3 g CaCO*<sub>*3*</sub>* and 19 cm*<sup>*3 *</sup>*of NaOH to be neutralised (from Experiment 2)*
- *This means that 0.3 g of CaCO*<sub>*3*</sub>* neutralised 57 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* NaOH in Experiment 2*
- *To find out how much extra CaCO*<sub>*3*</sub>* is needed so that 0.0 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* NaOH is used, we need to find out how much CaCO*<sub>*3*</sub>* is needed to neutralise the remaining 19 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* in Experiment 2*
- *57 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* is 3 x greater than 19 (57/19 = 3) and we know 0.3 g CaCO*<sub>*3*</sub>* was needed to neutralise 57 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* NaOH*
- *Therefore, an extra third of CaCO*<sub>*3*</sub>* is needed: 0.3/3 = 0.1 g*

A student investigated the solubility of salt A in water at various temperatures. Five experiments were carried out. Experiment 1: The student was provided with a boiling tube containing 12 g of salt A. A burette was filled with distilled water and 10.0 cm^3 of water was added to the boiling tube. The mixture of salt A and water was heated until all of the solid had dissolved. The boiling tube was removed from the heat and the solution was stirred with a thermometer and allowed to cool. improvement ..........................................................................................................

explanation ..........................................................................................................

- Don’t use a beaker of cold water to cool solution; **[1 mark] **

- Use second person / IT method to note formation of crystals; **[1 mark] **
- Repeat; **[1 mark] **

With **one **linked explanation:

- Different rate of heat losses; **[1 mark] **

**[Total: 2 marks] **

(1 dm<sup>3</sup> = 1000 cm<sup>3</sup>)
parts.solutionMd:
An experiment to find the mass of salts in 1 dm<sup>3</sup> of seawater would involve:

Any **six **from:

- Measured volume of seawater; **[1 mark]**
- Using measuring cylinder; **[1 mark]**
- Into evaporating dish/beaker; **[1 mark]**
- Pre-weighed; **[1 mark]**
- Evaporate/heat; **[1 mark]**
- To dryness/constant mass; **[1 mark]**
- Re-weigh; **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
Copper(II) oxide and carbon are both black solids. Copper(II) oxide reacts with dilute sulfuric acid to form aqueous copper(II) sulfate. Carbon does not react with dilute sulfuric acid.

Plan an experiment to investigate the percentage of copper(II) oxide in the mixture.
parts.solutionMd:
To investigate the percentage of copper(II) oxide in the mixture:

The method must use a minimum of **six** of the following:

- Weigh the mixture;** [1 mark]**
- Add an excess; **[1 mark]**
- Of sulfuric acid; **[1 mark]**
- Heat / stir; **[1 mark]**
- Filter the carbon / residue; **[1 mark] ***Ignore details about the evaporation of the copper(II) sulfate solution*
- Wash the carbon / residue; **[1 mark]**
- Dry the carbon / residue 
**OR **
Place in a warm oven / somewhere warm; **[1 mark]**
- Reweigh the carbon / residue;** [1 mark] **

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Chromatography can be used to test the purity of substances. The diagram shows the chromatogram of a coloured substance. ![q4c0620-s20-qp-43](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2022/07/q4c0620-s20-qp-43.png)

#### Extended Only

Draw a circle around the correct *R*<sub>f</sub> value for the spot labelled **X**.

0.2         0.4        0.8         1.2
parts.solutionMd:
b) The correct *R*<sub>f</sub> value for the spot labelled **X** is:

- 0.8 (circled); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

- *The maximum an **R*<sub>*f*</sub>* value can be is 1.0*

  - *This means that the spot has travelled with the solvent to the top / solvent front*
  - *Therefore, 1.2 is not a correct possibility *
- *You can estimate where spots with the other values would appear on the chromatography paper*

  - *0.2 is almost a quarter (0.25)*
  
    - *This means that the spot would appear just below a quarter of the way up from the baseline to the solvent front*
    - *Spot **X** appears above this spot, so the **R*<sub>*f*</sub>* value of X cannot be 0.2 *
  - *0.4 is close to a half (0.5)*
  
    - *This means that the spot would appear just below halfway up from the baseline to the solvent front*
    - *Spot **X** appears above this spot, so the **R*<sub>*f*</sub>* value of **X** cannot be 0.4 *
  - *0.8 is just over three quarters (0.75)*
  
    - *This means that the spot would appear just over three-quarters of the way up from the baseline to the solvent front*
    - *Spot **X** appears at about this point, so the **R*<sub>*f*</sub>* value of **X** is 0.8 *
- *You can also calculate the **R*<sub>*f*</sub>* value by measuring the distance from the baseline to the solvent front and measuring the distance from the baseline to spot **X*

  - *Using the equation** R*<sub>*f*</sub>* =  *$\frac{\mathrm{distance} \mathrm{travelled} \mathrm{by} \mathrm{substance}}{\mathrm{distance} \mathrm{travelled} \mathrm{by} \mathrm{solvent}}$* will give a more precise value*

Filtration

parts.solutionMd:

- 9O<sub>2</sub>; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

- *You could be expected to fully balance a chemical equation like this as well as be able to write it using the information given in the written part of the question *
- *To balance the oxygen atoms*

  - *On the right-hand side of the equation*
  
    - *There are 6CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* molecules, which means that there are 6 x 2 = 12 oxygen atoms*
    - *There are 6H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O molecules, which means that there are 6 x 1 = 6 oxygen atoms*
    - *This gives a total of 18 oxygen atoms*
  - *Since the oxygen on the left-hand side is diatomic (two oxygen atoms per one molecule of oxygen), this means that we need 9O*<sub>*2*</sub>* to balance the oxygen atoms*

- *You should be familiar with the test for sulfate ions in which acidified barium nitrate (or chloride) is added to the solution to be tested*

  - *If sulfate ions are present, a white precipitate of barium sulfate is formed*

test ______________________________

observations ______________________
parts.solutionMd:
b) A test for iodide ions is:

- Add (acidified aqueous) silver nitrate; **[1 mark]**
- Yellow precipitate; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *Acidified silver nitrate solution is used to identify the halide ions*
- *You do not need to state that it is acidified in this question, but sometimes this is required, so it is best to give this information*
- *The solution is acidified with nitric acid which removes any unwanted negative ions that may produce a precipitate with silver ions and give a false positive result*

  - *Careful**: It should not be acidified with hydrochloric acid as this introduces chloride ions that would produce a white precipitate with silver nitrate*
- *The colour of the precipitate indicates the halide ion present:*

  - *A white precipitate forms when chloride ions are present*
  - *A cream precipitate forms when bromide ions are present*
  - *A yellow precipitate forms when iodide ions are present*

parts.problemMd:
This question is about ammonium compounds.

The table shows the names and formulae of some ammonium compounds.

| **Name** | Ammonium nitrate | Ammonium carbonate |   |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Formula** | NH<sub>4</sub>NO<sub>3</sub> |   | NH<sub>4</sub>Cl |

i) Complete the table by giving the missing information.

[2]

ii) When ammonia reacts with nitric acid, ammonium nitrate is formed.

Write a chemical equation for this reaction.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
a)

i) The missing information in the table is:

- Ammonium carbonate formula = (NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>; **[1 mark]**
- NH<sub>4</sub>Cl name = ammonium chloride; **[1 mark]**

ii) The chemical equation for when ammonia reacts with nitric acid to form ammonium nitrate is:

- NH<sub>3</sub> + HNO<sub>3</sub> → NH<sub>4</sub>NO<sub>3</sub>; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *The ammonium ion is NH*<sub>*4*</sub><sup>*+*</sup>* *
- *The carbonate ion is CO*<sub>*3*</sub><sup>*2–*</sup>* *

  - *This means that you need two ammonium ions to balance the 2- charge from the carbonate ion*
  - *Therefore, the formula of ammonium carbonate is (NH*<sub>*4*</sub>*)*<sub>*2*</sub>*CO*<sub>*3*</sub>* *
- *NH*<sub>*4*</sub>*Cl contains the ammonium / NH*<sub>*4*</sub><sup>*+*</sup>* ion and the chloride / Cl*<sup>*–*</sup>* ion*

  - *Therefore, it is called ammonium chloride*
- *From the question, you know:*

  - *When ammonia reacts with nitric acid, ammonium nitrate is formed*
  
    - *Ammonia + nitric acid → ammonium nitrate *
  - *You are expected to know the formulae of ammonia and nitric acid*
  
    - *Ammonia = NH*<sub>*3*</sub>* *
    - *Nitric acid = HNO*<sub>*3*</sub>
  - *The formula of ammonium nitrate is NH*<sub>*4*</sub>*NO*<sub>*3*</sub>* *
  - *So, the chemical equation is:*
  
    - *NH*<sub>*3*</sub>* + HNO*<sub>*3*</sub>* → NH*<sub>*4*</sub>*NO*<sub>*3*</sub>* *
  - *No balancing is required for this equation*
  
    - *Previous exams have asked the same question using sulfuric acid to form ammonium sulfate*
    - *Although such an equation will need balancing, it was still only worth one mark! *

b) The results for each gaseous product from the thermal decomposition of ammonium chloride are:

Hydrogen chloride / HCl; **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

When ammonium chloride is heated, it undergoes thermal decomposition to form two gaseous products. The products are ammonia / NH3 AND Hydrogen chloride / HCl. Ammonia is a base, which means that its gas will turn damp indicator paper blue / purple. Hydrogen chloride is a strong acid, which means that it will turn damp indicator paper red.

#### Extended Only

The diagram shows the apparatus used to heat ammonium chloride.

![nh4cl-thermal-decomposition-testing](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-chemistry-23/12-experimental-techniques-and-chemical-analysis/12-3-identification-of-ions-and-gases/assets/008-nh4cl-thermal-decomposition-testing.png)

i) Suggest why the damp litmus paper is two different colours.

[1]

ii) Explain what happens to the damp litmus paper as the ammonium chloride is heated.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
c)

i) The damp litmus paper is two different colours because:

- Blue litmus paper 
**AND**
Red litmus paper is being used; **[1 mark]**

ii) Explanation of what happens to the damp litmus paper as the ammonium chloride is heated:

- Ammonia has a lower *M*<sub>r</sub> / mass than hydrogen chloride 
**AND **
Therefore, it travels **OR **diffuses quicker / faster; **[1 mark]**
- So, the (damp) red litmus paper will turn blue (first); **[1 mark]**
- The heavier / slower hydrogen chloride then turns both litmus papers red; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *Remember:** Litmus paper comes in red and blue to test for alkaline and acidic chemicals respectively *
- *Using both litmus papers suggests that you will be testing for ammonia gas **AND **hydrogen chloride gas*

  - *Many students will incorrectly guess:*
  
    - *That one of the gases turns both litmus papers red / blue and the other has no effect*
    - *That the red litmus paper will turn blue and the blue litmus paper will turn red - this answer suggests that each piece of litmus paper will only be affected by the gas it should be testing for, not the other gas produced*
- * The explanation about colour changes must be linked to the difference between ammonia and hydrogen chloride*

  - *You already know that one is alkaline and the other is acidic but this does not help explain the results*
  - *Ammonia has an **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of 14 + (3 x 1) = 17*
  - *Hydrogen chloride has an **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of 35.5 + 1 = 36.5*
  - *This means that ammonia is lighter and can travel faster*
  - *Therefore, ammonia travels / diffuses quicker and turns the red litmus paper blue*
  - *This means that both litmus papers are blue by the time that the hydrogen chloride gets there*
  - *So, both litmus papers will then turn red*
